abstract: We have developed a neural network which consists of cooperatively inter(cid:173) connected Grossberg on-center off-surround subnets and which can be used to optimize a function related to the log likelihood function for decoding convolu(cid:173) tional codes or more general FIR signal deconvolution problems. Connections in the network are confined to neighboring subnets, and it is representative of the types of networks which lend themselves to VLSI implementation. Analytical and experimental results for convergence and stability of the network have been found. The structure of the network can be used for distributed representation of data items while allowing for fault tolerance and replacement of faulty units. 1

paragraphs: The paper develops a neural network for decoding convolutional codes and for more general finite impulse response signal deconvolution problems. Its computation optimizes a function related to log likelihood, connecting the network's evolving state with the task of finding a plausible explanation for a received signal.

The architecture consists of cooperating Grossberg subnets with an on-center, off-surround organization. Connections run only between neighboring subnets. This local structure matters for implementation because it avoids requiring every part of the network to communicate directly with every other part. The authors identify it as a type of architecture suited to VLSI hardware.

The paper reports analytical and experimental results concerning convergence and stability, addressing how the network behaves as its computation unfolds. It also describes how the structure can distribute the representation of data items while supporting fault tolerance and replacement of faulty units. The contribution brings together a signal-processing objective, local interconnections, and a representation designed to accommodate failures in individual components.
summary.tldr: A network of locally connected subnets supports likelihood-related signal decoding, with analyses of stability and convergence.

title: A Trellis-Structured Neural Network

abstract: We have done an empirical study of the relation of the number of parameters (weights) in a feedforward net to generalization perfor(cid:173) mance. Two experiments are reported. In one, we use simulated data sets with well-controlled parameters, such as the signal-to-noise ratio of continuous-valued data. In the second, we train the network on vector-quantized mel cepstra from real speech samples. In each case, we use back-propagation to train the feedforward net to discriminate in a multiple class pattern classification problem. We report the results of these studies, and show the application of cross-validation techniques to prevent overfitting.

In the second, we train the network on vector-quantized mel cepstra from real speech samples. paragraphs: This paper empirically examines how the number of adjustable weights in a feedforward network relates to generalization. The concern is whether a network's learned classification behavior carries over beyond its training examples. Parameter count is the design variable under study, connecting network size to the reliability of learned decisions.

The authors use two experimental settings. One consists of simulated continuous-valued data with controlled properties, including signal-to-noise ratio. The other uses real speech represented by vector-quantized mel cepstra. In both settings, backpropagation trains the network to distinguish among multiple classes. The combination places the parameter question in both a controlled data setting and a speech application.

The paper reports the studies and demonstrates cross-validation techniques for preventing overfitting. Cross-validation makes performance on held-out data part of the assessment, rather than relying solely on how well training examples are fitted. The stated contribution is an empirical investigation of network size together with a practical method for controlling overfitting; the abstract does not assert a single optimal parameter count.
summary.tldr: Experiments on simulated data and real speech examine network size and demonstrate cross-validation as a way to prevent overfitting.

title: Generalization and Parameter Estimation in Feedforward Nets: Some Experiments

Practical Characteristics of Neural Network

paragraphs: This study compares eight neural and conventional classifiers on two speech recognition tasks and two artificial tasks. The implementations run on a serial computer. The set includes Gaussian classification, nearest neighbors, two backpropagation variants, hypersphere and feature-map methods, learning vector quantization, and a binary decision tree.

Error rates are statistically equivalent on almost all tasks, but the systems differ by orders of magnitude in practical resource requirements. The comparison considers memory, training time, classification time, and ease of adaptation. Nearest-neighbor methods train quickly but use the most memory. Trees classify quickly but are complicated to adapt, while backpropagation usually requires long training and intermediate memory.

The findings shift attention toward the conditions under which a classifier will operate. When error rates are similar, available storage, allowable preparation time, response speed, and adaptation needs become consequential selection criteria. The paper's main lesson is that evaluating recognition quality alone can miss large differences in the cost and practicality of obtaining that quality.
summary.tldr: Eight classifiers achieve mostly similar error rates but differ dramatically in memory, speed, and adaptability.

title: Practical Characteristics of Neural Network and Conventional Pattern Classifiers on Artificial and Speech Problems

abstract: Learning is posed as a problem of function estimation, for which two princi(cid:173) ples of solution are considered: empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization. These two principles are applied to two different state(cid:173) ments of the function estimation problem: global and local. Systematic improvements in prediction power are illustrated in application to zip-code recognition.
originalAbstract: Learning is posed as a problem of function estimation, for which two princi(cid:173) ples of solution are considered: empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization. These two principles are applied to two different state(cid:173) ments of the function estimation problem: global and local. Systematic improvements in prediction power are illustrated in application to zip-code recognition.

paragraphs: The paper treats learning as function estimation: using observations to choose a function that makes predictions. It examines two principles for making that choice, empirical risk minimization and structural risk minimization. The central concern is how the rule used to select a function affects its predictive power.

Empirical risk minimization centers on reducing error on the observed examples. Structural risk minimization also brings the structure of the candidate function families into the selection problem. The paper considers these principles under both global and local formulations of function estimation. This creates two linked questions: how to define the estimation task, and how to choose a solution within that formulation.

An application to zip-code recognition illustrates systematic improvements in prediction. The stated result connects the theoretical choices to a concrete recognition task, showing why the formulation of learning deserves attention alongside the eventual predictor. The paper's contribution is to organize function estimation around alternative selection principles and demonstrate their relevance to predictive performance.
summary.tldr: The paper compares empirical and structural risk minimization for global and local function estimation, illustrating predictive improvements in zip-code recognition.

title: Principles of Risk Minimization for Learning Theory

abstract: The Bayesian analysis of neural networks is difficult because a sim(cid:173) ple prior over weights implies a complex prior distribution over functions . In this paper we investigate the use of Gaussian process priors over functions, which permit the predictive Bayesian anal(cid:173) ysis for fixed values of hyperparameters to be carried out exactly using matrix operations. Two methods, using optimization and av(cid:173) eraging (via Hybrid Monte Carlo) over hyperparameters have been tested on a number of challenging problems and have produced excellent results.
originalAbstract: The Bayesian analysis of neural networks is difficult because a sim(cid:173) ple prior over weights implies a complex prior distribution over functions . In this paper we investigate the use of Gaussian process priors over functions, which permit the predictive Bayesian anal(cid:173) ysis for fixed values of hyperparameters to be carried out exactly using matrix operations. Two methods, using optimization and av(cid:173) eraging (via Hybrid Monte Carlo) over hyperparameters have been tested on a number of challenging problems and have produced excellent results.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Gaussian processes as a Bayesian approach to regression. Its motivation comes from a difficulty with neural networks: even a simple prior distribution over network weights can induce a complicated distribution over the functions the network represents. That complication makes Bayesian prediction difficult to carry out.

Gaussian processes place the prior directly over functions. For fixed hyperparameters, the predictive Bayesian calculation can then be performed exactly through matrix operations. This gives the approach a clear computational advantage in how prediction is expressed: the function-level prior leads to a tractable calculation once its controlling settings are specified.

The authors test two ways of handling those hyperparameters. One uses optimization to choose their values; the other averages over them using Hybrid Monte Carlo. This distinction matters because exact prediction at a fixed setting and accounting for uncertainty over settings are separate tasks. Both approaches are tested on several challenging problems, with results described as excellent. The paper thus presents direct function priors as a practical route to Bayesian regression.
summary.tldr: Gaussian process priors enable exact Bayesian regression calculations at fixed hyperparameters using matrix operations.

title: Gaussian Processes for Regression

abstract: We derive a smoothing regularizer for recurrent network models by requiring robustness in prediction performance to perturbations of the training data. The regularizer can be viewed as a generaliza(cid:173) tion of the first order Tikhonov stabilizer to dynamic models. The closed-form expression of the regularizer covers both time-lagged and simultaneous recurrent nets, with feedforward nets and one(cid:173) layer linear nets as special cases. We have successfully tested this regularizer in a number of case studies and found that it performs better than standard quadratic weight decay. 1

paragraphs: The paper develops a regularizer for recurrent neural networks by starting with a desired property: predictions should remain reliable when the training data are perturbed. A regularizer adds a preference to the learning objective, steering training toward particular kinds of solutions. Here, that preference comes from robustness to changes in the data.

The resulting smoothing penalty extends the first-order Tikhonov stabilizer to dynamic models. The authors derive a closed-form expression covering both time-lagged recurrent networks and networks with simultaneous recurrence. Feedforward networks and single-layer linear networks fall within the same expression as special cases, giving the method a common mathematical basis across several architectures.

In the reported case studies, the regularizer performed better than standard quadratic weight decay. Weight decay directly penalizes large weights, while this derivation ties the penalty to prediction sensitivity. The comparison therefore supports the practical value of regularizing a network according to how its predictions respond to perturbations, including when recurrence makes those responses depend on dynamic interactions.
summary.tldr: A robustness-derived smoothing penalty covers several recurrent architectures and outperforms quadratic weight decay in reported case studies.

title: A Smoothing Regularizer for Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We suggest a working definition of texture: Texture is stuff that is more compactly represented by its statistics than by specifying the configuration of its parts. This definition suggests that to fmd texture we look for outliers to the local statistics, and label as texture the regions with no outliers. We present a method, based upon this idea, for labeling points in natural scenes as belonging to texture regions, while simultaneously allowing us to label low(cid:173) level, bottom-up cues for visual attention. This method is based upon recent psychophysics results on processing of texture and popout. 1 WHAT IS TEXTURE, AND WHY DO WE WANT TO FIND IT? In a number of problems in computer VlSlon and image processing, one must distinguish between image regions that correspond to objects and those which correspond to texture, and perform different processing depending upon the type of region. Current computer vision algorithms assume one magically knows this region labeling. But what is texture? We have the notion that texture involves a pattern that is somehow homogeneous, or in which signal changes are "too complex" to describe, so that aggregate properties must be used instead (Saund, 1998). There is by no means a firm division between texture and objects; rather, the characterization often depends upon the scale of interest (Saund, 1998). • Email: rruth@parc.xerox.com 818

paragraphs: This paper proposes identifying texture through how economically an image region can be described. A region counts as texture when its statistics provide a more compact description than the exact arrangement of its parts. This working definition turns texture detection into a question about local regularity and departures from that regularity.

The method looks for points that are unusual relative to local statistics. Regions without such outliers receive texture labels. At the same time, the unusual points provide low-level, bottom-up cues for visual attention. The authors connect this approach to psychophysical findings about texture processing and visual popout, bringing the two kinds of labeling into one method.

The motivation is that image-processing systems often need to treat objects and texture differently but require a way to determine which regions belong to each. The supplied text also emphasizes that this distinction can depend on scale. The proposed statistical criterion supplies a practical way to label natural scenes while acknowledging that texture is a characterization made at a particular scale of interest.
summary.tldr: A local-statistics method labels texture where outliers are absent and uses outliers as cues for visual attention.

title: General-Purpose Localization of Textured Image Regions

abstract: Local "belief propagation" rules of the sort proposed by Pearl [15] are guaranteed to converge to the correct posterior probabilities in singly connected graphical models. Recently, a number of researchers have empirically demonstrated good performance of "loopy belief propagation"- using these same rules on graphs with loops. Perhaps the most dramatic instance is the near Shannon-limit performance of "Turbo codes", whose decoding algorithm is equivalent to loopy belief propagation. Except for the case of graphs with a single loop, there has been little theoretical understanding of the performance of loopy propagation. Here we analyze belief propagation in networks with arbitrary topologies when the nodes in the graph describe jointly Gaussian random variables. We give an analytical formula relating the true posterior probabilities with those calculated using loopy propagation. We give sufficient conditions for convergence and show that when belief propagation converges it gives the correct posterior means for all graph topologies, not just networks with a single loop. The related "max-product" belief propagation algorithm finds the maximum posterior probability estimate for singly connected networks. We show that, even for non-Gaussian probability distributions, the convergence points of the max-product algorithm in loopy networks are maxima over a particular large local neighborhood of the posterior probability. These results help clarify the empirical performance results and motivate using the powerful belief propagation algorithm in a broader class of networks.

We give an analytical formula relating the true posterior probabilities with those calculated using loopy propagation. We give sufficient conditions for convergence and show that when belief propagation converges it gives the correct posterior means for all graph topologies, not just networks with a single loop. The related "max-product" belief propagation algorithm finds the maximum posterior probability estimate for singly connected networks. We show that, even for non-Gaussian probability distributions, the convergence points of the max-product algorithm in loopy networks are maxima over a particular large local neighborhood of the posterior probability. These results help clarify the empirical performance results and motivate using the powerful belief propagation algorithm in a broader class of networks.

paragraphs: Belief propagation computes probabilistic information through local updates in a graph. Its correctness is established for singly connected models, while its empirical success on graphs containing loops raises harder theoretical questions. This paper analyzes arbitrary graph structures when the variables are jointly Gaussian, providing an analytical relationship between true posteriors and the results of loopy propagation.

The authors give sufficient conditions for convergence and prove that, whenever the algorithm converges in this Gaussian setting, its posterior means are correct. The qualification matters: arbitrary topology does not itself guarantee convergence, and correctness of the means is more specific than correctness of the entire posterior distribution.

The paper also studies max-product propagation beyond Gaussian distributions. Its convergence points in loopy networks maximize posterior probability over a particular large local neighborhood. This is a local optimality result rather than a guarantee of the global maximum. Together, the results explain specific forms of correctness that can survive loops and provide theoretical motivation for using propagation algorithms in a broader range of networks.
summary.tldr: For jointly Gaussian graphical models of any topology, belief propagation gives exact posterior means if it converges.

title: Correctness of Belief Propagation in Gaussian Graphical Models of Arbitrary Topology

Based on these criteria, the principle of "maximal inconsistency" is pro(cid:173) posed to form (approximately) optimal working sets. Experimental results show superior performance of the new algorithm in compar(cid:173) ison with traditional training of regression SVM without decompo(cid:173) sition. Similar results have been previously reported on decomposi(cid:173) tion algorithms for pattern recognition SVM. paragraphs: Training a regression support vector machine involves solving an optimization problem. This paper develops a decomposition algorithm that approaches training through smaller working sets. Building on existing decomposition principles, it focuses on how to choose those sets effectively, making working-set selection the central algorithmic question.

The authors derive new criteria for testing the optimality of a working set. From these criteria, they propose a selection principle called maximal inconsistency, intended to construct approximately optimal sets. The theoretical criteria therefore guide which part of the training problem the algorithm should address, rather than leaving this choice disconnected from optimality.

Experiments show superior performance relative to traditional regression SVM training without decomposition. The abstract also notes that similar findings had previously been reported for decomposition in pattern-recognition SVMs. The proposed method extends to regression-based SVM formulations for density estimation and integral equations. Its contribution combines a principled selection rule with empirical evidence for decomposition in regression training, without establishing superiority over every alternative decomposition method.
summary.tldr: A maximal-inconsistency rule selects approximately optimal working sets for decomposition-based regression SVM training.

title: An Improved Decomposition Algorithm for Regression Support Vector Machines

abstract: We introduce a novel method of constructing language models, which avoids some of the problems associated with recurrent neu(cid:173) ral networks. The method of creating a Prediction Fractal Machine (PFM) [1] is briefly described and some experiments are presented which demonstrate the suitability of PFMs for language modeling. PFMs distinguish reliably between minimal pairs, and their be(cid:173) havior is consistent with the hypothesis [4] that wellformedness is 'graded' not absolute. A discussion of their potential to offer fresh insights into language acquisition and processing follows.

PFMs distinguish reliably between minimal pairs, and their be(cid:173) havior is consistent with the hypothesis [4] that wellformedness is 'graded' not absolute. paragraphs: This paper introduces a method for constructing language models called Prediction Fractal Machines, or PFMs. The method is presented as avoiding some problems associated with recurrent neural networks. The authors briefly describe how PFMs are created and use experiments to examine their suitability for language modeling.

A central finding is that PFMs reliably distinguish minimal pairs: closely related language examples whose small differences matter to their wellformedness. Such comparisons test whether a model responds to distinctions that can be obscured when examples differ in many ways at once. The reported behavior therefore supports the method's ability to capture meaningful differences between language examples.

The models also behave consistently with the hypothesis that grammatical wellformedness comes in degrees rather than only absolute categories. This is evidence of compatibility with that hypothesis, not proof that grammaticality must always be graded. The paper discusses how PFMs might offer new insights into language acquisition and processing, extending the significance of the modeling results toward questions about how language is learned and understood.
summary.tldr: Prediction Fractal Machines distinguish minimal pairs and exhibit behavior consistent with graded grammatical wellformedness.

title: Graded Grammaticality in Prediction Fractal Machines

abstract: In many scientific and engineering applications, detecting and understanding differences between two groups of examples can be reduced to a classical problem of training a classifier for labeling new examples while making as few mistakes as possible. In the traditional classification setting, the resulting classifier is rarely analyzed in terms of the properties of the input data captured by the discriminative model. However, such analysis is crucial if we want to understand and visualize the detected differences. We propose an approach to interpretation of the statistical model in the original feature space that allows us to argue about the model in terms of the relevant changes to the input vectors. For each point in the input space, we define a discriminative direction to be the direction that moves the point towards the other class while introducing as little irrelevant change as possible with respect to the classifier function. We derive the discriminative direction for kernel-based classifiers, demonstrate the technique on several examples and briefly discuss its use in the statistical shape analysis, an application that originally motivated this work.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to interpret the differences a classifier detects between two groups. A classifier can assign labels accurately while leaving unclear which properties of the original inputs drive that distinction. The authors seek an interpretation expressed directly as changes to input vectors, making the learned distinction easier to understand and visualize.

For every point in input space, they define a discriminative direction. This direction moves the point toward the other class while making as little irrelevant change as possible with respect to the classifier’s function. The interpretation is therefore local to an input and tied to the particular model’s distinction between classes.

The authors derive this direction for kernel-based classifiers and demonstrate the technique on several examples. They also discuss statistical shape analysis, the application that motivated the work. The contribution is a way to translate a classifier’s behavior into relevant changes in the original feature space. This supports examination of what the statistical model has captured, beyond using it solely to label new examples.
summary.tldr: Discriminative directions interpret kernel classifiers through input changes that move toward another class while minimizing irrelevant change.

title: Discriminative Direction for Kernel Classifiers

abstract: The curse of dimensionality gives rise to prohibitive computational requirements that render infeasible the exact solution of large- scale stochastic control problems. We study an efficient method based on linear programming for approximating solutions to such prob(cid:173) lems. The approach "fits" a linear combination of pre- selected basis functions to the dynamic programming cost- to- go function. We develop bounds on the approximation error and present experi(cid:173) mental results in the domain of queueing network control, providing empirical support for the methodology.
originalAbstract: The curse of dimensionality gives rise to prohibitive computational requirements that render infeasible the exact solution of large- scale stochastic control problems. We study an efficient method based on linear programming for approximating solutions to such prob(cid:173) lems. The approach "fits" a linear combination of pre- selected basis functions to the dynamic programming cost- to- go function. We develop bounds on the approximation error and present experi(cid:173) mental results in the domain of queueing network control, providing empirical support for the methodology.

paragraphs: Large stochastic control problems require decisions whose consequences unfold under uncertainty. Dynamic programming addresses such problems through a cost-to-go function, which describes future cost from a given situation. Computing that function exactly can become prohibitively expensive as the problem's dimensionality grows, motivating a more manageable approximation.

The paper studies a linear programming method that represents the cost-to-go function as a weighted combination of preselected basis functions. These functions provide the building blocks of the approximation, and the optimization fits their combination. This shifts the task from finding an unrestricted function to selecting a representation within a chosen family.

The authors develop bounds on approximation error and test the method on queueing network control. The bounds supply a theoretical way to assess approximation quality, while the experiments provide empirical support in a concrete control domain. Together, these contributions support linear programming as an efficient approach to approximate dynamic programming without claiming that the approximation solves every large control problem exactly.
summary.tldr: Linear programming fits a compact cost-to-go approximation, supported by error bounds and queueing network control experiments.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming via Linear Programming

abstract: Statistical language models estimate the probability of a word occurring in a given context. The most common language models rely on a discrete enumeration of predictive contexts (e.g., n-grams) and consequently fail to capture and exploit statistical regularities across these contexts. In this paper, we show how to learn hierarchical, distributed representations of word contexts that maximize the predictive value of a statistical language model. The representations are initialized by unsupervised algorithms for linear and nonlinear dimensionality reduction [14], then fed as input into a hierarchical mixture of experts, where each expert is a multinomial distribution over predicted words [12]. While the distributed representations in our model are inspired by the neural probabilistic language model of Bengio et al. [2, 3], our particular architecture enables us to work with significantly larger vocabularies and training corpora. For example, on a large-scale bigram modeling task involving a sixty thousand word vocabulary and a training corpus of three million sentences, we demonstrate consistent improvement over class-based bigram models [10, 13]. We also discuss extensions of our approach to longer multiword contexts.

paragraphs: A statistical language model predicts how likely a word is in a given context. The paper argues that explicitly enumerating contexts, as in common n-gram approaches, misses statistical regularities shared across them. It instead learns hierarchical, distributed context representations with the goal of improving word prediction.

Unsupervised linear and nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods initialize these representations. They then serve as inputs to a hierarchical mixture of experts, with each expert supplying a probability distribution over words. This couples a learned representation of context with a structured prediction mechanism. The authors state that their architecture permits substantially larger vocabularies and training corpora than the neural probabilistic model that inspired the representations.

On a bigram task with a vocabulary of sixty thousand words and three million training sentences, the method consistently improves over class-based bigram models. This provides evidence that the representation and architecture are useful at the reported scale. The paper also discusses longer multiword contexts, while the concrete experimental finding described in the abstract concerns bigram prediction.
summary.tldr: Learned distributed context representations feed a hierarchical mixture of experts and improve large-scale bigram prediction over class-based models.

title: Hierarchical Distributed Representations for Statistical Language Modeling

abstract: Prior work has shown that features which appear to be biologically plausible as well as empirically useful can be found by sparse coding with a prior such as a laplacian (L1) that promotes sparsity. We show how smoother priors can pre- serve the beneﬁts of these sparse priors while adding stability to the Maximum A-Posteriori (MAP) estimate that makes it more useful for prediction problems. Additionally, we show how to calculate the derivative of the MAP estimate efﬁ- ciently with implicit differentiation. One prior that can be differentiated this way is KL-regularization. We demonstrate its effectiveness on a wide variety of appli- cations, and ﬁnd that online optimization of the parameters of the KL-regularized model can signiﬁcantly improve prediction performance.

We show how smoother priors can pre- serve the beneﬁts of these sparse priors while adding stability to the Maximum A-Posteriori (MAP) estimate that makes it more useful for prediction problems. Additionally, we show how to calculate the derivative of the MAP estimate efﬁ- ciently with implicit differentiation. One prior that can be differentiated this way is KL-regularization. paragraphs: Sparse coding seeks representations that explain data using relatively few active components. Earlier work found that sparsity-promoting priors, including an L1 prior, could produce useful features with apparent biological plausibility. This paper asks how to retain those benefits while making the inferred representation more stable and more useful for prediction.

The authors show that smoother priors can preserve the advantages of sparse priors while stabilizing the maximum a posteriori estimate. This estimate is the representation selected by balancing the observed data against the prior. They also show how to compute its derivative efficiently through implicit differentiation, making changes in the inferred representation mathematically accessible when adjusting the model.

KL regularization is one prior that supports this differentiation approach. The paper demonstrates its effectiveness across a variety of applications and reports that online optimization of the KL-regularized model's parameters can substantially improve prediction. The contribution connects representation learning with predictive optimization: the inferred features can be stable enough to use in prediction and differentiable enough to help improve the model producing them.
summary.tldr: Smoother sparse-coding priors support stable, efficiently differentiable representations, and online parameter optimization can improve prediction.

title: Differentiable Sparse Coding

abstract: In this theoretical contribution we provide mathematical proof that two of the most important classes of network learning - correlation-based differential Hebbian learning and reward-based temporal difference learning - are asymptotically equivalent when timing the learning with a local modulatory signal. This opens the opportunity to consistently reformulate most of the abstract reinforcement learning framework from a correlation based perspective that is more closely related to the biophysics of neurons.
originalAbstract: In this theoretical contribution we provide mathematical proof that two of the most important classes of network learning - correlation-based differential Hebbian learning and reward-based temporal difference learning - are asymptotically equivalent when timing the learning with a local modulatory signal. This opens the opportunity to consistently reformulate most of the abstract reinforcement learning framework from a correlation based perspective that is more closely related to the biophysics of neurons.

paragraphs: The paper connects two major ways of describing learning in networks. Differential Hebbian learning is based on correlations, whereas temporal difference learning is framed around rewards. These descriptions emphasize different learning signals, raising the question of whether they can nevertheless describe equivalent behavior under an appropriate formulation.

The authors prove an asymptotic equivalence when learning is timed by a local modulatory signal, described in the title as a third factor. Both parts of that statement matter: the equivalence is asymptotic, and it depends on the local signal controlling learning timing. The result therefore establishes a specific mathematical connection between the two learning frameworks.

The authors argue that this connection opens a route to reformulating much of abstract reinforcement learning from a correlation-based perspective closer to neuronal biophysics. That is an opportunity created by the proof, rather than a completed reformulation of the whole framework. Its significance lies in providing a theoretical bridge between reward-centered learning descriptions and more locally expressed mechanisms.
summary.tldr: A local timing signal makes differential Hebbian and temporal difference learning asymptotically equivalent in the paper's theoretical analysis.

title: On the asymptotic equivalence between differential Hebbian and temporal difference learning using a local third factor

abstract: We study unsupervised learning in a probabilistic generative model for occlusion. The model uses two types of latent variables: one indicates which objects are present in the image, and the other how they are ordered in depth. This depth order then determines how the positions and appearances of the objects present, specified in the model parameters, combine to form the image. We show that the object parameters can be learnt from an unlabelled set of images in which objects occlude one another. Exact maximum-likelihood learning is intractable. However, we show that tractable approximations to Expectation Maximization (EM) can be found if the training images each contain only a small number of objects on average. In numerical experiments it is shown that these approximations recover the correct set of object parameters. Experiments on a novel version of the bars test using colored bars, and experiments on more realistic data, show that the algorithm performs well in extracting the generating causes. Experiments based on the standard bars benchmark test for object learning show that the algorithm performs well in comparison to other recent component extraction approaches. The model and the learning algorithm thus connect research on occlusion with the research field of multiple-cause component extraction methods.

paragraphs: When objects overlap, the visible image depends both on which objects are present and on which ones are in front. This paper builds that distinction into a probabilistic generative model. One set of latent variables represents object presence, while another represents depth order, determining how the modeled positions and appearances combine into an image.

The goal is to learn object parameters from unlabeled images containing occlusion. Exact maximum-likelihood learning is intractable, so the authors develop approximations to Expectation Maximization. Their tractability depends on training images containing only a small number of objects on average. This condition makes learning feasible while retaining an explicit account of objects hiding parts of one another.

Numerical experiments show recovery of the correct object parameters. Tests with colored bars and more realistic data also show successful extraction of the underlying image-generating components, while standard bars experiments compare favorably with recent component-extraction methods. The contribution connects occlusion modeling with unsupervised discovery of multiple causes, showing how depth ordering can be incorporated into learning the objects that produce an image.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised model learns overlapping objects and their depth ordering using tractable approximations when images contain few objects on average.

title: Occlusive Components Analysis

abstract: Steinwart was the ﬁrst to prove universal consistency of support vector machine classiﬁcation. His proof analyzed the ‘standard’ support vector machine classiﬁer, which is restricted to binary classiﬁcation problems. In contrast, recent analysis has resulted in the common belief that several extensions of SVM classiﬁcation to more than two classes are inconsistent. Countering this belief, we proof the universal consistency of the multi-class support vector machine by Crammer and Singer. Our proof extends Steinwart’s techniques to the multi-class case.
originalAbstract: Steinwart was the ﬁrst to prove universal consistency of support vector machine classiﬁcation. His proof analyzed the ‘standard’ support vector machine classiﬁer, which is restricted to binary classiﬁcation problems. In contrast, recent analysis has resulted in the common belief that several extensions of SVM classiﬁcation to more than two classes are inconsistent. Countering this belief, we proof the universal consistency of the multi-class support vector machine by Crammer and Singer. Our proof extends Steinwart’s techniques to the multi-class case.

paragraphs: Consistency concerns whether a learning method approaches the best achievable classification performance as the amount of training data grows. Universal consistency asks for this statistical property across data distributions within the theorem's scope. Earlier work established such a result for the standard binary support vector machine, leaving the multiclass setting as a separate theoretical question.

This paper proves universal consistency for the multiclass support vector machine formulated by Crammer and Singer. The proof extends techniques previously used for binary SVM classification to the case of more than two classes. Its contribution is therefore a statistical guarantee for a specific multiclass formulation, obtained by broadening an existing proof approach.

The result counters a prevailing belief, motivated by earlier analysis, that several multiclass SVM extensions were inconsistent. It establishes that the Crammer–Singer method has the stated asymptotic learning property. This is a claim about behavior as data accumulate, and its significance lies in clarifying the theoretical status of that method rather than reporting a finite-dataset performance comparison.
summary.tldr: The paper proves universal consistency for the Crammer–Singer multiclass SVM by extending proof techniques from binary classification.

title: Universal Consistency of Multi-Class Support Vector Classification

abstract: Size, color, and orientation have long been considered elementary features whose attributes are extracted in parallel and available to guide the deployment of attention. If each is processed in the same fashion with simply a different set of local detectors, one would expect similar search behaviours on localizing an equivalent flickering change among identically laid out disks. We analyze feature transitions associated with saccadic search and find out that size, color, and orientation are not alike in dynamic attribute processing over time. The Markovian feature transition is attractive for size, repulsive for color, and largely reversible for orientation.

We analyze feature transitions associated with saccadic search and find out that size, color, and orientation are not alike in dynamic attribute processing over time. The Markovian feature transition is attractive for size, repulsive for color, and largely reversible for orientation.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether size, color, and orientation behave similarly when people search visually for a changing feature. These attributes have long been treated as elementary features that can be extracted in parallel to guide attention. If their processing differed only in the local detectors involved, equivalent changes in equivalent layouts would be expected to produce similar search behavior.

The authors analyze feature transitions during saccadic search, which involves shifts of gaze. The search setting uses identically arranged disks and asks about locating a flickering change. Holding the layout comparable makes the differences between feature types central to the question: does changing size guide search over time in the same way as changing color or orientation?

Their analysis finds distinct Markovian transition behavior: attraction for size, repulsion for color, and largely reversible transitions for orientation. The stated result concerns dynamic processing over time. It challenges the expectation that these three attributes share the same temporal search behavior simply because all are considered elementary visual features.
summary.tldr: Size, color, and orientation show different feature-transition patterns during saccadic search, challenging a uniform account of their temporal processing.

title: Feature Transitions with Saccadic Search: Size, Color, and Orientation Are Not Alike

abstract: For many structured prediction problems, complex models often require adopting approximate inference techniques such as variational methods or sampling, which generally provide no satisfactory accuracy guarantees. In this work, we propose sidestepping intractable inference altogether by learning ensembles of tractable sub-models as part of a structured prediction cascade. We focus in particular on problems with high-treewidth and large state-spaces, which occur in many computer vision tasks. Unlike other variational methods, our ensembles do not enforce agreement between sub-models, but filter the space of possible outputs by simply adding and thresholding the max-marginals of each constituent model. Our framework jointly estimates parameters for all models in the ensemble for each level of the cascade by minimizing a novel, convex loss function, yet requires only a linear increase in computation over learning or inference in a single tractable sub-model. We provide a generalization bound on the filtering loss of the ensemble as a theoretical justification of our approach, and we evaluate our method on both synthetic data and the task of estimating articulated human pose from challenging videos. We find that our approach significantly outperforms loopy belief propagation on the synthetic data and a state-of-the-art model on the pose estimation/tracking problem.

We find that our approach significantly outperforms loopy belief propagation on the synthetic data and a state-of-the-art model on the pose estimation/tracking problem.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can require searching an enormous space of interdependent outputs. This paper proposes a cascade of ensembles built from tractable submodels, targeting problems with large state spaces and complicated dependencies. The aim is to reduce the candidate output space without performing inference in a single intractable model.

Each submodel contributes max-marginal scores, which describe its best achievable score subject to particular output choices. The ensemble adds and thresholds these scores to filter candidates, without requiring the submodels to agree. At each cascade level, all model parameters are learned jointly using a convex loss. Computation increases only linearly relative to learning or inference in one tractable submodel.

The authors provide a generalization bound for filtering loss, giving theoretical support specifically for the ensemble’s filtering behavior. Tests on synthetic data and articulated human pose estimation from challenging videos show significant improvements over loopy belief propagation and a leading pose model, respectively. The results support using several manageable models to narrow the search in difficult structured prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: Structured ensemble cascades combine tractable models to filter large output spaces efficiently, with theoretical and empirical support.

title: Sidestepping Intractable Inference with Structured Ensemble Cascades

abstract: We propose a novel method for inferring whether X causes Y or vice versa from joint observations of X and Y. The basic idea is to model the observed data using probabilistic latent variable models, which incorporate the effects of unobserved noise. To this end, we consider the hypothetical effect variable to be a function of the hypothetical cause variable and an independent noise term (not necessarily additive). An important novel aspect of our work is that we do not restrict the model class, but instead put general non-parametric priors on this function and on the distribution of the cause. The causal direction can then be inferred by using standard Bayesian model selection. We evaluate our approach on synthetic data and real-world data and report encouraging results.
originalAbstract: We propose a novel method for inferring whether X causes Y or vice versa from joint observations of X and Y. The basic idea is to model the observed data using probabilistic latent variable models, which incorporate the effects of unobserved noise. To this end, we consider the hypothetical effect variable to be a function of the hypothetical cause variable and an independent noise term (not necessarily additive). An important novel aspect of our work is that we do not restrict the model class, but instead put general non-parametric priors on this function and on the distribution of the cause. The causal direction can then be inferred by using standard Bayesian model selection. We evaluate our approach on synthetic data and real-world data and report encouraging results.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether joint observations of two variables can help determine which one causes the other. Its approach compares probabilistic explanations for the two possible directions. Unobserved noise is explicitly included in those explanations, so the method considers how a candidate cause and hidden variation could jointly produce a candidate effect.

For each direction, the hypothetical effect is modeled as a function of the hypothetical cause and an independent noise term. The noise does not have to enter additively. The authors place general nonparametric priors on both the function and the cause distribution, allowing flexible explanations without restricting the functional model class in the proposed formulation.

Standard Bayesian model selection is then used to compare the causal directions. The authors evaluate the approach with synthetic and real-world data and describe the results as encouraging. The contribution is a flexible probabilistic comparison of directional explanations, with independence between the candidate cause and the noise serving as an explicit modeling assumption.
summary.tldr: Flexible latent-variable models compare causal directions through Bayesian model selection, assuming noise independent of the hypothetical cause.

title: Probabilistic latent variable models for distinguishing between cause and effect

abstract: Compositional models provide an elegant formalism for representing the visual appearance of highly variable objects. While such models are appealing from a theoretical point of view, it has been difficult to demonstrate that they lead to performance advantages on challenging datasets. Here we develop a grammar model for person detection and show that it outperforms previous high-performance systems on the PASCAL benchmark. Our model represents people using a hierarchy of deformable parts, variable structure and an explicit model of occlusion for partially visible objects. To train the model, we introduce a new discriminative framework for learning structured prediction models from weakly-labeled data.

While such models are appealing from a theoretical point of view, it has been difficult to demonstrate that they lead to performance advantages on challenging datasets. Here we develop a grammar model for person detection and show that it outperforms previous high-performance systems on the PASCAL benchmark. Our model represents people using a hierarchy of deformable parts, variable structure and an explicit model of occlusion for partially visible objects. To train the model, we introduce a new discriminative framework for learning structured prediction models from weakly-labeled data.

paragraphs: The paper develops a grammar model for detecting people in images. Compositional models describe an object's appearance through an arrangement of parts, making them appealing for objects with substantial visual variation. The challenge addressed here is whether that modeling flexibility can translate into better detection on a demanding benchmark.

The proposed representation combines a hierarchy of deformable parts, variable structure, and an explicit treatment of occlusion. These components allow the model to represent variation in how a person appears and to account for people who are only partly visible. The grammar provides a structured way to combine these aspects within one detector.

Training uses a new discriminative framework for structured prediction with weakly labeled data. This connects the flexible object representation to a learning procedure that can operate with incomplete labeling of its structure. On the PASCAL benchmark, the person detector outperforms previous high-performance systems. The reported result supplies empirical evidence that this particular compositional model delivers practical detection benefits alongside its representational appeal.
summary.tldr: A person-detection grammar combining deformable parts, variable structure, and occlusion modeling improves performance on PASCAL.

title: Object Detection with Grammar Models

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks define an exceptionallypowerful class of model, but are still limited by the lack of abilityto be spatially invariant to the input data in a computationally and parameterefficient manner. In this work we introduce a new learnable module, theSpatial Transformer, which explicitly allows the spatial manipulation ofdata within the network. This differentiable module can be insertedinto existing convolutional architectures, giving neural networks the ability toactively spatially transform feature maps, conditional on the feature map itself,without any extra training supervision or modification to the optimisation process. We show that the useof spatial transformers results in models which learn invariance to translation,scale, rotation and more generic warping, resulting in state-of-the-artperformance on several benchmarks, and for a numberof classes of transformations.
originalAbstract: Convolutional Neural Networks define an exceptionallypowerful class of model, but are still limited by the lack of abilityto be spatially invariant to the input data in a computationally and parameterefficient manner. In this work we introduce a new learnable module, theSpatial Transformer, which explicitly allows the spatial manipulation ofdata within the network. This differentiable module can be insertedinto existing convolutional architectures, giving neural networks the ability toactively spatially transform feature maps, conditional on the feature map itself,without any extra training supervision or modification to the optimisation process. We show that the useof spatial transformers results in models which learn invariance to translation,scale, rotation and more generic warping, resulting in state-of-the-artperformance on several benchmarks, and for a numberof classes of transformations.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks are powerful image models, but handling changes in position, size, orientation, and shape efficiently remains a challenge. The paper introduces the Spatial Transformer, a learnable module that explicitly changes the spatial arrangement of data inside a network. This gives the model a mechanism for adapting its internal representation to the input's geometry.

The module transforms a feature map based on the feature map itself, so the spatial operation is conditioned on the current input. It is differentiable and can be inserted into an existing convolutional architecture. Training requires neither extra supervision for the transformations nor changes to the optimization process, allowing the spatial behavior to be learned alongside the rest of the model.

The authors show models learning invariance to translation, scale, rotation, and more general warping, with state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks and transformation classes. These results demonstrate the usefulness of learning spatial manipulation within the network. The reported invariance is learned behavior in the studied settings, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every possible transformation.
summary.tldr: Spatial Transformers let neural networks learn input-dependent spatial transformations through ordinary training, improving robustness to several geometric changes.

title: Spatial Transformer Networks

abstract: Super-resolution is the problem of recovering a superposition of point sources using bandlimited measurements, which may be corrupted with noise. This signal processing problem arises in numerous imaging problems, ranging from astronomy to biology to spectroscopy, where it is common to take (coarse) Fourier measurements of an object. Of particular interest is in obtaining estimation procedures which are robust to noise, with the following desirable statistical and computational properties: we seek to use coarse Fourier measurements (bounded by some \emph{cutoff frequency}); we hope to take a (quantifiably) small number of measurements; we desire our algorithm to run quickly. Suppose we have $k$ point sources in $d$ dimensions, where the points are separated by at least $\Delta$ from each other (in Euclidean distance). This work provides an algorithm with the following favorable guarantees:1. The algorithm uses Fourier measurements, whose frequencies are bounded by $O(1/\Delta)$ (up to log factors). Previous algorithms require a \emph{cutoff frequency} which may be as large as $\Omega(\sqrt{d}/\Delta)$.2. The number of measurements taken by and the computational complexity of our algorithm are bounded by a polynomial in both the number of points $k$ and the dimension $d$, with \emph{no} dependence on the separation $\Delta$. In contrast, previous algorithms depended inverse polynomially on the minimal separation and exponentially on the dimension for both of these quantities.Our estimation procedure itself is simple: we take random bandlimited measurements (as opposed to taking an exponential number of measurements on the hyper-grid). Furthermore, our analysis and algorithm are elementary (based on concentration bounds of sampling and singular value decomposition).

paragraphs: Super-resolution seeks to recover point sources from measurements that contain only limited frequency information. The paper studies k sources in d dimensions, assuming a minimum Euclidean separation Δ between distinct sources. Its aim is to recover them using a controlled frequency range, few measurements, and manageable computation.

The proposed algorithm takes random bandlimited Fourier measurements. Its required cutoff frequency is O(1/Δ), up to logarithmic factors, whereas previous algorithms may require a cutoff as large as Ω(√d/Δ). This improves the stated dependence on dimension in the frequency requirement while retaining dependence on how closely the sources are spaced.

Both the measurement count and computational complexity are polynomial in k and d, with no dependence on Δ. The abstract contrasts this with earlier methods whose costs depend inverse-polynomially on separation and exponentially on dimension. The procedure and analysis use sampling concentration bounds and singular value decomposition. The distinction between frequency range and measurement count is central: closer sources still affect the cutoff, even though they do not enter the stated count and runtime bounds.
summary.tldr: Random Fourier measurements enable off-grid point-source recovery with polynomial measurement and runtime bounds and an improved frequency cutoff requirement.

title: Super-Resolution Off the Grid

abstract: Estimating distributions over large alphabets is a fundamental machine-learning tenet. Yet no method is known to estimate all distributions well. For example, add-constant estimators are nearly min-max optimal but often perform poorly in practice, and practical estimators such as absolute discounting, Jelinek-Mercer, and Good-Turing are not known to be near optimal for essentially any distribution.We describe the first universally near-optimal probability estimators. For every discrete distribution, they are provably nearly the best in the following two competitive ways. First they estimate every distribution nearly as well as the best estimator designed with prior knowledge of the distribution up to a permutation. Second, they estimate every distribution nearly as well as the best estimator designed with prior knowledge of the exact distribution, but as all natural estimators, restricted to assign the same probability to all symbols appearing the same number of times.Specifically, for distributions over $k$ symbols and $n$ samples, we show that for both comparisons, a simple variant of Good-Turing estimator is always within KL divergence of $(3+o(1))/n^{1/3}$ from the best estimator, and that a more involved estimator is within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min(k/n,1/\sqrt n))$. Conversely, we show that any estimator must have a KL divergence $\ge\tilde\Omega(\min(k/n,1/ n^{2/3}))$ over the best estimator for the first comparison, and $\ge\tilde\Omega(\min(k/n,1/\sqrt{n}))$ for the second.

For example, add-constant estimators are nearly min-max optimal but often perform poorly in practice, and practical estimators such as absolute discounting, Jelinek-Mercer, and Good-Turing are not known to be near optimal for essentially any distribution.We describe the first universally near-optimal probability estimators. For every discrete distribution, they are provably nearly the best in the following two competitive ways. First they estimate every distribution nearly as well as the best estimator designed with prior knowledge of the distribution up to a permutation. Second, they estimate every distribution nearly as well as the best estimator designed with prior knowledge of the exact distribution, but as all natural estimators, restricted to assign the same probability to all symbols appearing the same number of times.Specifically, for distributions over $k$ symbols and $n$ samples, we show that for both comparisons, a simple variant of Good-Turing estimator is always within KL divergence of $(3+o(1))/n^{1/3}$ from the best estimator, and that a more involved estimator is within $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\min(k/n,1/\sqrt n))$. Conversely, we show that any estimator must have a KL divergence $\ge\tilde\Omega(\min(k/n,1/ n^{2/3}))$ over the best estimator for the first comparison, and $\ge\tilde\Omega(\min(k/n,1/\sqrt{n}))$ for the second.

paragraphs: Estimating probabilities over many possible symbols creates a gap between worst-case theory and practical performance. This paper asks a more distribution-specific question: how close can an estimator come to a well-informed competitor for every discrete distribution? The answer depends on precisely what information or restrictions the competitor receives.

The first comparison gives the competitor knowledge of the distribution without revealing which probabilities belong to which symbols. The second gives exact distribution knowledge but requires equal estimated probabilities for symbols observed equally often. These benchmarks make the universal near-optimality claim specific: it concerns competition against these two defined classes.

A simple Good-Turing variant has an excess KL-divergence guarantee of (3 + o(1))/n^(1/3), where n is sample size. A more involved estimator achieves a bound of order min(k/n, 1/√n), up to logarithmic factors, for k symbols. Lower bounds match the latter rate for the second comparison up to logarithmic factors; the first comparison has a different stated lower bound. The results give Good-Turing a distribution-by-distribution theoretical justification.
summary.tldr: Competitive guarantees explain why a Good-Turing variant estimates every discrete distribution nearly as well as two carefully defined informed benchmarks.

title: Competitive Distribution Estimation: Why is Good-Turing Good

abstract: In this paper, we consider a non-convex loss-minimization problem of learning Supervised PageRank models, which can account for features of nodes and edges. We propose gradient-based and random gradient-free methods to solve this problem. Our algorithms are based on the concept of an inexact oracle and unlike the state-of-the-art gradient-based method we manage to provide theoretically the convergence rate guarantees for both of them. Finally, we compare the performance of the proposed optimization methods with the state of the art applied to a ranking task.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we consider a non-convex loss-minimization problem of learning Supervised PageRank models, which can account for features of nodes and edges. We propose gradient-based and random gradient-free methods to solve this problem. Our algorithms are based on the concept of an inexact oracle and unlike the state-of-the-art gradient-based method we manage to provide theoretically the convergence rate guarantees for both of them. Finally, we compare the performance of the proposed optimization methods with the state of the art applied to a ranking task.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train Supervised PageRank models by minimizing a nonconvex loss. These ranking models can incorporate features of both nodes and edges, allowing the learned ranking to reflect information beyond the graph's connections alone. The optimization problem is therefore a central part of fitting the ranking model to a task.

The authors propose two approaches: a gradient-based method and a randomized gradient-free method. Both are developed around an inexact oracle, meaning that the optimization framework accommodates approximate information supplied to the algorithm. This common perspective lets the paper analyze methods that use different kinds of information to guide their updates.

The main theoretical contribution is a convergence-rate guarantee for each method, which the authors contrast with the existing state-of-the-art gradient-based approach. They also compare the proposed methods with the state of the art on a ranking task. The abstract establishes the presence of that empirical comparison, while the stated advance is the availability of convergence guarantees for both optimization routes.
summary.tldr: Two inexact-oracle optimization methods provide convergence-rate guarantees for training nonconvex Supervised PageRank models.

title: Learning Supervised PageRank with Gradient-Based and Gradient-Free Optimization Methods

abstract: Constraint-based causal discovery from limited data is a notoriously difficult challenge due to the many borderline independence test decisions. Several approaches to improve the reliability of the predictions by exploiting redundancy in the independence information have been proposed recently. Though promising, existing approaches can still be greatly improved in terms of accuracy and scalability. We present a novel method that reduces the combinatorial explosion of the search space by using a more coarse-grained representation of causal information, drastically reducing computation time. Additionally, we propose a method to score causal predictions based on their confidence. Crucially, our implementation also allows one to easily combine observational and interventional data and to incorporate various types of available background knowledge. We prove soundness and asymptotic consistency of our method and demonstrate that it can outperform the state-of-the-art on synthetic data, achieving a speedup of several orders of magnitude. We illustrate its practical feasibility by applying it on a challenging protein data set.
originalAbstract: Constraint-based causal discovery from limited data is a notoriously difficult challenge due to the many borderline independence test decisions. Several approaches to improve the reliability of the predictions by exploiting redundancy in the independence information have been proposed recently. Though promising, existing approaches can still be greatly improved in terms of accuracy and scalability. We present a novel method that reduces the combinatorial explosion of the search space by using a more coarse-grained representation of causal information, drastically reducing computation time. Additionally, we propose a method to score causal predictions based on their confidence. Crucially, our implementation also allows one to easily combine observational and interventional data and to incorporate various types of available background knowledge. We prove soundness and asymptotic consistency of our method and demonstrate that it can outperform the state-of-the-art on synthetic data, achieving a speedup of several orders of magnitude. We illustrate its practical feasibility by applying it on a challenging protein data set.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from limited data often depends on deciding whether variables are statistically independent. When the evidence is borderline, individual decisions can make the resulting causal conclusions unreliable. Combining overlapping independence information can help, but searching through the possible causal explanations creates a substantial computational burden.

This paper reduces that burden through a coarser representation of causal information. By representing less detailed causal distinctions during the search, the method reduces the number of possibilities it must consider. It also assigns confidence scores to causal predictions, making the strength of a prediction part of the output. The implementation can combine observational data, intervention data, and several kinds of background knowledge.

The authors prove soundness and asymptotic consistency for their method. On synthetic data, they demonstrate that it can outperform existing methods and achieve speedups of several orders of magnitude. An application to a challenging protein dataset illustrates practical feasibility. These contributions connect computational efficiency with more informative causal predictions, while the empirical superiority remains a result demonstrated in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A coarser representation of causal information makes causal discovery faster while supporting confidence scores and combined sources of evidence.

title: Ancestral Causal Inference

abstract: A hallmark of human intelligence is the ability to ask rich, creative, and revealing questions. Here we introduce a cognitive model capable of constructing human-like questions. Our approach treats questions as formal programs that, when executed on the state of the world, output an answer. The model specifies a probability distribution over a complex, compositional space of programs, favoring concise programs that help the agent learn in the current context. We evaluate our approach by modeling the types of open-ended questions generated by humans who were attempting to learn about an ambiguous situation in a game. We find that our model predicts what questions people will ask, and can creatively produce novel questions that were not present in the training set. In addition, we compare a number of model variants, finding that both question informativeness and complexity are important for producing human-like questions.

A program takes the state of the world as input and returns an answer, giving questions a formal structure that can be combined and evaluated.

The model assigns probabilities across a compositional space of programs. It favors questions that are concise and informative in the current context. This connects the construction of a question with its learning value: the model considers both what the answer could reveal and the complexity of the program needed to ask for it.

The model predicts human question choices and generates novel questions absent from its training set. Comparisons among model variants indicate that both informativeness and complexity matter for human-like behavior. The results support a program-based account of question generation in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: A cognitive model generates human-like questions as programs, balancing how much they reveal against their complexity.

title: Question Asking as Program Generation

abstract: Early stopping of iterative algorithms is a widely-used form of regularization in statistical learning, commonly used in conjunction with boosting and related gradient-type algorithms. Although consistency results have been established in some settings, such estimators are less well-understood than their analogues based on penalized regularization. In this paper, for a relatively broad class of loss functions and boosting algorithms (including $L^2$-boost, LogitBoost and AdaBoost, among others), we connect the performance of a stopped iterate to the localized Rademacher/Gaussian complexity of the associated function class. This connection allows us to show that local fixed point analysis, now standard in the analysis of penalized estimators, can be used to derive optimal stopping rules. We derive such stopping rules in detail for various kernel classes, and illustrate the correspondence of our theory with practice for Sobolev kernel classes.

paragraphs: Stopping an iterative learning algorithm before it finishes can act as regularization: the stopping time helps control the model being learned. Although this practice is common in boosting and gradient-based methods, the paper notes that its statistical behavior has been less understood than regularization imposed through an explicit penalty.

The authors connect the performance of an intermediate, stopped model to localized Rademacher or Gaussian complexity. These quantities describe the complexity of relevant portions of the associated function class. Their analysis covers a relatively broad collection of losses and boosting algorithms, including L2-boost, LogitBoost, and AdaBoost. This creates a common basis for studying stopping across several methods.

The connection allows local fixed-point analysis, already used for penalized estimators, to produce optimal stopping rules in the settings considered. The paper works out these rules for various kernel classes and illustrates how the theory corresponds to practice for Sobolev kernels. Its central contribution is a principled link between function-class complexity and the choice of when to stop training.
summary.tldr: Localized complexity analysis yields principled, optimal stopping rules for a broad class of kernel boosting methods.

title: Early stopping for kernel boosting algorithms: A general analysis with localized complexities

abstract: Alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) has received tremendous interest for solving numerous problems in machine learning, statistics and signal processing. However, it is known that the performance of ADMM and many of its variants is very sensitive to the penalty parameter of a quadratic penalty applied to the equality constraints. Although several approaches have been proposed for dynamically changing this parameter during the course of optimization, they do not yield theoretical improvement in the convergence rate and are not directly applicable to stochastic ADMM. In this paper, we develop a new ADMM and its linearized variant with a new adaptive scheme to update the penalty parameter. Our methods can be applied under both deterministic and stochastic optimization settings for structured non-smooth objective function. The novelty of the proposed scheme lies at that it is adaptive to a local sharpness property of the objective function, which marks the key difference from previous adaptive scheme that adjusts the penalty parameter per-iteration based on certain conditions on iterates. On theoretical side, given the local sharpness characterized by an exponent $\theta\in(0, 1]$, we show that the proposed ADMM enjoys an improved iteration complexity of $\widetilde O(1/\epsilon^{1-\theta})$\footnote{$\widetilde O()$ suppresses a logarithmic factor.} in the deterministic setting and an iteration complexity of $\widetilde O(1/\epsilon^{2(1-\theta)})$ in the stochastic setting without smoothness and strong convexity assumptions. The complexity in either setting improves that of the standard ADMM which only uses a fixed penalty parameter. On the practical side, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithms converge comparably to, if not much faster than, ADMM with a fine-tuned fixed penalty parameter.

paragraphs: ADMM uses a quadratic penalty to enforce equality constraints, and its performance can depend strongly on the penalty's size. Here, ε is the target accuracy and the notation suppresses a logarithmic factor.

Experiments also show convergence comparable to, and sometimes much faster than, ADMM with a carefully tuned fixed penalty. The contribution therefore combines a structural explanation for faster convergence with evidence that adaptive penalization can be practically useful.
summary.tldr: An ADMM penalty scheme adapted to local objective sharpness improves conditional convergence bounds and performs competitively with carefully tuned fixed penalties.

title: ADMM without a Fixed Penalty Parameter: Faster Convergence with New Adaptive Penalization

abstract: Recent work has shown that fast, compact low-bitwidth neural networks can be surprisingly accurate. These networks use homogeneous binarization: all parameters in each layer or (more commonly) the whole model have the same low bitwidth (e.g., 2 bits). However, modern hardware allows efficient designs where each arithmetic instruction can have a custom bitwidth, motivating heterogeneous binarization, where every parameter in the network may have a different bitwidth. In this paper, we show that it is feasible and useful to select bitwidths at the parameter granularity during training. For instance a heterogeneously quantized version of modern networks such as AlexNet and MobileNet, with the right mix of 1-, 2- and 3-bit parameters that average to just 1.4 bits can equal the accuracy of homogeneous 2-bit versions of these networks. Further, we provide analyses to show that the heterogeneously binarized systems yield FPGA- and ASIC-based implementations that are correspondingly more efficient in both circuit area and energy efficiency than their homogeneous counterparts.
