paragraphs: Low-bitwidth neural networks reduce the precision used to represent parameters, making compact and fast implementations possible. Common approaches assign the same bitwidth across a layer or an entire model. This paper instead allows individual parameters to use different bitwidths, motivated by hardware that can efficiently support arithmetic instructions with customized precision.

The authors show that selecting bitwidths at the level of individual parameters during training is feasible and useful. Their examples include AlexNet and MobileNet models that mix 1-, 2-, and 3-bit parameters. With an appropriate mix averaging 1.4 bits per parameter, these networks can match the accuracy of corresponding homogeneous 2-bit versions.

The significance is that precision need not be allocated uniformly to preserve the demonstrated accuracy. Hardware analyses further indicate that the heterogeneous designs yield FPGA and ASIC implementations with better circuit-area and energy efficiency than their homogeneous counterparts. The paper therefore connects a training-time choice about parameter representation to both predictive performance and the efficiency of specialized hardware implementations.
summary.tldr: Choosing bitwidths per parameter can match homogeneous 2-bit network accuracy at an average of 1.4 bits while improving hardware efficiency.

title: Heterogeneous Bitwidth Binarization in Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We propose Graphical Generative Adversarial Networks (Graphical-GAN) to model structured data. Graphical-GAN conjoins the power of Bayesian networks on compactly representing the dependency structures among random variables and that of generative adversarial networks on learning expressive dependency functions. We introduce a structured recognition model to infer the posterior distribution of latent variables given observations. We generalize the Expectation Propagation (EP) algorithm to learn the generative model and recognition model jointly. Finally, we present two important instances of Graphical-GAN, i.e. Gaussian Mixture GAN (GMGAN) and State Space GAN (SSGAN), which can successfully learn the discrete and temporal structures on visual datasets, respectively.

Finally, we present two important instances of Graphical-GAN, i.e. Gaussian Mixture GAN (GMGAN) and State Space GAN (SSGAN), which can successfully learn the discrete and temporal structures on visual datasets, respectively.

paragraphs: Structured data contains dependencies that a generative model needs to represent. Graphical-GAN combines two approaches to this task: Bayesian networks provide a compact description of dependencies among random variables, while generative adversarial networks learn expressive functions for those dependencies. The framework brings explicit probabilistic structure into adversarial generative modeling.

The paper also introduces a structured recognition model for inferring latent variables from observations. This complements the generative direction, which describes how observations arise from hidden variables. To train both components together, the authors generalize Expectation Propagation. Joint learning therefore includes both the model of the data and the model used to infer its hidden explanation.

Two concrete versions demonstrate the framework. Gaussian Mixture GAN learns discrete structure in visual datasets, while State Space GAN learns temporal structure. These examples show how the general construction accommodates different forms of organization through its graphical specification. The stated results support the combination of structured dependencies, expressive adversarial components, and learned latent-variable inference as a workable approach to modeling visual data.
summary.tldr: Graphical-GAN combines Bayesian dependency structure with adversarial learning and structured inference to model discrete and temporal organization in visual data.

title: Graphical Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We present a simple and general framework for feature learning from point cloud. The key to the success of CNNs is the convolution operator that is capable of leveraging spatially-local correlation in data represented densely in grids (e.g. images). However, point cloud are irregular and unordered, thus a direct convolving of kernels against the features associated with the points will result in deserting the shape information while being variant to the orders. To address these problems, we propose to learn a X-transformation from the input points, which is used for simultaneously weighting the input features associated with the points and permuting them into latent potentially canonical order. Then element-wise product and sum operations of typical convolution operator are applied on the X-transformed features. The proposed method is a generalization of typical CNNs into learning features from point cloud, thus we call it PointCNN. Experiments show that PointCNN achieves on par or better performance than state-of-the-art methods on multiple challenging benchmark datasets and tasks.

paragraphs: Convolution works naturally on images because their grid gives nearby values a consistent spatial arrangement. Point clouds have irregular locations and no inherent ordering. Applying ordinary convolution directly to point features can therefore lose shape information and make the result depend on an arbitrary ordering of the points.

PointCNN addresses this problem by learning an X-transformation from the input points. The transformation both weights their associated features and rearranges them into a learned, potentially canonical order. Standard convolution-style multiplication and summation then operate on the transformed features. This makes the learned transformation the bridge between irregular point data and the familiar convolution operation.

The framework generalizes convolutional feature learning to point clouds while explicitly addressing their geometry and ordering difficulties. The ordering is described as potentially canonical, so the proposal should not be read as an unconditional guarantee of a unique ordering. Across multiple challenging benchmark datasets and tasks, the authors report performance matching or exceeding state-of-the-art methods, supporting the practical effectiveness of the transformation-based approach in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: PointCNN learns to weight and reorder point features before convolution, enabling effective feature learning on irregular point clouds.

title: PointCNN: Convolution On X-Transformed Points

abstract: Scattering transforms are non-trainable deep convolutional architectures that exploit the multi-scale resolution of a wavelet filter bank to obtain an appropriate representation of data. More importantly, they are proven invariant to translations, and stable to perturbations that are close to translations. This stability property dons the scattering transform with a robustness to small changes in the metric domain of the data. When considering network data, regular convolutions do not hold since the data domain presents an irregular structure given by the network topology. In this work, we extend scattering transforms to network data by using multi-resolution graph wavelets, whose computation can be obtained by means of graph convolutions. Furthermore, we prove that the resulting graph scattering transforms are stable to metric perturbations of the underlying network. This renders graph scattering transforms robust to changes on the network topology, making it particularly useful for cases of transfer learning, topology estimation or time-varying graphs.

paragraphs: Scattering transforms are deep convolutional representations with fixed, non-trainable components built around wavelets at multiple scales. Their appeal includes mathematical stability: suitable small changes in the data domain produce controlled changes in the representation. Extending this idea to network data is challenging because graph topology gives the domain an irregular structure where ordinary convolutions do not directly apply.

The paper constructs graph scattering transforms using multiresolution graph wavelets. These wavelets can be computed through graph convolutions, providing the basic operations needed to carry the scattering architecture onto networks. The result preserves the multiscale representation idea while adapting its computations to the graph domain.

The authors prove stability to metric perturbations of the underlying network. This supports robustness when network topology changes within the setting covered by the analysis. They identify transfer learning, topology estimation, and time-varying graphs as particularly relevant uses. The main finding is a theoretical stability guarantee for graph-based representations, giving a mathematical reason to expect controlled sensitivity to changes in their underlying network.
summary.tldr: Multiresolution graph wavelets extend scattering transforms to networks with proven stability to metric perturbations of the underlying graph.

title: Stability of Graph Scattering Transforms

abstract: Humans and animals are capable of flexibly switching between a multitude of tasks, each requiring rapid, sensory-informed decision making. Incoming stimuli are processed by a hierarchy of neural circuits consisting of millions of neurons with diverse feature selectivity. At any given moment, only a small subset of these carry task-relevant information. In principle, downstream processing stages could identify the relevant neurons through supervised learning, but this would require many example trials. Such extensive learning periods are inconsistent with the observed flexibility of humans or animals, who can adjust to changes in task parameters or structure almost immediately. Here, we propose a novel solution based on functionally-targeted stochastic modulation. It has been observed that trial-to-trial neural activity is modulated by a shared, low-dimensional, stochastic signal that introduces task-irrelevant noise. Counter-intuitively this noise is preferentially targeted towards task-informative neurons, corrupting the encoded signal. However, we hypothesize that this modulation offers a solution to the identification problem, labeling task-informative neurons so as to facilitate decoding. We simulate an encoding population of spiking neurons whose rates are modulated by a shared stochastic signal, and show that a linear decoder with readout weights approximating neuron-specific modulation strength can achieve near-optimal accuracy. Such a decoder allows fast and flexible task-dependent information routing without relying on hardwired knowledge of the task-informative neurons (as in maximum likelihood) or unrealistically many supervised training trials (as in regression).

paragraphs: A neural population can contain many signals, while only a small subset matters for the current task. Downstream circuits must identify that subset quickly to explain flexible behavior. Learning the relevant neurons through extensive supervised practice would be difficult to reconcile with the rapid task changes that humans and animals can manage.

The paper proposes that shared random modulation could help identify those neurons. Such modulation introduces noise and is preferentially directed toward task-informative neurons. The authors hypothesize that this seemingly harmful signal also labels useful information: a downstream decoder could use the strength of each neuron's modulation to determine how much to weight its activity.

In simulations of spiking neurons, a linear decoder whose weights approximate these modulation strengths achieves near-optimal accuracy. This supports the proposed mechanism for fast, task-dependent routing without predefined knowledge of the informative neurons or very large amounts of supervised training. The biological interpretation remains a hypothesis supported here by the simulated encoding and decoding system.
summary.tldr: Simulations suggest shared neural noise can mark task-relevant neurons and enable rapid, accurate information routing.

title: Flexible information routing in neural populations through stochastic comodulation

abstract: If you are predicting the label $y$ of a new object with $\hat y$, how confident are you that $y = \hat y$? Conformal prediction methods provide an elegant framework for answering such question by building a $100 (1 - \alpha)\%$ confidence region without assumptions on the distribution of the data. It is based on a refitting procedure that parses all the possibilities for $y$ to select the most likely ones. Although providing strong coverage guarantees, conformal set is impractical to compute exactly for many regression problems. We propose efficient algorithms to compute conformal prediction set using approximated solution of (convex) regularized empirical risk minimization. Our approaches rely on a new homotopy continuation technique for tracking the solution path with respect to sequential changes of the observations. We also provide a detailed analysis quantifying its complexity.

paragraphs: A prediction set expresses uncertainty by returning a collection of plausible outcomes instead of only one estimated value. Conformal prediction provides a framework for constructing such sets with a specified coverage level without assuming a particular data distribution. Its computational difficulty is that candidate outcomes are assessed through repeated model refitting.

For regression, exploring all possible values of a new outcome can make exact full conformal computation impractical. This paper proposes efficient algorithms that use approximate solutions to convex, regularized empirical risk minimization problems. The approach addresses the repeated optimization underlying the prediction set, where changing a candidate outcome changes the fitting problem.

The central technique is homotopy continuation: tracking how a solution evolves as observations change sequentially. Following this solution path provides a way to organize the work across related fitting problems. The authors also quantify the method's computational complexity. The contribution is thus a computational route toward full conformal prediction in regression, built around approximate optimization and an analysis of the effort required.
summary.tldr: Approximate homotopy tracks related optimization solutions to make full conformal prediction sets more practical to compute.

title: Computing Full Conformal Prediction Set with Approximate Homotopy

abstract: Tremendous amount of parameters make deep neural networks impractical to be deployed for edge-device-based real-world applications due to the limit of computational power and storage space. Existing studies have made progress on learning quantized deep models to reduce model size and energy consumption, i.e. converting full-precision weights ($r$'s) into discrete values ($q$'s) in a supervised training manner. However, the training process for quantization is non-differentiable, which leads to either infinite or zero gradients ($g_r$) w.r.t. $r$. To address this problem, most training-based quantization methods use the gradient w.r.t. $q$ ($g_q$) with clipping to approximate $g_r$ by Straight-Through-Estimator (STE) or manually design their computation. However, these methods only heuristically make training-based quantization applicable, without further analysis on how the approximated gradients can assist training of a quantized network. In this paper, we propose to learn $g_r$ by a neural network. Specifically, a meta network is trained using $g_q$ and $r$ as inputs, and outputs $g_r$ for subsequent weight updates. The meta network is updated together with the original quantized network. Our proposed method alleviates the problem of non-differentiability, and can be trained in an end-to-end manner. Extensive experiments are conducted with CIFAR10/100 and ImageNet on various deep networks to demonstrate the advantage of our proposed method in terms of a faster convergence rate and better performance. Codes are released at: \texttt{https://github.com/csyhhu/MetaQuant}

paragraphs: Quantization replaces full-precision network weights with discrete values to reduce model size and energy consumption. Training these compressed networks is difficult because the conversion is non-differentiable. The gradients needed to update the underlying weights are therefore unusable directly, motivating approximations such as straight-through estimators and manually designed gradient rules.

MetaQuant learns the update information with a second neural network. This meta network receives the full-precision weights and the gradients with respect to their quantized versions. It outputs gradients for updating the full-precision weights, and it is trained jointly with the quantized network. The method thus makes the gradient approximation itself part of the learning process.

The authors report faster convergence and better performance across experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet using various deep networks. These findings support learned gradient estimates as a useful alternative to fixed heuristics in the tested settings. The approach alleviates the training obstacle posed by non-differentiability and supports end-to-end optimization; it does not make the discrete quantization operation itself differentiable.
summary.tldr: MetaQuant jointly trains a meta network to supply useful weight-update gradients through non-differentiable quantization.

title: MetaQuant: Learning to Quantize by Learning to Penetrate Non-differentiable Quantization

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) testing is increasingly popular for evaluating a machine learning system's ability to generalize beyond the biases of a training set. OOD benchmarks are designed to present a different joint distribution of data and labels between training and test time. VQA-CP has become the standard OOD benchmark for visual question answering, but we discovered three troubling practices in its current use. First, most published methods rely on explicit knowledge of the construction of the OOD splits. They often rely on ``inverting'' the distribution of labels, e.g. answering mostly ``yes'' when the common training answer was ``no''. Second, the OOD test set is used for model selection. Third, a model's in-domain performance is assessed after retraining it on in-domain splits (VQA v2) that exhibit a more balanced distribution of labels. These three practices defeat the objective of evaluating generalization, and put into question the value of methods specifically designed for this dataset. We show that embarrassingly-simple methods, including one that generates answers at random, surpass the state of the art on some question types. We provide short- and long-term solutions to avoid these pitfalls and realize the benefits of OOD evaluation.

OOD benchmarks are designed to present a different joint distribution of data and labels between training and test time. VQA-CP has become the standard OOD benchmark for visual question answering, but we discovered three troubling practices in its current use. First, most published methods rely on explicit knowledge of the construction of the OOD splits. They often rely on ``inverting'' the distribution of labels, e.g. answering mostly ``yes'' when the common training answer was ``no''. Second, the OOD test set is used for model selection. Third, a model's in-domain performance is assessed after retraining it on in-domain splits (VQA v2) that exhibit a more balanced distribution of labels. These three practices defeat the objective of evaluating generalization, and put into question the value of methods specifically designed for this dataset. We show that embarrassingly-simple methods, including one that generates answers at random, surpass the state of the art on some question types. We provide short- and long-term solutions to avoid these pitfalls and realize the benefits of OOD evaluation.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution evaluation is intended to test whether a model generalizes when relationships between inputs and labels change. This paper examines VQA-CP, a visual question answering benchmark designed for that purpose. The authors find that common evaluation practices can reward knowledge of the benchmark’s construction, undermining what the resulting scores say about generalization.

They identify three problems. Methods often exploit explicit knowledge of how the splits were constructed, including reversing common training answers. Researchers use the out-of-distribution test set for model selection. They also assess in-domain performance after retraining on different, more balanced splits, so that assessment does not measure the same trained model’s behavior across the two settings.

The authors demonstrate the consequences with very simple methods, including a random-answer procedure that exceeds the state of the art on some question types. This is evidence of exploitable evaluation practices, rather than broad success at visual reasoning. The paper proposes short- and long-term remedies aimed at restoring the value of out-of-distribution evaluation and distinguishing benchmark-specific adaptation from the generalization the benchmark was meant to measure.
summary.tldr: An analysis of VQA-CP shows how benchmark-specific strategies and evaluation practices can undermine claims of out-of-distribution generalization.

title: On the Value of Out-of-Distribution Testing: An Example of Goodhart's Law

abstract: A central problem in machine learning and statistics is to model joint densities of random variables from data. Copulas are joint cumulative distribution functions with uniform marginal distributions and are used to capture interdependencies in isolation from marginals. Copulas are widely used within statistics, but have not gained traction in the context of modern deep learning. In this paper, we introduce ACNet, a novel differentiable neural network architecture that enforces structural properties and enables one to learn an important class of copulas--Archimedean Copulas. Unlike Generative Adversarial Networks, Variational Autoencoders, or Normalizing Flow methods, which learn either densities or the generative process directly, ACNet learns a generator of the copula, which implicitly defines the cumulative distribution function of a joint distribution. We give a probabilistic interpretation of the network parameters of ACNet and use this to derive a simple but efficient sampling algorithm for the learned copula. Our experiments show that ACNet is able to both approximate common Archimedean Copulas and generate new copulas which may provide better fits to data.

paragraphs: Modeling several random variables together requires describing both their individual distributions and their dependence on one another. Copulas separate these tasks by representing dependence through a joint cumulative distribution with uniform marginals. This paper brings that statistical approach into a differentiable neural architecture designed for the Archimedean family of copulas.

The proposed architecture, ACNet, enforces structural properties needed to learn this family. Its target is a copula generator, a mathematical object that implicitly determines the joint cumulative distribution function. This differs from directly learning a density or a data-generation process. The architecture therefore places neural learning inside a structured representation of statistical dependence.

The authors provide a probabilistic interpretation of ACNet’s parameters and use it to derive a simple, efficient sampling algorithm for the learned copula. Experiments show that ACNet can approximate common Archimedean copulas and construct new ones that may fit data better. The findings support a flexible way to learn dependence while preserving the structure of the chosen copula family, with sampling available from the resulting model.
summary.tldr: ACNet learns structurally valid Archimedean copulas and supports efficient sampling, with learned copulas that may fit data better.

title: Deep Archimedean Copulas

abstract: Knowledge graph (KG) embedding is well-known in learning representations of KGs. Many models have been proposed to learn the interactions between entities and relations of the triplets. However, long-term information among multiple triplets is also important to KG. In this work, based on the relational paths, which are composed of a sequence of triplets, we define the Interstellar as a recurrent neural architecture search problem for the short-term and long-term information along the paths. First, we analyze the difficulty of using a unified model to work as the Interstellar. Then, we propose to search for recurrent architecture as the Interstellar for different KG tasks. A case study on synthetic data illustrates the importance of the defined search problem. Experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the searched models and the efficiency of the proposed hybrid-search algorithm.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs describe relationships through triplets connecting entities and relations. Interstellar studies relational paths, where a sequence of triplets supplies both nearby context and longer-range information.

The paper formulates learning along these paths as a recurrent neural architecture search problem. It first analyzes the difficulty of using one unified model as the path-processing architecture. It then proposes searching for recurrent architectures suited to different knowledge graph tasks, making the architecture itself part of the solution rather than fixing the same design across tasks.

A synthetic case study illustrates why the search problem matters. Experiments on real datasets support the effectiveness of the resulting models and the efficiency of the proposed hybrid search algorithm. The contribution combines a modeling perspective with a search method: relationships across multiple triplets deserve explicit treatment, and the recurrent structure used to capture them can be selected for the task at hand.
summary.tldr: Interstellar searches for task-specific recurrent architectures that capture short- and long-range information along knowledge graph paths.

title: Interstellar: Searching Recurrent Architecture for Knowledge Graph Embedding

abstract: The ability to detect and count certain substructures in graphs is important for solving many tasks on graph-structured data, especially in the contexts of computational chemistry and biology as well as social network analysis. Inspired by this, we propose to study the expressive power of graph neural networks (GNNs) via their ability to count attributed graph substructures, extending recent works that examine their power in graph isomorphism testing and function approximation. We distinguish between two types of substructure counting: induced-subgraph-count and subgraph-count, and establish both positive and negative answers for popular GNN architectures. Specifically, we prove that Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs), 2-Weisfeiler-Lehman (2-WL) and 2-Invariant Graph Networks (2-IGNs) cannot perform induced-subgraph-count of substructures consisting of 3 or more nodes, while they can perform subgraph-count of star-shaped substructures. As an intermediary step, we prove that 2-WL and 2-IGNs are equivalent in distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, partly answering an open problem raised in Maron et al. (2019). We also prove positive results for k-WL and k-IGNs as well as negative results for k-WL with a finite number of iterations. We then conduct experiments that support the theoretical results for MPNNs and 2-IGNs. Moreover, motivated by substructure counting and inspired by Murphy et al. (2019), we propose the Local Relational Pooling model and demonstrate that it is not only effective for substructure counting but also able to achieve competitive performance on molecular prediction tasks.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates graph neural networks through their ability to count structural patterns. Such patterns matter in molecular, biological, and social graphs. It distinguishes ordinary subgraph counting from induced-subgraph counting: an induced match must also respect which connections are absent among the selected nodes. The distinction changes what a network needs to recognize.

The authors prove limits for message-passing networks, the 2-Weisfeiler-Lehman procedure, and 2-Invariant Graph Networks. These methods cannot perform induced counting of substructures with three or more nodes, although they can count star-shaped ordinary subgraphs. They also establish that 2-Weisfeiler-Lehman and 2-Invariant Graph Networks have equivalent power for distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs, and derive further positive results for higher-order methods and negative results for finite-iteration higher-order Weisfeiler-Lehman procedures.

Experiments support the theoretical findings for message-passing networks and 2-Invariant Graph Networks. Motivated by the counting problem, the authors introduce Local Relational Pooling, which performs effectively on substructure counting and competitively on molecular prediction. Together, the results make counting a concrete way to assess architecture capabilities and motivate alternative designs.
summary.tldr: Substructure counting exposes provable limits of common graph networks and motivates Local Relational Pooling for richer structural prediction.

title: Can Graph Neural Networks Count Substructures?

abstract: Normalizing flows (NFs) have become a prominent method for deep generative models that allow for an analytic probability density estimation and efficient synthesis. However, a flow-based network is considered to be inefficient in parameter complexity because of reduced expressiveness of bijective mapping, which renders the models unfeasibly expensive in terms of parameters. We present an alternative parameterization scheme called NanoFlow, which uses a single neural density estimator to model multiple transformation stages. Hence, we propose an efficient parameter decomposition method and the concept of flow indication embedding, which are key missing components that enable density estimation from a single neural network. Experiments performed on audio and image models confirm that our method provides a new parameter-efficient solution for scalable NFs with significant sublinear parameter complexity.
originalAbstract: Normalizing flows (NFs) have become a prominent method for deep generative models that allow for an analytic probability density estimation and efficient synthesis. However, a flow-based network is considered to be inefficient in parameter complexity because of reduced expressiveness of bijective mapping, which renders the models unfeasibly expensive in terms of parameters. We present an alternative parameterization scheme called NanoFlow, which uses a single neural density estimator to model multiple transformation stages. Hence, we propose an efficient parameter decomposition method and the concept of flow indication embedding, which are key missing components that enable density estimation from a single neural network. Experiments performed on audio and image models confirm that our method provides a new parameter-efficient solution for scalable NFs with significant sublinear parameter complexity.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows are generative models that support explicit probability-density calculation and efficient sample generation. Their transformations must be invertible, which constrains how each stage can represent data. Building expressive models through multiple such stages can therefore require a large number of parameters, making parameter efficiency an important scaling problem.

NanoFlow proposes using a single neural density estimator across multiple transformation stages. To make this shared estimator work, the paper introduces an efficient parameter decomposition and a flow indication embedding. The embedding supplies information about the transformation stage, allowing one neural network to participate in density estimation across the sequence rather than requiring fully separate estimators throughout.

Experiments on audio and image models support the resulting parameter efficiency. The authors report sublinear parameter complexity, meaning parameter requirements grow more slowly than a proportional increase as the flow scales in the studied scheme. The contribution is a way to parameterize larger flows more economically while retaining the density-estimation and synthesis capabilities that make this model family useful.
summary.tldr: NanoFlow shares a neural density estimator across transformation stages to scale normalizing flows with sublinear parameter complexity.

title: NanoFlow: Scalable Normalizing Flows with Sublinear Parameter Complexity

abstract: We propose an adaptively weighted stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics algorithm (SGLD), so-called contour stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (CSGLD), for Bayesian learning in big data statistics. The proposed algorithm is essentially a scalable dynamic importance sampler, which automatically flattens the target distribution such that the simulation for a multi-modal distribution can be greatly facilitated. Theoretically, we prove a stability condition and establish the asymptotic convergence of the self-adapting parameter to a unique fixed-point, regardless of the non-convexity of the original energy function; we also present an error analysis for the weighted averaging estimators. Empirically, the CSGLD algorithm is tested on multiple benchmark datasets including CIFAR10 and CIFAR100. The numerical results indicate its superiority over the existing state-of-the-art algorithms in training deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Bayesian learning can require sampling from distributions with several distinct peaks. The paper introduces contour stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or CSGLD, to make this sampling easier in large-data settings. It extends SGLD with weights that adapt during the simulation, making the method a scalable form of dynamic importance sampling.

The central idea is to automatically flatten the target distribution. This changes the landscape explored by the simulation so that sampling a distribution with multiple modes can be greatly facilitated. The method also uses weighted averaging estimators, and the paper analyzes the errors of those estimators alongside the adaptation mechanism.

The theoretical results include a stability condition and asymptotic convergence of the adapting parameter to a unique fixed point, despite possible nonconvexity of the original energy function. This is specifically a result about the adaptive parameter. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, indicate advantages over the compared state-of-the-art algorithms for training deep neural networks, connecting the sampling proposal to practical Bayesian learning.
summary.tldr: CSGLD adaptively flattens multimodal distributions to facilitate scalable Bayesian sampling, with convergence analysis and promising neural-network experiments.

title: A Contour Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics Algorithm for Simulations of Multi-modal Distributions

abstract: We study the problem of discovering the simplest latent variable that can make two observed discrete variables conditionally independent. The minimum entropy required for such a latent is known as common entropy in information theory. We extend this notion to Renyi common entropy by minimizing the Renyi entropy of the latent variable. To efficiently compute common entropy, we propose an iterative algorithm that can be used to discover the trade-off between the entropy of the latent variable and the conditional mutual information of the observed variables. We show two applications of common entropy in causal inference: First, under the assumption that there are no low-entropy mediators, it can be used to distinguish direct causation from spurious correlation among almost all joint distributions on simple causal graphs with two observed variables. Second, common entropy can be used to improve constraint-based methods such as PC or FCI algorithms in the small-sample regime, where these methods are known to struggle. We propose a modification to these constraint-based methods to assess if a separating set found by these algorithms are valid using common entropy. We finally evaluate our algorithms on synthetic and real data to establish their performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies how simple a hidden variable can be while explaining the dependence between two observed discrete variables. The target is a latent variable that makes the observations conditionally independent. Common entropy measures the smallest entropy such a variable needs; the authors also extend this idea using Renyi entropy.

An iterative algorithm explores the trade-off between latent-variable entropy and the dependence that remains between the observations after conditioning. This makes the problem useful beyond finding a single exact explanation: it provides a way to examine how the complexity of a hidden explanation relates to how much observed dependence it accounts for.

The authors develop two causal applications. Assuming there are no low-entropy mediators, common entropy can distinguish direct causation from spurious correlation for almost all joint distributions on the simple graphs studied. It can also help assess separating sets produced by PC or FCI when samples are scarce. Evaluations use synthetic and real data, supporting these applications within the stated settings.
summary.tldr: Common entropy measures the complexity of hidden explanations for dependence and supports causal inference under stated assumptions.

title: Applications of Common Entropy for Causal Inference

abstract: Applications of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in robotics are often limited by high data demand. On the other hand, approximate models are readily available in many robotics scenarios, making model-based approaches like planning a data-efficient alternative. Still, the performance of these methods suffers if the model is imprecise or wrong. In this sense, the respective strengths and weaknesses of RL and model-based planners are complementary. In the present work, we investigate how both approaches can be integrated into one framework that combines their strengths. We introduce Learning to Execute (L2E), which leverages information contained in approximate plans to learn universal policies that are conditioned on plans. In our robotic manipulation experiments, L2E exhibits increased performance when compared to pure RL, pure planning, or baseline methods combining learning and planning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for robotics often needs substantial interaction data. Planning can use an available model to reduce that demand, but its performance suffers when the model inaccurately describes the robot or its surroundings. This paper starts from the observation that these approaches have complementary strengths: learning can adapt behavior, while planning supplies useful structure from approximate knowledge.

Learning to Execute, or L2E, combines them by training universal policies conditioned on plans. An approximate plan becomes information supplied to the learned policy, connecting model-based guidance with learned execution. The central idea is to make use of what the plan contains even when the model that produced it is imprecise or wrong.

In robotic manipulation experiments, L2E performs better than pure reinforcement learning, pure planning, and the compared methods that combine learning with planning. These results support plan conditioning as a useful way to integrate the two approaches. The reported contribution is a framework for learning how to execute with approximate guidance, with its performance advantage demonstrated in the manipulation experiments.
summary.tldr: Learning to Execute trains policies conditioned on approximate plans, outperforming the tested planning, reinforcement-learning, and hybrid alternatives in robotic manipulation.

title: Learning to Execute: Efficient Learning of Universal Plan-Conditioned Policies in Robotics

abstract: In this paper, we present Conjoint Attentions (CAs), a class of novel learning-to-attend strategies for graph neural networks (GNNs). Besides considering the layer-wise node features propagated within the GNN, CAs can additionally incorporate various structural interventions, such as node cluster embedding, and higher-order structural correlations that can be learned outside of GNN, when computing attention scores. The node features that are regarded as significant by the conjoint criteria are therefore more likely to be propagated in the GNN. Given the novel Conjoint Attention strategies, we then propose Graph conjoint attention networks (CATs) that can learn representations embedded with significant latent features deemed by the Conjoint Attentions. Besides, we theoretically validate the discriminative capacity of CATs. CATs utilizing the proposed Conjoint Attention strategies have been extensively tested in well-established benchmarking datasets and comprehensively compared with state-of-the-art baselines. The obtained notable performance demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed Conjoint Attentions.

paragraphs: Attention in a graph neural network helps determine which node information receives emphasis as representations are propagated. This paper introduces Conjoint Attentions, which combine the node features available within a network layer with additional structural information. The aim is to make attention sensitive to useful graph organization beyond the current propagated features.

The structural inputs can include node-cluster embeddings and higher-order correlations learned outside the graph neural network. These signals participate in computing attention scores, making features judged significant by the combined criteria more likely to be propagated. The authors build Graph conjoint attention networks, or CATs, around these strategies so that learned representations incorporate the features selected through this broader attention mechanism.

The paper provides theoretical validation of CATs' discriminative capacity and evaluates them extensively on established benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art baselines. The reported performance supports the effectiveness of combining internal node features with external structural signals. Its contribution is a class of attention strategies together with network architectures that put those strategies into practice.
summary.tldr: Conjoint Attentions combine propagated node features with additional graph structure to guide information flow in graph neural networks.

title: Learning Conjoint Attentions for Graph Neural Nets

abstract: Deep neural networks have been used widely to learn the latent structure of datasets, across modalities such as images, shapes, and audio signals. However, existing models are generally modality-dependent, requiring custom architectures and objectives to process different classes of signals. We leverage neural fields to capture the underlying structure in image, shape, audio and cross-modal audiovisual domains in a modality-independent manner. We cast our task as one of learning a manifold, where we aim to infer a low-dimensional, locally linear subspace in which our data resides. By enforcing coverage of the manifold, local linearity, and local isometry, our model -- dubbed GEM -- learns to capture the underlying structure of datasets across modalities. We can then travel along linear regions of our manifold to obtain perceptually consistent interpolations between samples, and can further use GEM to recover points on our manifold and glean not only diverse completions of input images, but cross-modal hallucinations of audio or image signals. Finally, we show that by walking across the underlying manifold of GEM, we may generate new samples in our signal domains.

paragraphs: Models that learn compact representations of images, shapes, or audio often need different architectures and training objectives for each signal type. This paper uses neural fields to pursue a common approach across these domains, including audiovisual data. Its model, GEM, aims to capture the structure of a dataset in a low-dimensional manifold.

GEM encourages three properties: coverage of that manifold, locally linear behavior, and preservation of local distances. Together, these constraints organize the representation so nearby portions can support meaningful movement between samples. The authors report that following linear regions produces perceptually consistent interpolations, connecting the geometry of the learned space to changes in the represented signals.

The learned manifold also supports recovering representations from inputs, producing diverse image completions, and generating audio or image signals across modalities. Moving through the manifold can additionally produce new samples in the signal domains. The contribution is a shared representation-learning framework whose geometry supports several operations, rather than requiring a separate modality-specific formulation for each kind of signal.
summary.tldr: GEM learns structured neural-field manifolds across signal types, supporting interpolation, completion, cross-modal generation, and new samples.

title: Learning Signal-Agnostic Manifolds of Neural Fields

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) with linear function approximation under the adaptivity constraint. We consider two popular limited adaptivity models: the batch learning model and the rare policy switch model, and propose two efficient online RL algorithms for episodic linear Markov decision processes, where the transition probability and the reward function can be represented as a linear function of some known feature mapping. In specific, for the batch learning model, our proposed LSVI-UCB-Batch algorithm achieves an $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3H^3T} + dHT/B)$ regret, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping, $H$ is the episode length, $T$ is the number of interactions and $B$ is the number of batches. Our result suggests that it suffices to use only $\sqrt{T/dH}$ batches to obtain $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})$ regret. For the rare policy switch model, our proposed LSVI-UCB-RareSwitch algorithm enjoys an $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3H^3T[1+T/(dH)]^{dH/B}})$ regret, which implies that $dH\log T$ policy switches suffice to obtain the $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3H^3T})$ regret. Our algorithms achieve the same regret as the LSVI-UCB algorithm \citep{jin2020provably}, yet with a substantially smaller amount of adaptivity. We also establish a lower bound for the batch learning model, which suggests that the dependency on $B$ in our regret bound is tight.

paragraphs: An online reinforcement learning agent may be unable to update its behavior after every new observation. This paper studies two such restrictions: learning in batches and changing policies only rarely. The setting is episodic linear Markov decision processes, where rewards and transition probabilities have linear representations using known features.

The authors develop a separate algorithm for each restriction. For batch learning, their bound shows that roughly the square root of T divided by dH batches suffices to match the stated regret rate of LSVI-UCB, up to logarithmic factors. Here T counts interactions, d is feature dimension, and H is episode length. For rare policy switching, roughly dH log T switches suffice for that same rate.

These are sufficiency results: they establish that strong regret guarantees remain achievable with substantially less adaptation. A lower bound for batch learning additionally suggests that the batch-count dependence in the proposed upper bound is tight. Together, the results quantify how restricting updates affects learning under the paper's linear-model assumptions.
summary.tldr: For episodic linear decision processes, two algorithms match LSVI-UCB's regret rate using substantially fewer batches or policy changes.

title: Provably Efficient Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation under Adaptivity Constraints

abstract: Many concepts have been proposed for meta learning with neural networks (NNs), e.g., NNs that learn to reprogram fast weights, Hebbian plasticity, learned learning rules, and meta recurrent NNs. Our Variable Shared Meta Learning (VSML) unifies the above and demonstrates that simple weight-sharing and sparsity in an NN is sufficient to express powerful learning algorithms (LAs) in a reusable fashion. A simple implementation of VSML where the weights of a neural network are replaced by tiny LSTMs allows for implementing the backpropagation LA solely by running in forward-mode. It can even meta learn new LAs that differ from online backpropagation and generalize to datasets outside of the meta training distribution without explicit gradient calculation. Introspection reveals that our meta learned LAs learn through fast association in a way that is qualitatively different from gradient descent.

Its Variable Shared Meta Learning framework, or VSML, brings together ideas including fast weights, Hebbian plasticity, learned update rules, and meta recurrent networks. The central claim is that simple patterns of weight sharing and sparsity are sufficient to express powerful learning algorithms in a reusable form.

In a concrete implementation, ordinary network weights are replaced by tiny LSTMs. This construction can implement the backpropagation learning algorithm through forward execution alone. The distinction is about how the learning computation is represented and run: a recurrent neural mechanism can carry out a procedure normally associated with explicit backward gradient calculations.

VSML can also meta-learn algorithms that differ from online backpropagation and operate without explicit gradient calculation. The authors report that these learned procedures generalize to datasets outside the meta-training distribution. Inspection suggests that they learn through rapid association in a way qualitatively different from gradient descent. These results show that the framework can express a familiar algorithm while also discovering different learning behavior, rather than merely reproducing a fixed update rule.
summary.tldr: VSML uses shared, sparse neural computation to express backpropagation and meta-learn alternative learning algorithms that transfer beyond their training distribution.

title: Meta Learning Backpropagation And Improving It

abstract: The contrastive pre-training of a recognition model on a large dataset of unlabeled data often boosts the model’s performance on downstream tasks like image classification. However, in domains such as medical imaging, collecting unlabeled data can be challenging and expensive. In this work, we consider the task of medical image segmentation and adapt contrastive learning with meta-label annotations to scenarios where no additional unlabeled data is available. Meta-labels, such as the location of a 2D slice in a 3D MRI scan, often come for free during the acquisition process. We use these meta-labels to pre-train the image encoder, as well as in a semi-supervised learning step that leverages a reduced set of annotated data. A self-paced learning strategy exploiting the weak annotations is proposed to furtherhelp the learning process and discriminate useful labels from noise. Results on five medical image segmentation datasets show that our approach: i) highly boosts the performance of a model trained on a few scans, ii) outperforms previous contrastive and semi-supervised approaches, and iii) reaches close to the performance of a model trained on the full data.

This paper studies segmentation when no additional unlabeled data is available. It instead uses meta-labels already associated with acquisition, such as a two-dimensional slice’s location within a three-dimensional MRI scan.

These weak annotations guide both encoder pretraining and a semi-supervised learning stage using a reduced set of detailed annotations. A self-paced strategy further uses the meta-labels to distinguish useful supervision from noise. The approach therefore extracts training information from the available scans and their acquisition context, reducing reliance on either extra scans or extensive segmentation labels.

Across five medical segmentation datasets, the method substantially improves a model trained on only a few scans and outperforms previous contrastive and semi-supervised approaches. It also approaches the performance of a model trained on the full data. These empirical results suggest that acquisition metadata can provide valuable supervision when both scan availability and detailed annotation are constrained.
summary.tldr: Acquisition meta-labels and self-paced contrastive learning improve medical segmentation with few annotated scans and no additional unlabeled data.

title: Self-Paced Contrastive Learning for Semi-supervised Medical Image Segmentation with Meta-labels

abstract: One of the key challenges in training Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) is that target outputs typically come in the form of natural signals, such as labels for classification or images for generative models, and need to be encoded into spikes. This is done by handcrafting target spiking signals, which in turn implicitly fixes the mechanisms used to decode spikes into natural signals, e.g., rate decoding. The arbitrary choice of target signals and decoding rule generally impairs the capacity of the SNN to encode and process information in the timing of spikes. To address this problem, this work introduces a hybrid variational autoencoder architecture, consisting of an encoding SNN and a decoding Artificial Neural Network (ANN). The role of the decoding ANN is to learn how to best convert the spiking signals output by the SNN into the target natural signal. A novel end-to-end learning rule is introduced that optimizes a directed information bottleneck training criterion via surrogate gradients. We demonstrate the applicability of the technique in an experimental settings on various tasks, including real-life datasets.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through spikes, while their desired outputs are often ordinary labels or images. Training commonly bridges this mismatch by prescribing target spike patterns. That choice also implicitly fixes how spikes will be decoded, potentially restricting the network’s ability to use information carried by the timing of spikes.

The paper replaces a handcrafted decoding rule with a learned decoder. Its hybrid variational autoencoder combines a spiking neural network encoder with an artificial neural network decoder. The decoder learns to translate the encoder’s spike output into the target natural signal, making that translation part of the training problem.

The authors introduce an end-to-end learning rule that optimizes a directed information bottleneck objective through surrogate gradients. This provides a way to train the two components together while addressing the information represented by the spike sequence. Experiments across several tasks, including real-life datasets, demonstrate applicability. The stated result is evidence that learned decoding can support this hybrid architecture, rather than a claim of universal superiority across spiking-network tasks.
summary.tldr: A hybrid autoencoder learns to decode spike timing into ordinary outputs instead of fixing the decoding rule through handcrafted target spikes.

title: Learning to Time-Decode in Spiking Neural Networks Through the Information Bottleneck

abstract: The goal in label-imbalanced and group-sensitive classification is to optimize relevant metrics such as balanced error and equal opportunity. Classical methods, such as weighted cross-entropy, fail when training deep nets to the terminal phase of training (TPT), that is training beyond zero training error. This observation has motivated recent flurry of activity in developing heuristic alternatives following the intuitive mechanism of promoting larger margin for minorities. In contrast to previous heuristics, we follow a principled analysis explaining how different loss adjustments affect margins. First, we prove that for all linear classifiers trained in TPT, it is necessary to introduce multiplicative, rather than additive, logit adjustments so that the interclass margins change appropriately. To show this, we discover a connection of the multiplicative CE modification to the cost-sensitive support-vector machines. Perhaps counterintuitively, we also find that, at the start of training, the same multiplicative weights can actually harm the minority classes. Thus, while additive adjustments are ineffective in the TPT, we show that they can speed up convergence by countering the initial negative effect of the multiplicative weights. Motivated by these findings, we formulate the vector-scaling (VS) loss, that captures existing techniques as special cases. Moreover, we introduce a natural extension of the VS-loss to group-sensitive classification, thus treating the two common types of imbalances (label/group) in a unifying way. Importantly, our experiments on state-of-the-art datasets are fully consistent with our theoretical insights and confirm the superior performance of our algorithms. Finally, for imbalanced Gaussian-mixtures data, we perform a generalization analysis, revealing tradeoffs between balanced / standard error and equal opportunity.

This paper analyzes how changes to classification losses influence margins in that terminal phase. It addresses both unequal label frequencies and group-sensitive objectives such as equal opportunity.

A separate generalization analysis for imbalanced Gaussian mixtures exposes tradeoffs among balanced error, standard error, and equal opportunity, clarifying that the choice of performance objective matters.
summary.tldr: An analysis of early and late training motivates vector-scaling loss for label imbalance and group-sensitive classification.

title: Label-Imbalanced and Group-Sensitive Classification under Overparameterization

abstract: Most existing algorithms in decentralized online learning are conducted in the synchronous setting. However, synchronization makes these algorithms suffer from the straggler problem, i.e., fast learners have to wait for slow learners, which significantly reduces such algorithms' overall efficiency. To overcome this problem, we study decentralized online learning in the asynchronous setting, which allows different learners to work at their own pace. We first formulate the framework of Asynchronous Decentralized Online Convex Optimization, which specifies the whole process of asynchronous decentralized online learning using a sophisticated event indexing system. Then we propose the Asynchronous Decentralized Online Gradient-Push (AD-OGP) algorithm, which performs asymmetric gossiping communication and instantaneous model averaging. We further derive a regret bound of AD-OGP, which is a function of the network topology, the levels of processing delays, and the levels of communication delays. Extensive experiments show that AD-OGP runs significantly faster than its synchronous counterpart and also verify the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Decentralized online learning lets multiple learners update models and exchange information as data arrives. When updates are synchronized, faster learners must wait for slower ones. This straggler problem can reduce the efficiency of the whole system. The paper studies an asynchronous alternative in which each learner proceeds at its own pace.

The authors first formalize asynchronous decentralized online convex optimization using an event-indexing system. This provides a way to describe updates and communications that do not share a single synchronized step. They then introduce AD-OGP, an algorithm combining asymmetric gossip communication with instantaneous model averaging to coordinate learning across the network.

The theoretical analysis bounds regret, a measure of accumulated learning performance, in terms of network structure and both processing and communication delays. This explicitly connects the learning guarantee to conditions in the distributed system. Experiments show that AD-OGP runs significantly faster than its synchronous counterpart and support the theoretical results. The contribution therefore combines a formal account of asynchronous learning with an algorithm that demonstrates practical speed benefits.
summary.tldr: AD-OGP enables decentralized learners to work asynchronously, with delay-dependent regret guarantees and reported speed gains over synchronous learning.

title: Asynchronous Decentralized Online Learning

abstract: Recent advances in remote sensing products allow near-real time monitoring of the Earth’s surface. Despite increasing availability of near-daily time-series of satellite imagery, there has been little exploration of deep learning methods to utilize the unprecedented temporal density of observations. This is particularly interesting in crop monitoring where time-series remote sensing data has been used frequently to exploit phenological differences of crops in the growing cycle over time. In this work, we present DENETHOR: The DynamicEarthNET dataset for Harmonized, inter-Operabel, analysis-Ready, daily crop monitoring from space. Our dataset contains daily, analysis-ready Planet Fusion data together with Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical time-series for crop type classification in Northern Germany. Our baseline experiments underline that incorporating the available spatial and temporal information fully may not be straightforward and could require the design of tailored architectures. The dataset presents two main challenges to the community: Exploit the temporal dimension for improved crop classification and ensure that models can handle a domain shift to a different year.

paragraphs: DENETHOR supports research on identifying crop types from satellite observations collected over time. Crops change during their growing cycles, and these differences can help distinguish them. The authors focus on a growing opportunity: satellite imagery is becoming available nearly every day, but deep learning has made limited use of that dense sequence of observations.

The dataset covers Northern Germany and combines daily, analysis-ready Planet Fusion data with Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical time series. This gives researchers observations with both spatial detail and repeated measurements through time. The central modeling question is how to use that combined information effectively for crop classification.

Baseline experiments suggest that fully exploiting the available spatial and temporal information may require specially designed architectures. The dataset poses two connected challenges: improving classification through the temporal dimension and handling a shift to a different year. Success therefore involves learning from crop development over time while remaining effective when the year of observation changes.
summary.tldr: DENETHOR combines daily satellite observations for crop classification, challenging models to exploit time and generalize across years.

title: DENETHOR: The DynamicEarthNET dataset for Harmonized, inter-Operable, analysis-Ready, daily crop monitoring from space

abstract: Much of reinforcement learning theory is built on top of oracles that are computationally hard to implement. Specifically for learning near-optimal policies in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), existing algorithms either need to make strong assumptions about the model dynamics (e.g. deterministic transitions) or assume access to an oracle for solving a hard optimistic planning or estimation problem as a subroutine. In this work we develop the first oracle-free learning algorithm for POMDPs under reasonable assumptions. Specifically, we give a quasipolynomial-time end-to-end algorithm for learning in ``observable'' POMDPs, where observability is the assumption that well-separated distributions over states induce well-separated distributions over observations. Our techniques circumvent the more traditional approach of using the principle of optimism under uncertainty to promote exploration, and instead give a novel application of barycentric spanners to constructing policy covers.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision process, an agent must learn to act without directly seeing the underlying state. Existing theoretical algorithms often rely on strong assumptions about the dynamics or on an oracle that solves a computationally hard planning or estimation problem. Such an oracle leaves an important part of the computation unresolved.

This paper gives an end-to-end algorithm for observable POMDPs without relying on those hard subroutines. Observability has a specific meaning here: sufficiently different distributions over hidden states must produce sufficiently different distributions over observations. This assumption supplies a connection between what differs internally and what the agent can distinguish from its observations.

The algorithm runs in quasipolynomial time. Its exploration strategy uses barycentric spanners to construct policy covers, departing from the customary use of optimism under uncertainty. The contribution is therefore a computationally explicit learning result under the stated observability condition. It replaces an assumed hard oracle with an actual end-to-end procedure, while retaining a qualified runtime guarantee and a clear restriction on the environments considered.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a quasipolynomial-time, oracle-free learning algorithm for POMDPs satisfying a specified observability assumption.

title: Learning in Observable POMDPs, without Computationally Intractable Oracles

abstract: Bound propagation methods, when combined with branch and bound, are among the most effective methods to formally verify properties of deep neural networks such as correctness, robustness, and safety. However, existing works cannot handle the general form of cutting plane constraints widely accepted in traditional solvers, which are crucial for strengthening verifiers with tightened convex relaxations. In this paper, we generalize the bound propagation procedure to allow the addition of arbitrary cutting plane constraints, including those involving relaxed integer variables that do not appear in existing bound propagation formulations. Our generalized bound propagation method, GCP-CROWN, opens up the opportunity to apply general cutting plane methods for neural network verification while benefiting from the efficiency and GPU acceleration of bound propagation methods. As a case study, we investigate the use of cutting planes generated by off-the-shelf mixed integer programming (MIP) solver. We find that MIP solvers can generate high-quality cutting planes for strengthening bound-propagation-based verifiers using our new formulation. Since the branching-focused bound propagation procedure and the cutting-plane-focused MIP solver can run in parallel utilizing different types of hardware (GPUs and CPUs), their combination can quickly explore a large number of branches with strong cutting planes, leading to strong verification performance. Experiments demonstrate that our method is the first verifier that can completely solve the oval20 benchmark and verify twice as many instances on the oval21 benchmark compared to the best tool in VNN-COMP 2021, and also noticeably outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers on a wide range of benchmarks. GCP-CROWN is part of the $\alpha,\beta$-CROWN verifier, the VNN-COMP 2022 winner. Code is available at http://PaperCode.cc/GCP-CROWN.

title: General Cutting Planes for Bound-Propagation-Based Neural Network Verification

abstract: Data poisoning considers an adversary that distorts the training set of machine learning algorithms for malicious purposes. In this work, we bring to light one conjecture regarding the fundamentals of data poisoning, which we call the Lethal Dose Conjecture. The conjecture states: If $n$ clean training samples are needed for accurate predictions, then in a size-$N$ training set, only $\Theta(N/n)$ poisoned samples can be tolerated while ensuring accuracy. Theoretically, we verify this conjecture in multiple cases. We also offer a more general perspective of this conjecture through distribution discrimination. Deep Partition Aggregation (DPA) and its extension, Finite Aggregation (FA) are recent approaches for provable defenses against data poisoning, where they predict through the majority vote of many base models trained from different subsets of training set using a given learner. The conjecture implies that both DPA and FA are (asymptotically) optimal---if we have the most data-efficient learner, they can turn it into one of the most robust defenses against data poisoning. This outlines a practical approach to developing stronger defenses against poisoning via finding data-efficient learners. Empirically, as a proof of concept, we show that by simply using different data augmentations for base learners, we can respectively double and triple the certified robustness of DPA on CIFAR-10 and GTSRB without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Data poisoning attacks alter training examples to damage a learned model. This paper proposes a relationship between resistance to such attacks and the amount of clean data needed for accurate learning. Its Lethal Dose Conjecture says that if accurate prediction requires n clean examples, a training set of size N can tolerate poisoning on the order of N/n examples while retaining accuracy.

The authors verify the conjecture theoretically in multiple cases and develop a broader interpretation through distribution discrimination. It remains a conjecture in general. If it holds, Deep Partition Aggregation and Finite Aggregation are asymptotically optimal when supplied with the most data-efficient learner. These defenses combine votes from models trained on different training subsets.

This conditional result suggests a practical research direction: improve base learners' data efficiency to strengthen poisoning defenses. As a proof of concept, changing data augmentation doubles DPA's certified robustness on CIFAR-10 and triples it on GTSRB without sacrificing accuracy. Those experiments illustrate the proposed connection without constituting a general proof of the conjecture.
summary.tldr: The Lethal Dose Conjecture links poisoning tolerance to clean-data efficiency, with theoretical support in several cases and stronger empirical defenses.

title: Lethal Dose Conjecture on Data Poisoning

abstract: This paper targets at improving the generalizability of hypergraph neural networks in the low-label regime, through applying the contrastive learning approach from images/graphs (we refer to it as HyperGCL). We focus on the following question: How to construct contrastive views for hypergraphs via augmentations? We provide the solutions in two folds. First, guided by domain knowledge, we fabricate two schemes to augment hyperedges with higher-order relations encoded, and adopt three vertex augmentation strategies from graph-structured data. Second, in search of more effective views in a data-driven manner, we for the first time propose a hypergraph generative model to generate augmented views, and then an end-to-end differentiable pipeline to jointly learn hypergraph augmentations and model parameters. Our technical innovations are reflected in designing both fabricated and generative augmentations of hypergraphs. The experimental findings include: (i) Among fabricated augmentations in HyperGCL, augmenting hyperedges provides the most numerical gains, implying that higher-order information in structures is usually more downstream-relevant; (ii) Generative augmentations do better in preserving higher-order information to further benefit generalizability; (iii) HyperGCL also boosts robustness and fairness in hypergraph representation learning. Codes are released at https://github.com/weitianxin/HyperGCL.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of vertices, making their higher-order structure central to learning useful representations. This paper studies how contrastive learning can improve hypergraph neural networks when labels are scarce. Its main question is how to create augmented views that support learning while retaining information useful for downstream tasks.

The proposed HyperGCL approach explores both designed and learned augmentations. The authors construct two hyperedge augmentation schemes using domain knowledge and adapt three vertex augmentation strategies from graph learning. They also introduce a generative hypergraph model that produces augmented views. A differentiable training pipeline allows these augmentations and the neural network parameters to be learned together.

In the experiments, hyperedge changes provide the largest gains among the designed augmentations, suggesting that higher-order structure is often especially relevant to downstream predictions. Generative augmentations preserve that information better and further improve generalization. The authors also report improvements in robustness and fairness. These findings make view construction a substantive modeling choice, rather than merely a preparatory step before contrastive training.
summary.tldr: HyperGCL improves learning with scarce labels by designing or learning hypergraph augmentations that preserve useful higher-order relationships.

title: Augmentations in Hypergraph Contrastive Learning: Fabricated and Generative

abstract: Video-quality measurement is a critical task in video processing. Nowadays, many implementations of new encoding standards - such as AV1, VVC, and LCEVC - use deep-learning-based decoding algorithms with perceptual metrics that serve as optimization objectives. But investigations of the performance of modern video- and image-quality metrics commonly employ videos compressed using older standards, such as AVC. In this paper, we present a new benchmark for video-quality metrics that evaluates video compression. It is based on a new dataset consisting of about 2,500 streams encoded using different standards, including AVC, HEVC, AV1, VP9, and VVC. Subjective scores were collected using crowdsourced pairwise comparisons. The list of evaluated metrics includes recent ones based on machine learning and neural networks. The results demonstrate that new no-reference metrics exhibit high correlation with subjective quality and approach the capability of top full-reference metrics.

Yet evaluations of newer metrics often rely on videos compressed with older standards. This paper introduces a benchmark designed to examine quality measurement across a broader set of compression standards.

The accompanying dataset contains about 2,500 encoded video streams covering AVC, HEVC, AV1, VP9, and VVC. Human judgments are collected through crowdsourced pairwise comparisons, providing subjective scores against which automated metrics can be assessed. The evaluation includes recent methods based on machine learning and neural networks.

The results show that newer no-reference metrics correlate strongly with subjective quality and approach the capability of leading full-reference metrics. No-reference methods assess quality without access to an original reference video, making this comparison especially relevant to their usefulness. summary.tldr: A multi-standard video compression benchmark finds newer no-reference quality metrics approaching leading full-reference methods in agreement with human judgments.

title: Video compression dataset and benchmark of learning-based video-quality metrics

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a general framework for modeling sequential decision making problems, at the core of which lies the dilemma of exploitation and exploration. An agent failing to explore systematically will inevitably fail to learn efficiently. Optimism in the face of uncertainty (OFU) is a conventionally successful strategy for efficient exploration. An agent following the OFU principle explores actively and efficiently. However, when applied to model-based RL, it involves specifying a confidence set of the underlying model and solving a series of nonlinear constrained optimization, which can be computationally intractable. This paper proposes an algorithm, Bayesian optimistic optimization (BOO), which adopts a dynamic weighting technique for enforcing the constraint rather than explicitly solving a constrained optimization problem. BOO is a general algorithm proved to be sample-efficient for models in a finite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We also develop techniques for effective optimization and show through some simulation experiments that BOO is competitive with the existing algorithms.
