paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent must balance using what it knows with exploring uncertain possibilities. Optimism in the face of uncertainty encourages exploration by considering favorable possibilities that remain consistent with available evidence. In model-based reinforcement learning, implementing this idea can require a confidence set of plausible models and repeated nonlinear constrained optimization, which may be computationally intractable.

Bayesian optimistic optimization, or BOO, changes how those constraints are handled. It uses dynamic weighting to enforce the constraint rather than explicitly solving the constrained optimization problem. This preserves the goal of optimistic exploration while changing the computational procedure used to pursue it. The authors also develop techniques intended to make the optimization effective.

The paper proves sample efficiency for models in a finite-dimensional reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a specified mathematical class of models. That condition defines the scope of the stated theoretical guarantee. Simulation experiments find BOO competitive with existing algorithms. Together, the theory and experiments support dynamic weighting as an alternative implementation of optimism for model-based learning.
summary.tldr: BOO uses dynamic weighting to implement optimistic exploration, with a sample-efficiency guarantee for a specified model class and competitive simulation results.

title: Bayesian Optimistic Optimization: Optimistic Exploration for Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a sequence-to-set method that can transform any sequence generative model based on maximum likelihood to a set generative model where we can evaluate the utility/probability of any set. An efficient importance sampling algorithm is devised to tackle the computational challenge of learning our sequence-to-set model. We present GRU2Set, which is an instance of our sequence-to-set method and employs the famous GRU model as the sequence generative model.To further obtain permutation invariant representation of sets, we devise the SetNN model which is also an instance of the sequence-to-set model. A direct application of our models is to learn an order/set distribution from a collection of e-commerce orders, which is an essential step in many important operational decisions such as inventory arrangement for fast delivery. Based on the intuition that small-sized sets are usually easier to learn than large sets, we propose a size-bias trick that can help learn better set distributions with respect to the $\ell_1$-distance evaluation metric. Two e-commerce order datasets, TMALL and HKTVMALL, are used to conduct extensive experiments to show the effectiveness of our models. The experimental results demonstrate that our models can learn better set/order distributions from order data than the baselines. Moreover, no matter what model we use, applying the size-bias trick can always improve the quality of the set distribution learned from data.

paragraphs: Many collections, such as the items in an e-commerce order, are naturally treated as sets rather than ordered sequences. This paper proposes a general method for converting a maximum-likelihood sequence generator into a set generator. The resulting model can evaluate the probability or utility of a set.

Learning the converted model creates a computational challenge, which the authors address with importance sampling. They present GRU2Set as an implementation based on a GRU sequence model and introduce SetNN to obtain representations that are invariant to permutations. They also propose a size-bias technique, motivated by the idea that smaller sets are usually easier to learn, to improve distribution quality measured by L1 distance.

Experiments on TMALL and HKTVMALL order data show better learned set distributions than the evaluated baselines. The size-bias technique improves distribution quality across the models used in the experiments. Learning such order distributions can support operational decisions, including inventory arrangement for faster delivery. The contribution therefore connects sequence-modeling tools with probability estimation for unordered collections.
summary.tldr: A sequence-to-set framework adapts sequence generators to unordered collections and improves e-commerce order-distribution learning in the reported experiments.

title: Sequence-to-Set Generative Models

abstract: In this paper, we propose to use the concept of local fairness for auditing and ranking redistricting plans. Given a redistricting plan, a deviating group is a population-balanced contiguous region in which a majority of individuals are of the same interest and in the minority of their respective districts; such a set of individuals have a justified complaint with how the redistricting plan was drawn. A redistricting plan with no deviating groups is called locally fair. We show that the problem of auditing a given plan for local fairness is NP-complete. We present an MCMC approach for auditing as well as ranking redistricting plans. We also present a dynamic programming based algorithm for the auditing problem that we use to demonstrate the efficacy of our MCMC approach. Using these tools, we test local fairness on real-world election data, showing that it is indeed possible to find plans that are almost or exactly locally fair. Further, we show that such plans can be generated while sacrificing very little in terms of compactness and existing fairness measures such as competitiveness of the districts or seat shares of the plans.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a local criterion for evaluating electoral district plans. A complaint arises when a contiguous, population-balanced region contains a majority sharing an interest whose members are minorities in their assigned districts. Such a region is called a deviating group. A plan is locally fair when no group meeting this definition exists.

This criterion examines how district boundaries divide geographically connected populations with shared interests. The authors prove that auditing a plan for local fairness is NP-complete, establishing a computational obstacle to checking the condition in general. They develop an MCMC approach for auditing and ranking plans, alongside a dynamic-programming auditing algorithm used to assess the MCMC method’s effectiveness.

Tests using real election data find plans that are exactly or nearly locally fair. The authors also show that such plans can be produced with little sacrifice in compactness, district competitiveness, or plan-level seat shares in the examined settings. The findings make local fairness a practical additional perspective for evaluating redistricting, with evidence that it can coexist with established criteria rather than necessarily demanding large tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: The paper defines local fairness for redistricting and develops methods that find nearly or exactly fair plans in real election data.

title: All Politics is Local: Redistricting via Local Fairness

abstract: Due to its high sample complexity, simulation is, as of today, critical for the successful application of reinforcement learning. Many real-world problems, however, exhibit overly complex dynamics, making their full-scale simulation computationally slow. In this paper, we show how to factorize large networked systems of many agents into multiple local regions such that we can build separate simulators that run independently and in parallel. To monitor the influence that the different local regions exert on one another, each of these simulators is equipped with a learned model that is periodically trained on real trajectories. Our empirical results reveal that distributing the simulation among different processes not only makes it possible to train large multi-agent systems in just a few hours but also helps mitigate the negative effects of simultaneous learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often needs extensive simulation, but simulating an entire large networked system can be slow because of its complex dynamics. This paper addresses that computational bottleneck for systems containing many agents. It divides the system into local regions so that separate simulators can run independently and in parallel.

The local regions still exert influence on one another. To represent those effects, each local simulator includes a learned influence model that is periodically trained on real trajectories. This is the central design choice: local simulation is made independent at execution time while learned models account for interactions beyond each region.

The empirical results show that distributing simulation across processes enables training of large multi-agent systems within a few hours in the studied settings. The authors also find that the approach reduces negative effects associated with agents learning simultaneously. Its significance therefore extends beyond simulation speed: the local construction also helps with the interaction between multiple changing learners.
summary.tldr: Parallel local simulators with learned cross-region influence models accelerate multi-agent training and empirically reduce problems caused by simultaneous learning.

title: Distributed Influence-Augmented Local Simulators for Parallel MARL in Large Networked Systems

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have shown substantial promise in processing spatio-temporal data, mimicking biological neuronal mechanisms, and saving computational power. However, most SNNs use fixed model regardless of their locations in the network. This limits SNNs’ capability of transmitting precise information in the network, which becomes worse for deeper SNNs. Some researchers try to use specified parametric models in different network layers or regions, but most still use preset or suboptimal parameters. Inspired by the neuroscience observation that different neuronal mechanisms exist in disparate brain regions, we propose a new spiking neuronal mechanism, named learnable thresholding, to address this issue. Utilizing learnable threshold values, learnable thresholding enables flexible neuronal mechanisms across layers, proper information flow within the network, and fast network convergence. In addition, we propose a moderate dropout method to serve as an enhancement technique to minimize inconsistencies between independent dropout runs. Finally, we evaluate the robustness of the proposed learnable thresholding and moderate dropout for image classification with different initial thresholds for various types of datasets. Our proposed methods produce superior results compared to other approaches for almost all datasets with fewer timesteps. Our codes are available at https://github.com/sq117/LTMD.git.

Inspired by differences between neuronal mechanisms across brain regions, they propose learning the thresholds that govern spiking behavior instead of relying on preset values.

Learnable thresholding allows neuronal behavior to vary across layers through training. The intended benefits are more appropriate information flow and faster convergence. The paper also introduces moderate dropout, an additional training technique designed to reduce inconsistencies between independent dropout runs. Together, the two methods address both the behavior of individual neurons and variability introduced during training.

The authors evaluate image classification across different kinds of datasets and initial threshold settings. Their methods outperform comparison approaches on almost all evaluated datasets while using fewer timesteps. The result supports adapting thresholds as a useful part of training spiking networks, with moderate dropout providing a complementary enhancement. The reported superiority remains an empirical finding across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Learnable spiking thresholds and moderate dropout improve image-classification results on almost all tested datasets while requiring fewer timesteps.

title: LTMD: Learning Improvement of Spiking Neural Networks with Learnable Thresholding Neurons and Moderate Dropout

abstract: This paper investigates the network load balancing problem in data centers (DCs) where multiple load balancers (LBs) are deployed, using the multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework. The challenges of this problem consist of the heterogeneous processing architecture and dynamic environments, as well as limited and partial observability of each LB agent in distributed networking systems, which can largely degrade the performance of in-production load balancing algorithms in real-world setups. Centralised training and distributed execution (CTDE) RL scheme has been proposed to improve MARL performance, yet it incurs -- especially in distributed networking systems, which prefer distributed and plug-and-play design schemes -- additional communication and management overhead among agents. We formulate the multi-agent load balancing problem as a Markov potential game, with a carefully and properly designed workload distribution fairness as the potential function. A fully distributed MARL algorithm is proposed to approximate the Nash equilibrium of the game. Experimental evaluations involve both an event-driven simulator and a real-world system, where the proposed MARL load balancing algorithm shows close-to-optimal performance in simulations and superior results over in-production LBs in the real-world system.

paragraphs: Data centers may use several load balancers to distribute work across heterogeneous processing resources. Each balancer sees only part of a changing system, complicating coordinated decisions. Although centralized training can help multi-agent reinforcement learning, it adds communication and management overhead in networking systems that favor distributed components and straightforward deployment.

This paper models load balancing as a Markov potential game. Its potential function is a carefully designed measure of fairness in workload distribution, linking the agents' decisions to a shared system-level quantity. The authors then propose a fully distributed multi-agent learning algorithm that approximates a Nash equilibrium of this game, where individual agents have little incentive to change their policies unilaterally.

Evaluation uses both an event-driven simulator and a real system. The method achieves close-to-optimal performance in simulation and outperforms production load balancers in the real-system tests. Here, fairness refers to how workloads are distributed. The results suggest that this game-based formulation can support effective coordination while accommodating the distributed operation of the network.
summary.tldr: A fully distributed reinforcement-learning method uses workload fairness to coordinate load balancers and performs strongly in simulations and a real system.

title: Learning Distributed and Fair Policies for Network Load Balancing as Markov Potential Game

abstract: In this paper, we study multi-block min-max bilevel optimization problems, where the upper level is non-convex strongly-concave minimax objective and the lower level is a strongly convex objective, and there are multiple blocks of dual variables and lower level problems. Due to the intertwined multi-block min-max bilevel structure, the computational cost at each iteration could be prohibitively high, especially with a large number of blocks. To tackle this challenge, we present two single-loop randomized stochastic algorithms, which require updates for only a constant number of blocks at each iteration. Under some mild assumptions on the problem, we establish their sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^4)$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point. This matches the optimal complexity order for solving stochastic nonconvex optimization under a general unbiased stochastic oracle model. Moreover, we provide two applications of the proposed method in multi-task deep AUC (area under ROC curve) maximization. Experimental results validate our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

This paper studies a version containing many blocks of dual variables and lower-level problems. Its upper objective is nonconvex and strongly concave in the respective variables, while the lower objectives are strongly convex. Updating all blocks can make each iteration expensive.

The authors propose two randomized stochastic algorithms that operate in a single loop. Each iteration updates only a constant number of blocks, addressing the cost associated with having many coupled components. Under the paper's assumptions, both algorithms require O(1/epsilon⁴) samples to find an epsilon-stationary point, a solution meeting an approximate stationarity criterion.

That complexity order matches the optimal order for general stochastic nonconvex optimization under an unbiased stochastic oracle model. The guarantee concerns stationarity under the stated structure and assumptions. The authors also give two applications in multi-task deep AUC maximization, where the learning objective concerns area under the ROC curve. Experimental results support the theory and demonstrate the methods' effectiveness on these applications.
summary.tldr: Two randomized algorithms reduce per-iteration block updates while retaining a conditional O(1/epsilon⁴) sample-complexity guarantee.

title: Multi-block Min-max Bilevel Optimization with Applications in Multi-task Deep AUC Maximization

abstract: Associative memory plays an important role in human intelligence and its mechanisms have been linked to attention in machine learning. While the machine learning community's interest in associative memories has recently been rekindled, most work has focused on memory recall ($read$) over memory learning ($write$). In this paper, we present BayesPCN, a hierarchical associative memory capable of performing continual one-shot memory writes without meta-learning. Moreover, BayesPCN is able to gradually forget past observations ($forget$) to free its memory. Experiments show that BayesPCN can recall corrupted i.i.d. high-dimensional data observed hundreds to a thousand ``timesteps'' ago without a large drop in recall ability compared to the state-of-the-art offline-learned parametric memory models.

paragraphs: An associative memory retrieves a stored observation from an incomplete or corrupted version of it. The paper argues that recent machine-learning work has emphasized retrieval more than the process of adding new memories. BayesPCN addresses the writing side by introducing a hierarchical memory that can continually store observations after seeing them once, without relying on meta-learning.

The model also supports gradual forgetting of previous observations to free memory. Writing, recall, and forgetting therefore appear as complementary capabilities of the same system. This matters for continual memory use: the model is designed to incorporate incoming observations over time, while also providing a mechanism for releasing capacity occupied by older ones.

Experiments examine recall of corrupted, high-dimensional observations drawn independently from the same distribution. BayesPCN retrieves data encountered hundreds to a thousand time steps earlier without a large decline in recall relative to leading parametric memories trained offline. The stated finding is that continual one-shot writing can coexist with strong delayed recall in this experimental setting, bringing attention to how memories are learned as well as read.
summary.tldr: BayesPCN combines continual one-shot memory writing, gradual forgetting, and strong recall of corrupted observations from hundreds of time steps earlier.

title: BayesPCN: A Continually Learnable Predictive Coding Associative Memory

abstract: We present CELL-E 2, a novel bidirectional transformer that can generate images depicting protein subcellular localization from the amino acid sequences (and vice versa). Protein localization is a challenging problem that requires integrating sequence and image information, which most existing methods ignore. CELL-E 2 extends the work of CELL-E, not only capturing the spatial complexity of protein localization and produce probability estimates of localization atop a nucleus image, but also being able to generate sequences from images, enabling de novo protein design. We train and finetune CELL-E 2 on two large-scale datasets of human proteins. We also demonstrate how to use CELL-E 2 to create hundreds of novel nuclear localization signals (NLS). Results and interactive demos are featured at https://bohuanglab.github.io/CELL-E_2/.

paragraphs: CELL-E 2 connects two ways of describing a protein: its amino acid sequence and images showing where it localizes inside a cell. The paper treats localization as a problem requiring both sequence information and spatial information. Its transformer works in both directions, generating localization images from sequences and generating sequences from images.

Building on CELL-E, the model represents the spatial complexity of localization and produces probability estimates over a nucleus image. This gives the sequence-to-image direction a spatial output, showing how localization is distributed in the image. The reverse direction supports de novo protein design by allowing image information to guide the generation of new sequences.

This application illustrates how a bidirectional model can connect localization prediction with sequence generation. The stated contribution is the ability to move between these representations and use that connection for design; the abstract does not claim experimental biological validation of every generated signal.
summary.tldr: CELL-E 2 translates between protein sequences and localization images, supporting spatial prediction and generation of new protein sequences.

title: CELLE-2: Translating Proteins to Pictures and Back with a Bidirectional Text-to-Image Transformer

abstract: Robust fine-tuning aims to achieve competitive in-distribution (ID) performance while maintaining the out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness of a pre-trained model when transferring it to a downstream task. Recently, projected gradient descent has been successfully used in robust fine-tuning by constraining the deviation from the initialization of the fine-tuned model explicitly through projection. However, algorithmically, two limitations prevent this method from being adopted more widely, scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we propose a new projection-based fine-tuning algorithm, Fast Trainable Projection (FTP) for computationally efficient learning of per-layer projection constraints, resulting in an average 35% speedup on our benchmarks compared to prior works. FTP can be combined with existing optimizers such as AdamW, and be used in a plug-and-play fashion. Finally, we show that FTP is a special instance of hyper-optimizers that tune the hyper-parameters of optimizers in a learnable manner through nested differentiation. Empirically, we show superior robustness on OOD datasets, including domain shifts and natural corruptions, across four different vision tasks with five different pre-trained models. Additionally, we demonstrate that FTP is broadly applicable and beneficial to other learning scenarios such as low-label and continual learning settings thanks to its easy adaptability. The code will be available at https://github.com/GT-RIPL/FTP.git.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained model should improve performance on a downstream task while preserving its ability to handle unfamiliar data. Projection-based methods pursue this balance by explicitly restricting how far the updated model can move from its initial parameters. The paper addresses the scalability and efficiency problems that can make this approach difficult to use.

Fast Trainable Projection, or FTP, efficiently learns separate projection constraints for different layers. It can work with existing optimizers such as AdamW, making it usable as an addition to established training procedures. The authors also connect FTP to hyper-optimizers: methods that learn optimizer hyperparameters through nested differentiation.

On the reported benchmarks, FTP delivers an average 35% speedup over prior work. Experiments across four vision tasks and five pretrained models show superior robustness to domain shifts and natural corruptions. The authors also demonstrate benefits in low-label and continual learning settings. Together, these findings suggest that learning how tightly to constrain each layer can make robust fine-tuning both more practical and more effective in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FTP efficiently learns layer-specific projection constraints, improving robust fine-tuning with an average 35% benchmark speedup over prior work.

title: Fast Trainable Projection for Robust Fine-tuning

abstract: Estimating frequencies of elements appearing in a data stream is a key task in large-scale data analysis. Popular sketching approaches to this problem (e.g., CountMin and CountSketch) come with worst-case guarantees that probabilistically bound the error of the estimated frequencies for any possible input. The work of Hsu et al.~(2019) introduced the idea of using machine learning to tailor sketching algorithms to the specific data distribution they are being run on. In particular, their learning-augmented frequency estimation algorithm uses a learned heavy-hitter oracle which predicts which elements will appear many times in the stream. We give a novel algorithm, which in some parameter regimes, already theoretically outperforms the learning based algorithm of Hsu et al. *without* the use of any predictions. Augmenting our algorithm with heavy-hitter predictions further reduces the error and improves upon the state of the art. Empirically, our algorithms achieve superior performance in all experiments compared to prior approaches.

paragraphs: Frequency estimation asks how often each element appears in a data stream. Sketching algorithms provide probabilistic error guarantees for arbitrary inputs, while learning-augmented approaches try to improve estimates by exploiting the particular distribution being processed. One existing approach uses predictions of heavy hitters: elements expected to occur especially frequently in the stream.

This paper introduces a new algorithm that can improve on that earlier learning-based method even without predictions. The theoretical improvement holds in some parameter regimes, so the claim is conditional rather than a blanket advantage across all settings. Adding heavy-hitter predictions to the new algorithm reduces error further and improves on the state of the art.

The authors also report superior performance over prior approaches in every experiment they conducted. The results separate two sources of progress: a stronger underlying estimation algorithm and an additional benefit from learned predictions. This distinction matters when assessing learning-augmented methods, because improvements in the algorithm itself can change how much advantage should be attributed to the predictive component.
summary.tldr: A new frequency estimator improves on an earlier prediction-based method in some regimes without predictions, and benefits further from heavy-hitter forecasts.

title: Improved Frequency Estimation Algorithms with and without Predictions

abstract: Various deep learning models have been proposed for 3D bone shape reconstruction from two orthogonal (biplanar) X-ray images.However, it is unclear how these models compare against each other since they are evaluated on different anatomy, cohort and (often privately held) datasets.Moreover, the impact of the commonly optimized image-based segmentation metrics such as dice score on the estimation of clinical parameters relevant in 2D-3D bone shape reconstruction is not well known.To move closer toward clinical translation, we propose a benchmarking framework that evaluates tasks relevant to real-world clinical scenarios, including reconstruction of fractured bones, bones with implants, robustness to population shift, and error in estimating clinical parameters.Our open-source platform provides reference implementations of 8 models (many of whose implementations were not publicly available), APIs to easily collect and preprocess 6 public datasets, and the implementation of automatic clinical parameter and landmark extraction methods. We present an extensive evaluation of 8 2D-3D models on equal footing using 6 public datasets comprising images for four different anatomies.Our results show that attention-based methods that capture global spatial relationships tend to perform better across all anatomies and datasets; performance on clinically relevant subgroups may be overestimated without disaggregated reporting; ribs are substantially more difficult to reconstruct compared to femur, hip and spine; and the dice score improvement does not always bring corresponding improvement in the automatic estimation of clinically relevant parameters.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a bone’s three-dimensional shape from two perpendicular X-rays has attracted many deep learning approaches. Comparing them is difficult when studies use different anatomies, patient groups, and private datasets. This paper establishes a shared benchmark so that reconstruction models can be evaluated on comparable data and on outcomes relevant to clinical use.

The platform supplies reference implementations of eight models, tools to collect and preprocess six public datasets, and automatic extraction of clinical parameters and landmarks. Its evaluations cover four anatomies and include fractured bones, implants, changes in the population being evaluated, and errors in clinical measurements. This broadens comparison beyond a single image segmentation score.

Attention-based models that capture global spatial relationships tend to perform better across the evaluated datasets and anatomies. Ribs prove substantially harder than femur, hip, and spine. The authors also find that aggregate results can overestimate performance for clinically relevant subgroups, and better Dice scores do not always yield better clinical measurements. The findings make the choice of evaluation target consequential.
summary.tldr: A shared benchmark compares eight X-ray-to-3D reconstruction models and shows why clinical measurements and subgroup results matter alongside segmentation scores.

title: Benchmarking Encoder-Decoder Architectures for Biplanar X-ray to 3D Bone Shape Reconstruction

abstract: Continual learning entails learning a sequence of tasks and balancing their knowledge appropriately. With limited access to old training samples, much of the current work in deep neural networks has focused on overcoming catastrophic forgetting of old tasks in gradient-based optimization. However, the normalization layers provide an exception, as they are updated interdependently by the gradient and statistics of currently observed training samples, which require specialized strategies to mitigate recency bias. In this work, we focus on the most popular Batch Normalization (BN) and provide an in-depth theoretical analysis of its sub-optimality in continual learning. Our analysis demonstrates the dilemma between balance and adaptation of BN statistics for incremental tasks, which potentially affects training stability and generalization. Targeting on these particular challenges, we propose Adaptive Balance of BN (AdaB$^2$N), which incorporates appropriately a Bayesian-based strategy to adapt task-wise contributions and a modified momentum to balance BN statistics, corresponding to the training and testing stages. By implementing BN in a continual learning fashion, our approach achieves significant performance gains across a wide range of benchmarks, particularly for the challenging yet realistic online scenarios (e.g., up to 7.68\%, 6.86\% and 4.26\% on Split CIFAR-10, Split CIFAR-100 and Split Mini-ImageNet, respectively). Our code is available at https://github.com/lvyilin/AdaB2N.

Its behavior depends jointly on gradient updates and statistics from currently observed samples, creating a problem that requires attention beyond ordinary weight optimization.

The authors theoretically analyze a dilemma between adapting normalization statistics to new tasks and balancing contributions from earlier ones. This tension can affect training stability and generalization. Their method, Adaptive Balance of BN, combines a Bayesian strategy for adjusting task-wise contributions with modified momentum for balancing statistics, addressing training and testing respectively.

Experiments show significant gains across multiple continual learning benchmarks, especially online settings. The reported maximum improvements are 7.68% on Split CIFAR-10, 6.86% on Split CIFAR-100, and 4.26% on Split Mini-ImageNet. These findings identify normalization statistics as an important part of continual learning and support explicitly managing how successive tasks contribute to them.
summary.tldr: AdaB²N reduces recency bias in continual learning by adapting task contributions and balancing Batch Normalization statistics.

title: Overcoming Recency Bias of Normalization Statistics in Continual Learning: Balance and Adaptation

abstract: We study the problem of learning mixtures of linear classifiers under Gaussian covariates.Given sample access to a mixture of $r$ distributions on $\mathbb{R}^n$ of the form $(\mathbf{x},y_{\ell})$, $\ell \in [r]$,where $\mathbf{x}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_n)$ and$y_\ell=\mathrm{sign}(\langle\mathbf{v}_{\ell},\mathbf{x}\rangle)$for an unknown unit vector $\mathbf{v}_{\ell}$,the goal is to learn the underlying distribution in total variation distance. Our main result is a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound suggesting that known algorithms for this problem are essentially best possible,even for the special case of uniform mixtures.In particular, we show that the complexity of any SQ algorithm for the problem is $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\Delta) \log(r)}$,where $\Delta$ is a lower bound on the pairwise $\ell_2$-separation between the $\mathbf{v}_{\ell}$'s.The key technical ingredient underlying our result is a new construction of spherical designs on the unit sphere that may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies data generated by a mixture of linear classifiers. Inputs follow a standard Gaussian distribution, and each component labels an input according to which side of an unknown linear boundary it lies on. The goal is to learn the joint data distribution accurately in total variation distance, given samples from the mixture.

The main result establishes a lower bound in the Statistical Query framework. Its complexity dependence has the form n raised to poly(1/Δ) times log(r), where n is the input dimension, r is the number of mixture components, and Δ lower-bounds the separation between their direction vectors. The result applies even when all mixture components have equal weight.

This bound suggests that known algorithms are essentially optimal within the stated framework, revealing a substantial barrier to more efficient learning as the mixture structure becomes harder. The proof relies on a new construction of spherical designs on the unit sphere. That construction is also presented as a mathematical contribution that may be useful independently of this learning problem.
summary.tldr: A Statistical Query lower bound suggests existing methods for learning Gaussian-input mixtures of linear classifiers are essentially optimal.

title: SQ Lower Bounds for Learning Mixtures of Linear Classifiers

abstract: In the quest to advance human-centric natural language generation (NLG) systems, ensuring alignment between NLG models and human preferences is crucial. For this alignment, current popular methods leverage a reinforcement learning (RL) approach with a reward model trained on feedback from humans. However, inherent disagreements due to the subjective nature of human preferences pose a significant challenge for training the reward model, resulting in a deterioration of the NLG performance. To tackle this issue, previous approaches typically rely on majority voting or averaging to consolidate multiple inconsistent preferences into a merged one. Although straightforward to understand and execute, such methods suffer from an inability to capture the nuanced degrees of disaggregation among humans and may only represent a specialized subset of individuals, thereby lacking the ability to quantitatively disclose the universality of human preferences. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel approach, which employs a Bayesian framework to account for the distribution of disagreements among human preferences as training a preference model, and names it as $\textbf{d-PM}$. Besides, considering the RL strategy's inefficient and complex training process over the training efficiency, we further propose utilizing the contrastive learning strategy to train the NLG model with the preference scores derived from the d-PM model. Extensive experiments on two human-centric NLG tasks, i.e., emotional support conversation and integrity ``Rule-of-Thumb'' generation, show that our method consistently exceeds previous SOTA models in both automatic and human evaluations.

paragraphs: Human preferences can disagree even when people judge the same language output. This creates a challenge for systems that learn a reward model from feedback and then optimize generated text against it. Collapsing judgments through majority voting or averaging can hide the extent of disagreement and produce a preference signal that mainly reflects a subset of people.

The paper proposes d-PM, a Bayesian preference model that accounts for the distribution of disagreement during training. This makes variation across human judgments part of the modeling problem. The authors then use scores from d-PM to train the language generation model through contrastive learning, addressing the complexity and inefficiency they associate with reinforcement learning training.

Experiments cover emotional support conversations and the generation of integrity-related rules of thumb. The method consistently exceeds previous state-of-the-art models in both automatic measures and human evaluations on these tasks. The findings support preserving information about disagreement when constructing the preference signal used to guide generation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian preference model captures human disagreement and supplies scores for contrastive training that improves results on two language generation tasks.

title: Aligning Language Models with Human Preferences via a Bayesian Approach

abstract: Black-box hard-label adversarial attack on text is a practical and challenging task, as the text data space is inherently discrete and non-differentiable, and only the predicted label is accessible. Research on this problem is still in the embryonic stage and only a few methods are available. Nevertheless, existing methods rely on the complex heuristic algorithm or unreliable gradient estimation strategy, which probably fall into the local optimum and inevitably consume numerous queries, thus are difficult to craft satisfactory adversarial examples with high semantic similarity and low perturbation rate in a limited query budget. To alleviate above issues, we propose a simple yet effective framework to generate high quality textual adversarial examples under the black-box hard-label attack scenarios, named HQA-Attack. Specifically, after initializing an adversarial example randomly, HQA-attack first constantly substitutes original words back as many as possible, thus shrinking the perturbation rate. Then it leverages the synonym set of the remaining changed words to further optimize the adversarial example with the direction which can improve the semantic similarity and satisfy the adversarial condition simultaneously. In addition, during the optimizing procedure, it searches a transition synonym word for each changed word, thus avoiding traversing the whole synonym set and reducing the query number to some extent. Extensive experimental results on five text classification datasets, three natural language inference datasets and two real-world APIs have shown that the proposed HQA-Attack method outperforms other strong baselines significantly.

paragraphs: A hard-label text attack attempts to change a model’s prediction while seeing only its predicted class. It has no access to confidence scores, and text changes are discrete. The challenge is to create an adversarial example that preserves meaning, changes few words, and requires relatively few model queries.

HQA-Attack begins with a randomly initialized adversarial example and repeatedly restores original words wherever possible. This reduces the amount of altered text. It then searches synonyms for the words that remain changed, seeking improvements in semantic similarity while preserving the adversarial outcome. The process therefore balances textual fidelity with the requirement that the model still makes the targeted error.

To reduce queries, the method searches for an intermediate synonym for each changed word instead of traversing the entire synonym set. Evaluations cover five text-classification datasets, three natural-language-inference datasets, and two real-world APIs. The authors report significant improvements over strong baselines. These findings support the proposed sequence of restoring words and refining substitutions as an effective approach under the tested hard-label conditions.
summary.tldr: HQA-Attack refines word substitutions to produce meaning-preserving adversarial text using only predicted labels and fewer unnecessary queries.

title: HQA-Attack: Toward High Quality Black-Box Hard-Label Adversarial Attack on Text

abstract: Training reliable deep learning models which avoid making overconfident but incorrect predictions is a longstanding challenge. This challenge is further exacerbated when learning has to be differentially private: protection provided to sensitive data comes at the price of injecting additional randomness into the learning process. In this work, we conduct a thorough empirical investigation of selective classifiers---that can abstain under uncertainty---under a differential privacy constraint. We find that some popular selective prediction approaches are ineffective in a differentially private setting because they increase the risk of privacy leakage. At the same time, we identify that a recent approach that only uses checkpoints produced by an off-the-shelf private learning algorithm stands out as particularly suitable under DP. Further, we show that differential privacy does not just harm utility but also degrades selective classification performance. To analyze this effect across privacy levels, we propose a novel evaluation mechanism which isolates selective prediction performance across model utility levels at full coverage. Our experimental results show that recovering the performance level attainable by non-private models is possible but comes at a considerable coverage cost as the privacy budget decreases.

paragraphs: Selective classifiers can decline to answer when uncertain, aiming to avoid confident mistakes. Differential privacy complicates this goal because private training adds randomness. The paper empirically studies how abstention methods behave under privacy constraints, considering both their suitability for privacy protection and their ability to distinguish reliable predictions.

Some popular selective prediction methods are found unsuitable because they increase privacy-leakage risk. A recent method using only checkpoints from an off-the-shelf private training algorithm is particularly suitable. The study also finds that privacy degrades selective classification performance as well as ordinary predictive utility. A proposed evaluation mechanism separates selective prediction behavior across different levels of full-coverage model utility.

The experiments show that private models can recover performance levels attainable by non-private models, but doing so requires a substantial reduction in coverage as the privacy budget decreases. Coverage is the share of cases on which a model answers. The findings therefore expose a practical tradeoff: stronger privacy can require abstaining on considerably more inputs to retain comparable predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Private selective classifiers can recover non-private performance in experiments, but stronger privacy demands substantially more abstention.

title: Training Private Models That Know What They Don’t Know

abstract: Input gradients have a pivotal role in a variety of applications, including adversarial attack algorithms for evaluating model robustness, explainable AI techniques for generating saliency maps, and counterfactual explanations. However, saliency maps generated by traditional neural networks are often noisy and provide limited insights. In this paper, we demonstrate that, on the contrary, the saliency maps of 1-Lipschitz neural networks, learnt with the dual loss of an optimal transportation problem, exhibit desirable XAI properties:They are highly concentrated on the essential parts of the image with low noise, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art explanation approaches across various models and metrics. We also prove that these maps align unprecedentedly well with human explanations on ImageNet. To explain the particularly beneficial properties of the saliency map for such models, we prove this gradient encodes both the direction of the transportation plan and the direction towards the nearest adversarial attack. Following the gradient down to the decision boundary is no longer considered an adversarial attack, but rather a counterfactual explanation that explicitly transports the input from one class to another. Thus, Learning with such a loss jointly optimizes the classification objective and the alignment of the gradient , i.e. the saliency map, to the transportation plan direction. These networks were previously known to be certifiably robust by design, and we demonstrate that they scale well for large problems and models, and are tailored for explainability using a fast and straightforward method.

paragraphs: Input gradients describe how a neural network's output changes as its input changes, making them useful for visual explanations and robustness analysis. In conventional networks, gradient-based saliency maps can be noisy. This paper studies 1-Lipschitz networks trained with the dual loss of an optimal transport problem and finds that their gradients provide particularly useful explanations.

The authors prove that the gradient encodes both the direction of a transport plan and the direction toward the nearest adversarial attack. This gives the gradient a geometric meaning tied to movement between classes. Following it toward the decision boundary can therefore be interpreted as a counterfactual explanation showing how an input is transported from one class toward another.

The reported saliency maps concentrate on essential image regions with little noise and outperform state-of-the-art explanation approaches across the evaluated models and metrics. The authors also establish strong alignment with human explanations on ImageNet and demonstrate scaling to large models and problems. The contribution connects the training objective, classification behavior, and explanatory gradient within networks already known for certified robustness.
summary.tldr: Optimal-transport training gives 1-Lipschitz networks informative gradients, connecting clear saliency maps to transport directions and counterfactual explanations.

title: On the explainable properties of 1-Lipschitz Neural Networks: An Optimal Transport Perspective

abstract: In the current landscape of pervasive smartphones and tablets, apps frequently exist across both platforms.Although apps share most graphic user interfaces (GUIs) and functionalities across phones and tablets, developers often rebuild from scratch for tablet versions, escalating costs and squandering existing design resources.Researchers are attempting to collect data and employ deep learning in automated GUIs development to enhance developers' productivity.There are currently several publicly accessible GUI page datasets for phones, but none for pairwise GUIs between phones and tablets.This poses a significant barrier to the employment of deep learning in automated GUI development.In this paper, we introduce the Papt dataset, a pioneering pairwise GUI dataset tailored for Android phones and tablets, encompassing 10,035 phone-tablet GUI page pairs sourced from 5,593 unique app pairs.We propose novel pairwise GUI collection approaches for constructing this dataset and delineate its advantages over currently prevailing datasets in the field.Through preliminary experiments on this dataset, we analyze the present challenges of utilizing deep learning in automated GUI development.

paragraphs: Phone and tablet versions of an application often share functionality and much of their interface design. Nevertheless, developers may rebuild tablet interfaces from scratch, increasing effort and leaving existing design work underused. Research on automating this process needs examples of corresponding interfaces across devices, rather than collections containing only phone screens.

The paper introduces Papt, a dataset of paired Android phone and tablet graphical interfaces. It contains 10,035 page pairs drawn from 5,593 distinct application pairs. Pairing is the central contribution: each example connects the two device-specific interfaces, providing data for studying their relationship. The authors also propose new approaches for collecting these paired pages.

The work describes advantages over existing interface datasets and uses preliminary experiments to examine challenges in deep-learning-based interface development. Its main result is a research resource and a collection methodology, alongside an initial investigation of the automation problem. This gives researchers paired evidence for studying interface reuse across phones and tablets, an area the authors identify as lacking publicly available datasets.
summary.tldr: Papt provides paired Android phone and tablet interface pages to support research on automated cross-device interface development.

title: Pairwise GUI Dataset Construction Between Android Phones and Tablets

abstract: Large language models have shown tremendous performance in a variety of tasks. In-context learning -- the ability to improve at a task after being provided with a number of demonstrations -- is seen as one of the main contributors to their success. In the present paper, we demonstrate that the in-context learning abilities of large language models can be recursively improved via in-context learning itself. We coin this phenomenon meta-in-context learning. Looking at two idealized domains, a one-dimensional regression task and a two-armed bandit task, we show that meta-in-context learning adaptively reshapes a large language model's priors over expected tasks. Furthermore, we find that meta-in-context learning modifies the in-context learning strategies of such models. Finally, we broaden the scope of our investigation to encompass two diverse benchmarks: one focusing on real-world regression problems and the other encompassing multiple NLP tasks. In both cases, we observe competitive performance comparable to that of traditional learning algorithms. Taken together, our work improves our understanding of in-context learning and paves the way toward adapting large language models to the environment they are applied purely through meta-in-context learning rather than traditional finetuning.

The authors call the resulting phenomenon meta-in-context learning: contextual experience changes how the model learns from subsequent examples.

The study first examines two idealized settings, one-dimensional regression and a two-armed bandit task. In these settings, meta-in-context learning reshapes the model's prior expectations about the tasks it will encounter. It also changes the strategies the model uses for in-context learning, showing effects on both its expectations and its learning behavior.

The authors then examine benchmarks covering real-world regression and multiple natural language processing tasks. In both, they report performance competitive with traditional learning algorithms. Together, the findings support contextual adaptation as a route toward matching language models to their environments. The demonstrated contribution concerns modifying learning behavior through context, with broader environment adaptation presented as a direction enabled by those results.
summary.tldr: Language models can use context to change their task expectations and improve how they learn from further demonstrations.

title: Meta-in-context learning in large language models

abstract: Deep learning practice is increasingly driven by powerful foundation models (FM), pre-trained at scale and then fine-tuned for specific tasks of interest. A key property of this workflow is the efficacy of performing sparse or parameter-efficient fine-tuning, meaning that by updating only a tiny fraction of the whole FM parameters on a downstream task can lead to surprisingly good performance, often even superior to a full model update. However, it is not clear what is the optimal and principled way to select which parameters to update. Although a growing number of sparse fine-tuning ideas have been proposed, they are mostly not satisfactory, relying on hand-crafted heuristics or heavy approximation. In this paper we propose a novel Bayesian sparse fine-tuning algorithm: we place a (sparse) Laplace prior for each parameter of the FM, with the mean equal to the initial value and the scale parameter having a hyper-prior that encourages small scale. Roughly speaking, the posterior means of the scale parameters indicate how important it is to update the corresponding parameter away from its initial value when solving the downstream task. Given the sparse prior, most scale parameters are small a posteriori, and the few large-valued scale parameters identify those FM parameters that crucially need to be updated away from their initial values. Based on this, we can threshold the scale parameters to decide which parameters to update or freeze, leading to a principled sparse fine-tuning strategy. To efficiently infer the posterior distribution of the scale parameters, we adopt the Langevin MCMC sampler, requiring only two times the complexity of the vanilla SGD. Tested on popular NLP benchmarks as well as the VTAB vision tasks, our approach shows significant improvement over the state-of-the-arts (e.g., 1% point higher than the best SOTA when fine-tuning RoBERTa for GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks).

title: BayesTune: Bayesian Sparse Deep Model Fine-tuning

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated promising results in various applications by learning policies from previously collected datasets, reducing the need for online exploration and interactions. However, real-world scenarios usually involve partial observability, which brings crucial challenges of the deployment of offline RL methods: i) the policy trained on data with full observability is not robust against the masked observations during execution, and ii) the information of which parts of observations are masked is usually unknown during training. In order to address these challenges, we present Offline RL with DiscrEte pRoxy representations (ORDER), a probabilistic framework which leverages novel state representations to improve the robustness against diverse masked observabilities. Specifically, we propose a discrete representation of the states and use a proxy representation to recover the states from masked partial observable trajectories. The training of ORDER can be compactly described as the following three steps. i) Learning the discrete state representations on data with full observations, ii) Training the decision module based on the discrete representations, and iii) Training the proxy discrete representations on the data with various partial observations, aligning with the discrete representations. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate ORDER, showcasing its effectiveness in offline RL for diverse partially observable scenarios and highlighting the significance of discrete proxy representations in generalization performance.ORDER is a flexible framework to employ any offline RL algorithms and we hope that ORDER can pave the way for the deployment of RL policy against various partial observabilities in the real world.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data, but deployment may hide information that was available during training. A policy trained with complete observations can then become unreliable. The challenge is greater when the particular observation components that will be missing are unknown in advance.

ORDER addresses this problem through discrete state representations and proxy representations inferred from partially observed trajectories. Training first learns discrete representations from fully observed data, then trains a decision module using those representations. A third stage learns proxy representations from data with varied partial observations, aligning them with the representations obtained from complete observations.

The alignment gives the decision module a common representational target even when its available observations change. Experiments across diverse partially observable scenarios demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and highlight the role of discrete proxies in generalization. ORDER is designed to accommodate different offline reinforcement learning algorithms. Its stated training setup uses fully observed data to establish the representations that the partial-observation proxies learn to recover.
summary.tldr: ORDER aligns representations from partial observations with discrete full-state representations to improve offline policy robustness.

title: Offline RL with Discrete Proxy Representations for Generalizability in POMDPs

abstract: We present DiffInfinite, a hierarchical diffusion model that generates arbitrarily large histological images while preserving long-range correlation structural information. Our approach first generates synthetic segmentation masks, subsequently used as conditions for the high-fidelity generative diffusion process. The proposed sampling method can be scaled up to any desired image size while only requiring small patches for fast training. Moreover, it can be parallelized more efficiently than previous large-content generation methods while avoiding tiling artifacts. The training leverages classifier-free guidance to augment a small, sparsely annotated dataset with unlabelled data. Our method alleviates unique challenges in histopathological imaging practice: large-scale information, costly manual annotation, and protective data handling. The biological plausibility of DiffInfinite data is evaluated in a survey by ten experienced pathologists as well as a downstream classification and segmentation task. Samples from the model score strongly on anti-copying metrics which is relevant for the protection of patient data.

The paper addresses these challenges with a hierarchical diffusion system that separates the generation of tissue structure from the generation of detailed image appearance.

The system first creates synthetic segmentation masks and then uses them to condition image generation. Its sampling method can scale to any desired image size while training requires only small patches. The authors also describe more efficient parallelization than previous large-content generation methods while avoiding tiling artifacts. Classifier-free guidance allows training to combine a small, sparsely annotated dataset with unlabeled data.

Generated samples also score strongly on anti-copying metrics, which is relevant to protecting patient data. These results provide evidence about plausibility and copying behavior; the abstract does not present the anti-copying scores as a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: DiffInfinite uses generated masks and patch-based diffusion to synthesize large histology images with coherent structure.

title: DiffInfinite: Large Mask-Image Synthesis via Parallel Random Patch Diffusion in Histopathology

abstract: Exponential generalization bounds with near-optimal rates have recently been established for uniformly stable algorithms~\citep{feldman2019high,bousquet2020sharper}. We seek to extend these best known high probability bounds from deterministic learning algorithms to the regime of randomized learning. One simple approach for achieving this goal is to define the stability for the expectation over the algorithm's randomness, which may result in sharper parameter but only leads to guarantees regarding the on-average generalization error. Another natural option is to consider the stability conditioned on the algorithm's randomness, which is way more stringent but may lead to generalization with high probability jointly over the randomness of sample and algorithm. The present paper addresses such a tension between these two alternatives and makes progress towards relaxing it inside a classic framework of confidence-boosting. To this end, we first introduce a novel concept of $L_2$-uniform stability that holds uniformly over data but in second-moment over the algorithm's randomness. Then as a core contribution of this work, we prove a strong exponential bound on the first-moment of generalization error under the notion of $L_2$-uniform stability. As an interesting consequence of the bound, we show that a bagging-based meta algorithm leads to near-optimal generalization with high probability jointly over the randomness of data and algorithm. We further substantialize these generic results to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to derive sharper exponential bounds for convex or non-convex optimization with natural time-decaying learning rates, which have not been possible to prove with the existing stability-based generalization guarantees.

Randomized algorithms introduce a tension: averaging over internal randomness can yield favorable stability measures but only average guarantees, while conditioning on that randomness imposes a stronger requirement to obtain high-probability guarantees over both data and algorithm.

The paper introduces L2-uniform stability, which is uniform over data but measures algorithmic randomness through a second moment. Under this notion, the authors prove a strong exponential bound on the first moment of generalization error. They then use a bagging-based meta-algorithm within a confidence-boosting framework to obtain near-optimal generalization guarantees holding with high probability over both sources of randomness.

The theory is also applied to stochastic gradient descent for convex and nonconvex optimization with naturally decaying learning rates. It yields sharper exponential bounds than existing stability-based guarantees could establish in these settings. The advance is a new way to manage randomized stability, together with a confidence-boosting construction that converts the analysis into stronger probabilistic guarantees.
summary.tldr: L2-uniform stability enables sharper randomized-learning generalization bounds and, through bagging-based confidence boosting, near-optimal high-probability guarantees.

title: $L_2$-Uniform Stability of Randomized Learning Algorithms: Sharper Generalization Bounds and Confidence Boosting

abstract: This work addresses the fundamental linear inverse problem in compressive sensing (CS) by introducing a new type of regularizing generative prior. Our proposed method utilizes ideas from classical dictionary-based CS and, in particular, sparse Bayesian learning (SBL), to integrate a strong regularization towards sparse solutions. At the same time, by leveraging the notion of conditional Gaussianity, it also incorporates the adaptability from generative models to training data. However, unlike most state-of-the-art generative models, it is able to learn from a few compressed and noisy data samples and requires no optimization algorithm for solving the inverse problem. Additionally, similar to Dirichlet prior networks, our model parameterizes a conjugate prior enabling its application for uncertainty quantification. We support our approach theoretically through the concept of variational inference and validate it empirically using different types of compressible signals.

paragraphs: This paper tackles compressive sensing: recovering a signal from compressed linear measurements. It introduces a generative prior that combines a preference for sparse solutions with the ability to adapt to training data. The motivation is to bring together the structural guidance of classical sparse reconstruction and the flexibility of learned generative models.

The method draws on dictionary-based compressive sensing and sparse Bayesian learning to encourage sparsity. Conditional Gaussian structure supplies the connection to a data-adaptive generative model. The resulting approach can learn from a small number of compressed, noisy samples and does not require an optimization algorithm to solve the inverse problem.

The model also parameterizes a conjugate prior, enabling uncertainty quantification alongside reconstruction. The authors support the construction theoretically using variational inference and evaluate it on different types of compressible signals. Its contribution is therefore a combined treatment of sparse reconstruction, learning from limited measurements, and uncertainty, with empirical validation across the signal types studied.
summary.tldr: A sparse Bayesian generative prior learns from limited noisy compressed data and supports reconstruction with uncertainty quantification.

title: Sparse Bayesian Generative Modeling for Compressive Sensing

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with adaptive steps is widely used to train deep neural networks and generative models. Most theoretical results assume that it is possible to obtain unbiased gradient estimators, which is not the case in several recent deep learning and reinforcement learning applications that use Monte Carlo methods.This paper provides a comprehensive non-asymptotic analysis of SGD with biased gradients and adaptive steps for non-convex smooth functions. Our study incorporates time-dependent bias and emphasizes the importance of controlling the bias of the gradient estimator. In particular, we establish that Adagrad, RMSProp, and AMSGRAD, an exponential moving average variant of Adam, with biased gradients, converge to critical points for smooth non-convex functions at a rate similar to existing results in the literature for the unbiased case. Finally, we provide experimental results using Variational Autoenconders (VAE) and applications to several learning frameworks that illustrate our convergence results and show how the effect of bias can be reduced by appropriate hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: Adaptive gradient methods are widely used in deep learning, but their theory often assumes gradient estimates are unbiased. Some learning systems use Monte Carlo procedures that do not satisfy that assumption. This paper studies adaptive stochastic optimization when gradient estimates have bias, including bias that changes over time.

The analysis concerns smooth, non-convex objectives and gives guarantees for finite amounts of computation. It emphasizes controlling estimation bias and establishes convergence to critical points for Adagrad, RMSProp, and AMSGRAD with biased gradients. The reported rates are similar to existing results for unbiased gradients. Convergence to a critical point concerns vanishing gradients; it does not by itself identify a global optimum.

The authors also present experiments with variational autoencoders and applications to several learning frameworks. These illustrate the theoretical results and show that suitable hyperparameter tuning can reduce the influence of bias. The contribution connects adaptive optimization theory to settings where unbiased estimation is unavailable, while making bias control an explicit part of the convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes adaptive optimization with biased gradients and shows how controlling bias supports convergence for smooth non-convex objectives.

title: Non-asymptotic Analysis of Biased Adaptive Stochastic Approximation

abstract: AI models are increasingly prevalent in high-stakes environments, necessitating thorough assessment of their capabilities and risks. Benchmarks are popular for measuring these attributes and for comparing model performance, tracking progress, and identifying weaknesses in foundation and non-foundation models. They can inform model selection for downstream tasks and influence policy initiatives. However, not all benchmarks are the same: their quality depends on their design and usability. In this paper, we develop an assessment framework considering 40 best practices across a benchmark's life cycle and evaluate 25 AI benchmarks against it. We find that there exist large quality differences and that commonly used benchmarks suffer from significant issues. We further find that most benchmarks do not report statistical significance of their results nor can results be easily replicated. To support benchmark developers in aligning with best practices, we provide a checklist for minimum quality assurance based on our assessment. We also develop a living repository of benchmark assessments to support benchmark comparability.

paragraphs: AI benchmarks influence how people compare models, track progress, identify weaknesses, and choose systems for practical tasks. They can also inform policy. BetterBench examines the quality of these measuring tools themselves: a benchmark's usefulness depends on how it is designed and how easily others can use and reproduce its evaluation.

The authors create an assessment framework covering 40 best practices across a benchmark's life cycle and apply it to 25 AI benchmarks. They find substantial differences in quality, including significant problems in commonly used benchmarks. Most of the assessed benchmarks do not report the statistical significance of their results, and their results are not easily replicated. These findings complicate the interpretation of reported model comparisons.

The paper turns the assessment into practical resources: a minimum-quality checklist for benchmark developers and a living repository of benchmark assessments. The checklist helps developers align their work with the proposed practices, while the repository supports comparison between benchmarks. The contribution is an organized way to examine whether evaluation tools provide a dependable basis for judging AI systems.
summary.tldr: BetterBench assesses 25 AI benchmarks against 40 best practices, exposing substantial quality gaps and providing resources to improve evaluation.

title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices

abstract: Unsupervised Multiplex Graph Learning (UMGL) aims to learn node representations on various edge types without manual labeling. However, existing research overlooks a key factor: the reliability of the graph structure. Real-world data often exhibit a complex nature and contain abundant task-irrelevant noise, severely compromising UMGL's performance. Moreover, existing methods primarily rely on contrastive learning to maximize mutual information across different graphs, limiting them to multiplex graph redundant scenarios and failing to capture view-unique task-relevant information. In this paper, we focus on a more realistic and challenging task: to unsupervisedly learn a fused graph from multiple graphs that preserve sufficient task-relevant information while removing task-irrelevant noise. Specifically, our proposed Information-aware Unsupervised Multiplex Graph Fusion framework (InfoMGF) uses graph structure refinement to eliminate irrelevant noise and simultaneously maximizes view-shared and view-unique task-relevant information, thereby tackling the frontier of non-redundant multiplex graph. Theoretical analyses further guarantee the effectiveness of InfoMGF. Comprehensive experiments against various baselines on different downstream tasks demonstrate its superior performance and robustness. Surprisingly, our unsupervised method even beats the sophisticated supervised approaches. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/zxlearningdeep/InfoMGF.

paragraphs: A multiplex graph represents several kinds of relationships among nodes. Learning from these graphs without labels requires deciding which connections and information to preserve. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: unreliable connections introduce irrelevant noise, and emphasizing agreement between graphs can overlook useful information that appears in only one relationship type.

InfoMGF learns a fused graph while refining the structures of its component graphs. Its objective preserves both information shared across views and information unique to individual views, while removing task-irrelevant noise. This matters when the different relationship types contribute complementary evidence, rather than largely repeating the same information.

The authors provide theoretical analyses supporting the framework and evaluate it across multiple downstream tasks. They report stronger performance and robustness than the compared baselines, including better results than sophisticated supervised approaches in their evaluation. These findings support treating graph quality and view-specific information as central parts of unsupervised fusion, rather than assuming that the original connections are reliable or that agreement captures everything useful.
summary.tldr: InfoMGF improves unsupervised graph fusion by removing irrelevant connections while preserving both shared and view-specific useful information.

title: Beyond Redundancy: Information-aware Unsupervised Multiplex Graph Structure Learning

abstract: Foundation models possess strong capabilities in reasoning and memorizing across modalities. To further unleash the power of foundation models, we present FIND, a generalized interface for aligning foundation models' embeddings with unified image and dataset-level understanding spanning modality and granularity. As shown in Fig.1, a lightweight transformer interface without tuning any foundation model weights is enough for segmentation, grounding, and retrieval in an interleaved manner. The proposed interface has the following favorable attributes: (1) Generalizable. It applies to various tasks spanning retrieval, segmentation, etc., under the same architecture and weights. (2) Interleavable. With the benefit of multi-task multi-modal training, the proposed interface creates an interleaved shared embedding space. (3) Extendable. The proposed interface is adaptive to new tasks, and new models. In light of the interleaved embedding space, we introduce FIND-Bench, which introduces new training and evaluation annotations to the COCO dataset for interleaved segmentation and retrieval. We are the first work aligning foundations models' embeddings for interleave understanding. Meanwhile, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on FIND-Bench and competitive performance on standard retrieval and segmentation settings.

FIND introduces a lightweight Transformer interface that connects those embeddings while leaving the foundation models' weights unchanged. The aim is to support understanding at different levels, from regions within an image to relationships across a dataset.

The interface supports segmentation, grounding, and retrieval through the same architecture and weights. Multitask, multimodal training creates a shared embedding space in which these capabilities can be interleaved. The authors also describe the interface as extendable to new models and tasks. This makes the alignment layer the central mechanism for coordinating existing model capabilities across different forms of input and output.

To evaluate this combined behavior, the paper introduces FIND-Bench, adding training and evaluation annotations to COCO for interleaved segmentation and retrieval. FIND achieves state-of-the-art performance on that benchmark and competitive results on standard retrieval and segmentation settings. The distinction matters: its strongest reported result concerns the new benchmark designed around the interface's combined capabilities.
summary.tldr: FIND aligns frozen foundation-model embeddings through a lightweight interface that jointly supports segmentation, grounding, and retrieval.

title: Interfacing Foundation Models' Embeddings

abstract: The block tensor of trifocal tensors provides crucial geometric information on the three-view geometry of a scene. The underlying synchronization problem seeks to recover camera poses (locations and orientations up to a global transformation) from the block trifocal tensor. We establish an explicit Tucker factorization of this tensor, revealing a low multilinear rank of $(6,4,4)$ independent of the number of cameras under appropriate scaling conditions. We prove that this rank constraint provides sufficient information for camera recovery in the noiseless case. The constraint motivates a synchronization algorithm based on the higher-order singular value decomposition of the block trifocal tensor. Experimental comparisons with state-of-the-art global synchronization methods on real datasets demonstrate the potential of this algorithm for significantly improving location estimation accuracy. Overall this work suggests that higher-order interactions in synchronization problems can be exploited to improve performance, beyond the usual pairwise-based approaches.
