paragraphs: Dual Query addresses the problem of answering many questions about a dataset while maintaining differential privacy. The challenge becomes computationally severe when each record has many attributes. The paper explicitly retains the unavoidable worst-case cost: its complexity can grow exponentially with the number of dimensions.

The practical contribution is to package the difficult computation into a compactly specified integer program. Standard solvers can handle this subproblem without themselves implementing a private optimization algorithm. The overall procedure has proven privacy and accuracy guarantees, so the non-private solution of that internal optimization problem is part of the analyzed private method.

Experiments show that this organization can work well despite the worst-case complexity. The authors report efficiently and accurately answering millions of queries on the Netflix dataset, which has more than 17,000 attributes, and describe an improvement of multiple orders of magnitude over the state of the art. The result demonstrates substantial practical reach without claiming to eliminate the underlying computational difficulty.
summary.tldr: Dual Query uses standard integer-program solvers within a provably private algorithm to answer large query collections effectively in practice.

title: Dual Query: Practical Private Query Release for High Dimensional Data

abstract: In imitation learning, an agent learns how to behave in an environment with an unknown cost function by mimicking expert demonstrations. Existing imitation learning algorithms typically involve solving a sequence of planning or reinforcement learning problems. Such algorithms are therefore not directly applicable to large, high-dimensional environments, and their performance can significantly degrade if the planning problems are not solved to optimality. Under the apprenticeship learning formalism, we develop alternative model-free algorithms for finding a parameterized stochastic policy that performs at least as well as an expert policy on an unknown cost function, based on sample trajectories from the expert. Our approach, based on policy gradients, scales to large continuous environments with guaranteed convergence to local minima.

paragraphs: Imitation learning uses expert demonstrations to learn behavior when the underlying cost function is unknown. The paper addresses the computational burden of approaches that repeatedly solve planning or reinforcement-learning problems. Those intermediate problems can be difficult in large environments, and imperfect solutions can substantially damage imitation performance.

Within the apprenticeship-learning formalism, the authors develop model-free algorithms that work from sample trajectories supplied by an expert. They seek a parameterized stochastic policy that performs at least as well as the expert under an unknown cost function. Their approach uses policy gradients, putting optimization of the policy at the center of the learning procedure.

The algorithms are designed to scale to large continuous environments and have a guarantee of convergence to local minima. That guarantee describes the optimization destination and does not establish that every resulting policy reaches a global optimum. The contribution is an alternative route to apprenticeship learning that addresses the burden of repeated planning while retaining a stated local-convergence guarantee for its policy-gradient approach.
summary.tldr: Model-free policy-gradient algorithms pursue apprenticeship learning in large continuous environments with guaranteed convergence to local minima.

title: Model-Free Imitation Learning with Policy Optimization

abstract: The prevalent approach to sequence to sequence learning maps an input sequence to a variable length output sequence via recurrent neural networks. We introduce an architecture based entirely on convolutional neural networks. Compared to recurrent models, computations over all elements can be fully parallelized during training to better exploit the GPU hardware and optimization is easier since the number of non-linearities is fixed and independent of the input length. Our use of gated linear units eases gradient propagation and we equip each decoder layer with a separate attention module. We outperform the accuracy of the deep LSTM setup of Wu et al. (2016) on both WMT’14 English-German and WMT’14 English-French translation at an order of magnitude faster speed, both on GPU and CPU.

Compared to recurrent models, computations over all elements can be fully parallelized during training to better exploit the GPU hardware and optimization is easier since the number of non-linearities is fixed and independent of the input length. Our use of gated linear units eases gradient propagation and we equip each decoder layer with a separate attention module. We outperform the accuracy of the deep LSTM setup of Wu et al. (2016) on both WMT’14 English-German and WMT’14 English-French translation at an order of magnitude faster speed, both on GPU and CPU.

paragraphs: Sequence-to-sequence learning turns an input such as a sentence into an output whose length can differ. Recurrent networks traditionally perform this job, but their sequential computations make it difficult to use parallel hardware fully. This paper asks whether convolutions can provide a faster and more effective alternative for the entire model.

The proposed architecture uses convolutional networks throughout. Gated linear units help gradients propagate, while a separate attention module in every decoder layer lets the output computation consult the input. During training, computations across sequence elements can run in parallel. The number of nonlinear transformations also stays independent of sequence length, which the authors identify as an optimization advantage.

On WMT’14 English–German and English–French translation, the model exceeds the accuracy of the deep LSTM setup of Wu et al. while reporting an order-of-magnitude speed advantage on both CPU and GPU. These translation results establish that recurrence is not necessary for strong sequence modeling in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: A fully convolutional sequence model improves translation accuracy and speed over the compared recurrent model.

title: Convolutional Sequence to Sequence Learning

abstract: Using unitary (instead of general) matrices in artificial neural networks (ANNs) is a promising way to solve the gradient explosion/vanishing problem, as well as to enable ANNs to learn long-term correlations in the data. This approach appears particularly promising for Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). In this work, we present a new architecture for implementing an Efficient Unitary Neural Network (EUNNs); its main advantages can be summarized as follows. Firstly, the representation capacity of the unitary space in an EUNN is fully tunable, ranging from a subspace of SU(N) to the entire unitary space. Secondly, the computational complexity for training an EUNN is merely $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per parameter. Finally, we test the performance of EUNNs on the standard copying task, the pixel-permuted MNIST digit recognition benchmark as well as the Speech Prediction Test (TIMIT). We find that our architecture significantly outperforms both other state-of-the-art unitary RNNs and the LSTM architecture, in terms of the final performance and/or the wall-clock training speed. EUNNs are thus promising alternatives to RNNs and LSTMs for a wide variety of applications.

This paper introduces an Efficient Unitary Neural Network architecture, or EUNN. Its design addresses how broadly a network can represent unitary transformations and how much computation that representation requires.

The representation capacity is tunable, ranging from a subspace of SU(N) to the full unitary space. This makes the extent of the available transformations an explicit architectural choice. The authors also report training complexity of O(1) per parameter, a computational property that complements the adjustable representation capacity.

summary.tldr: EUNNs offer tunable unitary representation capacity and efficient training, with reported gains in task performance and/or training speed.

title: Tunable Efficient Unitary Neural Networks (EUNN) and their application to RNNs

abstract: In this paper, we study the gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT) when the output space is high dimensional and sparse. For example, in multilabel classification, the output space is a $L$-dimensional 0/1 vector, where $L$ is number of labels that can grow to millions and beyond in many modern applications. We show that vanilla GBDT can easily run out of memory or encounter near-forever running time in this regime, and propose a new GBDT variant, GBDT-SPARSE, to resolve this problem by employing $L_0$ regularization. We then discuss in detail how to utilize this sparsity to conduct GBDT training, including splitting the nodes, computing the sparse residual, and predicting in sublinear time. Finally, we apply our algorithm to extreme multilabel classification problems, and show that the proposed GBDT-SPARSE achieves an order of magnitude improvements in model size and prediction time over existing methods, while yielding similar performance.

We show that vanilla GBDT can easily run out of memory or encounter near-forever running time in this regime, and propose a new GBDT variant, GBDT-SPARSE, to resolve this problem by employing $L_0$ regularization. paragraphs: Gradient boosted decision trees become difficult to use when each prediction has an enormous number of possible output coordinates. Extreme multilabel classification is one example: the label vector may contain millions of entries, although relatively few are active. The paper shows that ordinary GBDT can require excessive memory or impractically long computation in this setting.

The proposed GBDT-SPARSE method introduces L0 regularization to exploit sparse outputs. The authors develop the associated training machinery, including how to split tree nodes and compute sparse residuals. They also explain how to make predictions in time that grows sublinearly with the output dimension, making sparsity relevant throughout the procedure.

On extreme multilabel classification problems, the method achieves reported order-of-magnitude improvements in model size and prediction time over existing methods while maintaining similar predictive performance. The result connects the structure of the output space to computational savings. It shows that accommodating sparse outputs explicitly can make boosted trees more practical when the number of possible labels is very large.
summary.tldr: GBDT-SPARSE exploits sparse outputs to reduce model size and prediction time while retaining similar multilabel classification performance.

title: Gradient Boosted Decision Trees for High Dimensional Sparse Output

abstract: We study the bias of generic optimization methods, including Mirror Descent, Natural Gradient Descent and Steepest Descent with respect to different potentials and norms, when optimizing underdetermined linear models or separable linear classification problems. We ask the question of whether the global minimum (among the many possible global minima) reached by optimization can be characterized in terms of the potential or norm, and indecently of hyper-parameter choices, such as stepsize and momentum.
originalAbstract: We study the bias of generic optimization methods, including Mirror Descent, Natural Gradient Descent and Steepest Descent with respect to different potentials and norms, when optimizing underdetermined linear models or separable linear classification problems. We ask the question of whether the global minimum (among the many possible global minima) reached by optimization can be characterized in terms of the potential or norm, and indecently of hyper-parameter choices, such as stepsize and momentum.

paragraphs: An optimization problem can have many equally good global solutions, leaving a further question: which one does a particular training method select? This paper studies that selection behavior, called implicit bias, for underdetermined linear models and separable linear classification problems. The focus is on the preference introduced by the optimization procedure itself.

The methods considered include Mirror Descent, Natural Gradient Descent, and Steepest Descent under different potentials and norms. These choices describe the geometry used by an optimizer to determine its updates. The authors investigate whether this geometry provides a way to characterize the solution that optimization ultimately reaches among the available possibilities.

A central part of the question is whether such a characterization can be independent of hyperparameters such as step size and momentum. That distinction matters because it separates a method's geometric preference from effects of its particular settings. The abstract presents the scope and research question rather than announcing a general answer, so the contribution described here is an investigation of when optimization geometry can explain solution selection.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates whether optimization geometry characterizes the solutions selected in linear learning problems independently of hyperparameters.

title: Characterizing Implicit Bias in Terms of Optimization Geometry

abstract: The problem of estimating causal effects of treatments from observational data falls beyond the realm of supervised learning {—} because counterfactual data is inaccessible, we can never observe the true causal effects. In the absence of "supervision", how can we evaluate the performance of causal inference methods? In this paper, we use influence functions {—} the functional derivatives of a loss function {—} to develop a model validation procedure that estimates the estimation error of causal inference methods. Our procedure utilizes a Taylor-like expansion to approximate the loss function of a method on a given dataset in terms of the influence functions of its loss on a "synthesized", proximal dataset with known causal effects. Under minimal regularity assumptions, we show that our procedure is consistent and efficient. Experiments on 77 benchmark datasets show that using our procedure, we can accurately predict the comparative performances of state-of-the-art causal inference methods applied to a given observational study.

paragraphs: Evaluating causal-effect estimates from observational data is difficult because the needed counterfactual outcomes are inaccessible. Unlike ordinary supervised prediction, there is no directly observed causal target against which to score every estimate. This paper develops a validation procedure for estimating the error of causal inference methods despite that missing supervision.

The procedure uses influence functions, which describe how a loss changes under changes to the underlying data distribution. It constructs a nearby synthetic dataset with known causal effects, then uses a Taylor-like expansion involving influence functions to approximate a method’s loss on the observational dataset. The known effects in the synthetic setting provide the reference for this approximation.

Under minimal regularity assumptions, the authors establish consistency and efficiency for the procedure. Experiments on 77 benchmark datasets show that it can accurately predict the relative performance of state-of-the-art causal inference methods for a given observational study. This supports using the procedure to compare candidate methods when true effects cannot be observed directly, while keeping the theoretical guarantees tied to their stated regularity conditions.
summary.tldr: Influence functions transfer validation information from a nearby synthetic dataset to estimate and compare causal-inference errors on observational data.

title: Validating Causal Inference Models via Influence Functions

abstract: We prove that for an $L$-layer fully-connected linear neural network, if the width of every hidden layer is $\widetilde{\Omega}\left(L \cdot r \cdot d_{out} \cdot \kappa^3 \right)$, where $r$ and $\kappa$ are the rank and the condition number of the input data, and $d_{out}$ is the output dimension, then gradient descent with Gaussian random initialization converges to a global minimum at a linear rate. The number of iterations to find an $\epsilon$-suboptimal solution is $O(\kappa \log(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$. Our polynomial upper bound on the total running time for wide deep linear networks and the $\exp\left(\Omega\left(L\right)\right)$ lower bound for narrow deep linear neural networks [Shamir, 2018] together demonstrate that wide layers are necessary for optimizing deep models.

The number of iterations to find an $\epsilon$-suboptimal solution is $O(\kappa \log(\frac{1}{\epsilon}))$. paragraphs: This paper studies how hidden-layer width affects optimization in deep, fully connected linear networks. Its main theorem gives a sufficient width condition under which gradient descent, starting from Gaussian random initialization, converges to a global minimum at a linear rate. The setting isolates depth and width within networks composed of linear layers.

For an L-layer network, each hidden layer must have width at least on the order of L times the input rank, output dimension, and cubed input condition number, up to logarithmic factors. Under that condition, reaching an epsilon-suboptimal solution requires O(kappa log(1/epsilon)) iterations, where kappa is the input condition number. This makes the dependence on data conditioning explicit.

The authors combine their polynomial running-time upper bound for wide networks with an existing exponential-in-depth lower bound for narrow deep linear networks. Together, these results establish a theoretical optimization advantage for width in the studied setting. The sufficient threshold supplies a regime with guaranteed convergence; it does not establish that every narrower individual network must be difficult to optimize.
summary.tldr: Sufficiently wide deep linear networks admit fast global convergence guarantees for gradient descent with Gaussian initialization.

title: Width Provably Matters in Optimization for Deep Linear Neural Networks

abstract: In data summarization we want to choose $k$ prototypes in order to summarize a data set. We study a setting where the data set comprises several demographic groups and we are restricted to choose $k_i$ prototypes belonging to group $i$. A common approach to the problem without the fairness constraint is to optimize a centroid-based clustering objective such as $k$-center. A natural extension then is to incorporate the fairness constraint into the clustering problem. Existing algorithms for doing so run in time super-quadratic in the size of the data set, which is in contrast to the standard $k$-center problem being approximable in linear time. In this paper, we resolve this gap by providing a simple approximation algorithm for the $k$-center problem under the fairness constraint with running time linear in the size of the data set and $k$. If the number of demographic groups is small, the approximation guarantee of our algorithm only incurs a constant-factor overhead.

paragraphs: Data summarization can be framed as selecting a small set of prototypes to represent a larger dataset. This paper considers datasets containing several demographic groups and requires a specified number of selected prototypes from each group. Fairness here is expressed through those selection quotas, making demographic representation part of the optimization problem itself.

The authors incorporate these constraints into the k-center clustering objective. Existing algorithms for this constrained problem take more than quadratic time in dataset size, whereas ordinary k-center admits a linear-time approximation. That difference creates a computational obstacle to using constrained prototype selection on larger datasets.

The paper supplies a simple approximation algorithm with running time linear in dataset size and in the number of prototypes. When the number of demographic groups is small, its approximation guarantee incurs only a constant-factor overhead. This is a conditional quality guarantee rather than a claim of exact optimization. The result narrows the efficiency gap between unconstrained summarization and summarization that must satisfy explicit demographic quotas.
summary.tldr: A fast approximation algorithm selects k-center prototypes under demographic quotas, with constant-factor overhead when there are few groups.

title: Fair k-Center Clustering for Data Summarization

abstract: We introduce an approach to learn representations based on the Lorentzian distance in hyperbolic geometry. Hyperbolic geometry is especially suited to hierarchically-structured datasets, which are prevalent in the real world. Current hyperbolic representation learning methods compare examples with the Poincaré distance. They try to minimize the distance of each node in a hierarchy with its descendants while maximizing its distance with other nodes. This formulation produces node representations close to the centroid of their descendants. To obtain efficient and interpretable algorithms, we exploit the fact that the centroid w.r.t the squared Lorentzian distance can be written in closed-form. We show that the Euclidean norm of such a centroid decreases as the curvature of the hyperbolic space decreases. This property makes it appropriate to represent hierarchies where parent nodes minimize the distances to their descendants and have smaller Euclidean norm than their children. Our approach obtains state-of-the-art results in retrieval and classification tasks on different datasets.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations in hyperbolic geometry, which is well suited to hierarchical data. The authors focus on how distance shapes the position of a parent relative to its descendants. Existing approaches described in the abstract use Poincaré distance to bring related nodes together and separate other nodes, placing a node near a centroid of its descendants.

The proposed approach uses Lorentzian distance and exploits a useful mathematical property: the centroid under squared Lorentzian distance has a closed-form expression. This supports efficient and interpretable algorithms. The authors also show that the Euclidean norm of this centroid decreases as the curvature of the hyperbolic space decreases.

That property fits a hierarchical representation in which parents minimize distances to descendants and have smaller Euclidean norms than their children. The geometry therefore supplies both a way to compute representative centers and a meaningful relationship between hierarchy and position. Experiments report state-of-the-art retrieval and classification results on different datasets, supporting the usefulness of this distance-based construction.
summary.tldr: Lorentzian distance provides closed-form centroids for efficient hyperbolic representations that reflect hierarchical relationships.

title: Lorentzian Distance Learning for Hyperbolic Representations

abstract: Despite the progress in voice conversion, many-to-many voice conversion trained on non-parallel data, as well as zero-shot voice conversion, remains under-explored. Deep style transfer algorithms, generative adversarial networks (GAN) in particular, are being applied as new solutions in this field. However, GAN training is very sophisticated and difficult, and there is no strong evidence that its generated speech is of good perceptual quality. In this paper, we propose a new style transfer scheme that involves only an autoencoder with a carefully designed bottleneck. We formally show that this scheme can achieve distribution-matching style transfer by training only on self-reconstruction loss. Based on this scheme, we proposed AutoVC, which achieves state-of-the-art results in many-to-many voice conversion with non-parallel data, and which is the first to perform zero-shot voice conversion.

In this paper, we propose a new style transfer scheme that involves only an autoencoder with a carefully designed bottleneck. We formally show that this scheme can achieve distribution-matching style transfer by training only on self-reconstruction loss. Based on this scheme, we proposed AutoVC, which achieves state-of-the-art results in many-to-many voice conversion with non-parallel data, and which is the first to perform zero-shot voice conversion.

paragraphs: Voice conversion changes the voice style of speech. This paper addresses conversion among multiple speakers using non-parallel recordings, meaning training does not require matching utterances across speakers. It also addresses zero-shot conversion, extending voice conversion beyond the speakers available during training. These settings make the choice of training method particularly important.

The proposed approach uses an autoencoder with a carefully designed bottleneck. An autoencoder learns to reconstruct its input through an intermediate representation; the bottleneck constrains that representation. The authors formally show that their scheme can achieve distribution-matching style transfer while training only with self-reconstruction loss. This provides a theoretical basis for learning the transfer without a separate adversarial training objective.

AutoVC implements this scheme for speech. The authors report state-of-the-art results for many-to-many conversion with non-parallel data and describe it as the first system to perform zero-shot voice conversion. The contribution connects a relatively simple reconstruction objective with a deliberately structured architecture, showing that this combination can support capabilities otherwise pursued through more complicated training methods.
summary.tldr: AutoVC uses a carefully constrained autoencoder trained only on reconstruction to achieve strong voice conversion results, including zero-shot conversion.

title: AutoVC: Zero-Shot Voice Style Transfer with Only Autoencoder Loss

abstract: Modern deep learning models employ considerably more parameters than required to fit the training data. Whereas conventional statistical wisdom suggests such models should drastically overfit, in practice these models generalize remarkably well. An emerging paradigm for describing this unexpected behavior is in terms of a \emph{double descent} curve, in which increasing a model’s capacity causes its test error to first decrease, then increase to a maximum near the interpolation threshold, and then decrease again in the overparameterized regime. Recent efforts to explain this phenomenon theoretically have focused on simple settings, such as linear regression or kernel regression with unstructured random features, which we argue are too coarse to reveal important nuances of actual neural networks. We provide a precise high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of generalization under kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel, which characterizes the behavior of wide neural networks optimized with gradient descent. Our results reveal that the test error has nonmonotonic behavior deep in the overparameterized regime and can even exhibit additional peaks and descents when the number of parameters scales quadratically with the dataset size.

paragraphs: Double descent describes test error that falls, rises near the capacity needed to fit training data, and then falls again as capacity increases further. This paper asks whether that picture captures the behavior of neural networks deeply into the overparameterized regime. It argues that simpler theoretical models can miss relevant structure.

The authors provide a precise high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of kernel regression using the neural tangent kernel. This kernel characterizes the behavior of wide neural networks optimized with gradient descent. The analysis examines generalization in this structured setting, allowing the relationship between parameter count, dataset size, and test error to have more than one characteristic scale.

The results show that test error can remain nonmonotonic well beyond the interpolation threshold. Additional peaks and descents can appear when parameter count scales quadratically with dataset size. The findings refine the double-descent picture within the paper's neural-tangent-kernel asymptotic analysis.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional neural tangent kernel analysis reveals that test error can exhibit additional peaks and descents deep in the overparameterized regime.

title: The Neural Tangent Kernel in High Dimensions: Triple Descent and a Multi-Scale Theory of Generalization

abstract: We present a novel communication-efficient Newton-type algorithm for finite-sum optimization over a distributed computing environment. Our method, named DINO, overcomes both theoretical and practical shortcomings of similar existing methods. Under minimal assumptions, we guarantee global sub-linear convergence of DINO to a first-order stationary point for general non-convex functions and arbitrary data distribution over the network. Furthermore, for functions satisfying Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality, we show that DINO enjoys a linear convergence rate. Our proposed algorithm is practically parameter free, in that it will converge regardless of the selected hyper-parameters, which are easy to tune. Additionally, its sub-problems are simple linear least-squares, for which efficient solvers exist, and numerical simulations demonstrate the efficiency of DINO as compared with similar alternatives.

The paper focuses on communication efficiency as well as optimization behavior. Its guarantees allow arbitrary distributions of data across the network, making data placement an explicit part of the setting.

Under minimal assumptions, the authors establish global sublinear convergence to a first-order stationary point for general nonconvex functions. A stationary point is a point where the gradient vanishes; this guarantee does not by itself identify a global minimum. For objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality, they prove the stronger result of linear convergence.

The implementation uses linear least-squares subproblems, for which efficient solvers are available. The authors describe DINO as practically parameter free because it converges regardless of the selected hyperparameters within their stated framework, while still allowing easy tuning. Numerical simulations report efficiency relative to similar alternatives. Together, these results connect distributed convergence guarantees with subproblems designed to be straightforward to solve.
summary.tldr: DINO combines communication-efficient distributed Newton-type optimization with stationary-point guarantees and linear convergence under the PL condition.

title: DINO: Distributed Newton-Type Optimization Method

abstract: Gating mechanisms are widely used in neural network models, where they allow gradients to backpropagate easily through depth or time. However, their saturation property introduces problems of its own. For example, in recurrent models these gates need to have outputs near 1 to propagate information over long time-delays, which requires them to operate in their saturation regime and hinders gradient-based learning of the gate mechanism. We address this problem by deriving two synergistic modifications to the standard gating mechanism that are easy to implement, introduce no additional hyperparameters, and improve learnability of the gates when they are close to saturation. We show how these changes are related to and improve on alternative recently proposed gating mechanisms such as chrono-initialization and Ordered Neurons. Empirically, our simple gating mechanisms robustly improve the performance of recurrent models on a range of applications, including synthetic memorization tasks, sequential image classification, language modeling, and reinforcement learning, particularly when long-term dependencies are involved.

To carry information over long delays, a gate often needs an output close to one. In that saturated region, gradient-based learning has difficulty adjusting the gate itself.

The paper derives two complementary modifications to standard gating that improve learning near saturation. The changes are straightforward to implement and add no hyperparameters. summary.tldr: Two simple gating modifications improve recurrent networks' ability to learn near saturation, with empirical gains especially on long-term dependencies.

title: Improving the Gating Mechanism of Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian optimization has demonstrated impressive success in finding the optimum input x$\ast$ and output f$\ast$ = f(x$\ast$) = max f(x) of a black-box function f. In some applications, however, the optimum output is known in advance and the goal is to find the corresponding optimum input. Existing work in Bayesian optimization (BO) has not effectively exploited the knowledge of f$\ast$ for optimization. In this paper, we consider a new setting in BO in which the knowledge of the optimum output is available. Our goal is to exploit the knowledge about f$\ast$ to search for the input x$\ast$ efficiently. To achieve this goal, we first transform the Gaussian process surrogate using the information about the optimum output. Then, we propose two acquisition functions, called confidence bound minimization and expected regret minimization, which exploit the knowledge about the optimum output to identify the optimum input more efficient. We show that our approaches work intuitively and quantitatively better performance against standard BO methods. We demonstrate real applications in tuning a deep reinforcement learning algorithm on the CartPole problem and XGBoost on Skin Segmentation dataset in which the optimum values are publicly available.

paragraphs: The paper examines a special optimization setting: the best possible output of a black-box function is already known, but the input that achieves it is unknown. Knowing the target value does not solve the search problem, yet it provides information that standard Bayesian optimization methods have not effectively used.

The authors first transform the Gaussian process surrogate to incorporate the known optimum output. They then introduce two rules for selecting the next input to evaluate: confidence bound minimization and expected regret minimization. Both use the known target value to guide the search for an input that reaches it, bringing that information into the model and the evaluation decision.

It also demonstrates applications to tuning a deep reinforcement learning algorithm on CartPole and XGBoost on the Skin Segmentation dataset, where optimum values are publicly available. The contribution is specifically useful when the optimum output is available in advance, turning that prior knowledge into a search advantage.
summary.tldr: The paper uses a known optimum output to guide Bayesian optimization toward the unknown input that achieves it.

title: Knowing The What But Not The Where in Bayesian Optimization

abstract: The F-measure is a widely used performance measure for multi-label classification, where multiple labels can be active in an instance simultaneously (e.g. in image tagging, multiple tags can be active in any image). In particular, the F-measure explicitly balances recall (fraction of active labels predicted to be active) and precision (fraction of labels predicted to be active that are actually so), both of which are important in evaluating the overall performance of a multi-label classifier. As with most discrete prediction problems, however, directly optimizing the F-measure is computationally hard. In this paper, we explore the question of designing convex surrogate losses that are calibrated for the F-measure – specifically, that have the property that minimizing the surrogate loss yields (in the limit of sufficient data) a Bayes optimal multi-label classifier for the F-measure. We show that the F-measure for an $s$-label problem, when viewed as a $2^s \times 2^s$ loss matrix, has rank at most $s^2+1$, and apply a result of Ramaswamy et al. (2014) to design a family of convex calibrated surrogates for the F-measure. The resulting surrogate risk minimization algorithms can be viewed as decomposing the multi-label F-measure learning problem into $s^2+1$ binary class probability estimation problems. We also provide a quantitative regret transfer bound for our surrogates, which allows any regret guarantees for the binary problems to be transferred to regret guarantees for the overall F-measure problem, and discuss a connection with the algorithm of Dembczynski et al. (2013). Our experiments confirm our theoretical findings.

This paper constructs convex substitute losses whose optimization is aligned with the F-measure in the limit of sufficient data.

The key observation is structural. Although the F-measure loss matrix for s labels has 2^s rows and columns, its rank is at most s^2 + 1. The authors use this low-rank property to build a family of calibrated surrogate losses. Their learning algorithms can be interpreted as solving s^2 + 1 binary probability estimation problems.

Calibration means that minimizing the surrogate risk yields a Bayes optimal classifier for the F-measure in the stated limiting setting. The paper also supplies a quantitative regret bound that transfers guarantees from the binary problems to the overall task. Experiments support the theory, connecting a tractable collection of probability estimates to the original evaluation objective.
summary.tldr: A low-rank property of the multi-label F-measure enables convex surrogate losses with calibration and regret-transfer guarantees.

title: Convex Calibrated Surrogates for the Multi-Label F-Measure

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel noise-robust semi-supervised deep generative model by jointly tackling noisy labels and outliers simultaneously in a unified robust semi-supervised variational autoencoder (URSVAE). Typically, the uncertainty of of input data is characterized by placing uncertainty prior on the parameters of the probability density distributions in order to ensure the robustness of the variational encoder towards outliers. Subsequently, a noise transition model is integrated naturally into our model to alleviate the detrimental effects of noisy labels. Moreover, a robust divergence measure is employed to further enhance the robustness, where a novel variational lower bound is derived and optimized to infer the network parameters. By proving the influence function on the proposed evidence lower bound is bounded, the enormous potential of the proposed model in the classification in the presence of the compound noise is demonstrated. The experimental results highlight the superiority of the proposed framework by the evaluating on image classification tasks and comparing with the state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised classification can encounter both incorrect labels and outlying inputs. This paper develops a unified robust semi-supervised variational autoencoder, URSVAE, to address these two forms of noise together. The motivation is that protecting a model against only one source of contamination leaves the other able to distort learning.

The model places uncertainty priors on parameters of probability distributions to improve the encoder's robustness to outliers. A noise-transition model addresses label errors, while a robust divergence measure adds another source of protection. The authors derive a new variational lower bound and optimize it to learn the network parameters within the combined framework.

The analysis proves that the influence function of the proposed evidence lower bound is bounded, providing a specific theoretical robustness property. Image-classification experiments report superiority over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. Together, the analysis and experiments support jointly modeling outliers and noisy labels, without turning bounded influence into a claim that arbitrary combinations of noise can always be overcome.
summary.tldr: URSVAE jointly addresses noisy labels and outliers through uncertainty modeling, label-noise transitions, and a robust training objective.

title: Unified Robust Semi-Supervised Variational Autoencoder

abstract: Many cluster similarity indices are used to evaluate clustering algorithms, and choosing the best one for a particular task remains an open problem. We demonstrate that this problem is crucial: there are many disagreements among the indices, these disagreements do affect which algorithms are preferred in applications, and this can lead to degraded performance in real-world systems. We propose a theoretical framework to tackle this problem: we develop a list of desirable properties and conduct an extensive theoretical analysis to verify which indices satisfy them. This allows for making an informed choice: given a particular application, one can first select properties that are desirable for the task and then identify indices satisfying these. Our work unifies and considerably extends existing attempts at analyzing cluster similarity indices: we introduce new properties, formalize existing ones, and mathematically prove or disprove each property for an extensive list of validation indices. This broader and more rigorous approach leads to recommendations that considerably differ from how validation indices are currently being chosen by practitioners. Some of the most popular indices are even shown to be dominated by previously overlooked ones.

paragraphs: Cluster similarity indices help evaluate clustering algorithms, but different indices can disagree about which algorithm is better. This paper shows that those disagreements matter in applications and can contribute to degraded system performance. Choosing an evaluation measure is therefore a consequential part of selecting a clustering method.

The authors develop a framework based on desirable mathematical properties. They introduce new properties, formalize existing ones, and prove or disprove whether a broad collection of indices satisfies each property. This produces a structured account of what the measures reward and how their behavior differs, extending earlier attempts to compare them.

The proposed selection process starts with an application’s requirements: identify the properties that matter, then choose indices that satisfy them. The resulting recommendations differ substantially from common practice, and some popular indices are dominated by previously overlooked alternatives under the analysis. The contribution is a principled way to choose validation measures according to desired behavior, making the evaluation criterion itself subject to scrutiny.
summary.tldr: A property-based analysis explains consequential disagreements among clustering evaluation indices and supports choosing measures according to application needs.

title: Systematic Analysis of Cluster Similarity Indices: How to Validate Validation Measures

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are often billed as "universal distribution learners", but precisely what distributions they can represent and learn is still an open question. Heavy-tailed distributions are prevalent in many different domains such as financial risk-assessment, physics, and epidemiology. We observe that existing GAN architectures do a poor job of matching the asymptotic behavior of heavy-tailed distributions, a problem that we show stems from their construction. Additionally, common loss functions produce unstable or near-zero gradients when faced with the infinite moments and large distances between outlier points characteristic of heavy-tailed distributions. We address these problems with the Pareto GAN. A Pareto GAN leverages extreme value theory and the functional properties of neural networks to learn a distribution that matches the asymptotic behavior of the marginal distributions of the features. We identify issues with standard loss functions and propose the use of alternative metric spaces that enable stable and efficient learning. Finally, we evaluate our proposed approach on a variety of heavy-tailed datasets.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed distributions assign meaningful probability to extreme observations, making their far-out behavior important to model. This paper examines why existing generative adversarial networks struggle to reproduce that behavior. It identifies a representational problem arising from their construction, alongside an optimization problem caused by common training losses.

For heavy-tailed data, infinite moments and large distances between outliers can make those losses produce unstable gradients or gradients close to zero. Pareto GAN addresses representation using extreme value theory and properties of neural-network functions. Its aim is to learn the correct asymptotic behavior of each feature’s marginal distribution, meaning the behavior of individual features far into their tails.

The paper also proposes alternative metric spaces to enable stable and efficient learning despite the difficulties with conventional losses. Evaluations use a variety of heavy-tailed datasets. The approach connects architectural expressiveness with the geometry of the training objective, addressing both the ability to represent extreme behavior and the ability to learn it effectively.
summary.tldr: Pareto GAN combines tail-aware representation and alternative metric spaces to learn heavy-tailed data more stably.

title: Pareto GAN: Extending the Representational Power of GANs to Heavy-Tailed Distributions

abstract: Across many data domains, co-occurrence statistics about the joint appearance of objects are powerfully informative. By transforming unsupervised learning problems into decompositions of co-occurrence statistics, spectral algorithms provide transparent and efficient algorithms for posterior inference such as latent topic analysis and community detection. As object vocabularies grow, however, it becomes rapidly more expensive to store and run inference algorithms on co-occurrence statistics. Rectifying co-occurrence, the key process to uphold model assumptions, becomes increasingly more vital in the presence of rare terms, but current techniques cannot scale to large vocabularies. We propose novel methods that simultaneously compress and rectify co-occurrence statistics, scaling gracefully with the size of vocabulary and the dimension of latent space. We also present new algorithms learning latent variables from the compressed statistics, and verify that our methods perform comparably to previous approaches on both textual and non-textual data.

paragraphs: Patterns of which objects appear together can reveal hidden structure, such as topics in text or communities in other data. Spectral methods extract that structure by decomposing co-occurrence statistics. As the vocabulary grows, however, storing and processing those statistics becomes expensive, making an otherwise efficient inference strategy harder to use.

There is also a modeling issue: co-occurrence statistics need rectification to uphold the assumptions behind inference. This becomes especially important when rare terms are present, yet existing rectification techniques do not scale to large vocabularies. The paper proposes methods that compress and rectify the statistics together, addressing representation size and model compatibility in the same process.

The authors then develop algorithms that learn latent variables directly from the compressed statistics. Their methods scale with both vocabulary size and latent-space dimension, and evaluations on textual and non-textual data show performance comparable to previous approaches. The contribution is therefore an integrated route from large co-occurrence data to usable compressed representations and subsequent inference, while retaining comparable empirical performance.
summary.tldr: Joint compression and rectification make co-occurrence-based latent inference scale to larger vocabularies while maintaining comparable reported performance.

title: On-the-fly Rectification for Robust Large-Vocabulary Topic Inference

abstract: In hypothesis testing, a \emph{false discovery} occurs when a hypothesis is incorrectly rejected due to noise in the sample. When adaptively testing multiple hypotheses, the probability of a false discovery increases as more tests are performed. Thus the problem of \emph{False Discovery Rate (FDR) control} is to find a procedure for testing multiple hypotheses that accounts for this effect in determining the set of hypotheses to reject. The goal is to minimize the number (or fraction) of false discoveries, while maintaining a high true positive rate (i.e., correct discoveries). In this work, we study False Discovery Rate (FDR) control in multiple hypothesis testing under the constraint of differential privacy for the sample. Unlike previous work in this direction, we focus on the \emph{online setting}, meaning that a decision about each hypothesis must be made immediately after the test is performed, rather than waiting for the output of all tests as in the offline setting. We provide new private algorithms based on state-of-the-art results in non-private online FDR control. Our algorithms have strong provable guarantees for privacy and statistical performance as measured by FDR and power. We also provide experimental results to demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms in a variety of data environments.

paragraphs: Repeated hypothesis testing creates opportunities to mistake noise for a real discovery. False discovery rate control addresses this problem while trying to preserve the ability to detect true effects. This paper adds a second requirement: the testing procedure must protect the underlying sample through differential privacy.

The focus is online testing, where each hypothesis requires an immediate decision after its test is performed. The procedure cannot wait until every test result is available before choosing which hypotheses to reject. This timing requirement distinguishes the problem from offline private testing and makes the sequence of decisions central to the algorithm's design.

The authors construct private algorithms from leading non-private online false discovery rate methods. They provide provable guarantees for privacy and for statistical performance, measured through false discovery rate and power, the ability to make correct discoveries. Experiments across several data environments demonstrate the algorithms' efficacy. The contribution brings privacy protection and statistical error control together in a setting requiring decisions as tests arrive.
summary.tldr: PAPRIKA provides differentially private online hypothesis testing with guarantees for false discovery rate and statistical power.

title: PAPRIKA: Private Online False Discovery Rate Control

abstract: Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) provides a principled and generic framework to model real world sequential decision making processes but yet remains unsolved, especially for high dimensional continuous space and unknown models. The main challenge lies in how to accurately obtain the belief state, which is the probability distribution over the unobservable environment states given historical information. Accurately calculating this belief state is a precondition for obtaining an optimal policy of POMDPs. Recent advances in deep learning techniques show great potential to learn good belief states. However, existing methods can only learn approximated distribution with limited flexibility. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{F}l\textbf{O}w-based \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{BE}lief \textbf{S}tate model (FORBES), which incorporates normalizing flows into the variational inference to learn general continuous belief states for POMDPs. Furthermore, we show that the learned belief states can be plugged into downstream RL algorithms to improve performance. In experiments, we show that our methods successfully capture the complex belief states that enable multi-modal predictions as well as high quality reconstructions, and results on challenging visual-motor control tasks show that our method achieves superior performance and sample efficiency.
originalAbstract: Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) provides a principled and generic framework to model real world sequential decision making processes but yet remains unsolved, especially for high dimensional continuous space and unknown models. The main challenge lies in how to accurately obtain the belief state, which is the probability distribution over the unobservable environment states given historical information. Accurately calculating this belief state is a precondition for obtaining an optimal policy of POMDPs. Recent advances in deep learning techniques show great potential to learn good belief states. However, existing methods can only learn approximated distribution with limited flexibility. In this paper, we introduce the \textbf{F}l\textbf{O}w-based \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{BE}lief \textbf{S}tate model (FORBES), which incorporates normalizing flows into the variational inference to learn general continuous belief states for POMDPs. Furthermore, we show that the learned belief states can be plugged into downstream RL algorithms to improve performance. In experiments, we show that our methods successfully capture the complex belief states that enable multi-modal predictions as well as high quality reconstructions, and results on challenging visual-motor control tasks show that our method achieves superior performance and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision problem, the agent cannot directly see the complete environment state. A belief state represents its uncertainty as a probability distribution conditioned on past information. Learning this distribution is particularly challenging when hidden states are continuous and high dimensional, and the environment model is unknown.

FORBES combines recurrent belief-state learning with normalizing flows inside variational inference. Its purpose is to make the learned distribution more flexible than the approximations used by existing methods. Rather than forcing uncertainty into a restrictive shape, the model can represent more complicated possibilities about the hidden state. The resulting belief representation can then serve as input to downstream reinforcement learning algorithms.

The experiments show complex learned beliefs supporting predictions with multiple modes and high-quality reconstructions. On challenging tasks involving visual input and motor control, the authors report improved performance and sample efficiency. These findings connect the quality of uncertainty representation with downstream decision-making results: the learned beliefs are useful both for describing possible states and for supporting control in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: FORBES uses normalizing flows to learn flexible belief distributions that improve control performance and sample efficiency in the reported experiments.

title: Flow-based Recurrent Belief State Learning for POMDPs

abstract: We develop a general framework unifying several gradient-based stochastic optimization methods for empirical risk minimization problems both in centralized and distributed scenarios. The framework hinges on the introduction of an augmented graph consisting of nodes modeling the samples and edges modeling both the inter-device communication and intra-device stochastic gradient computation. By designing properly the topology of the augmented graph, we are able to recover as special cases the renowned Local-SGD and DSGD algorithms, and provide a unified perspective for variance-reduction (VR) and gradient-tracking (GT) methods such as SAGA, Local-SVRG and GT-SAGA. We also provide a unified convergence analysis for smooth and (strongly) convex objectives relying on a proper structured Lyapunov function, and the obtained rate can recover the best known results for many existing algorithms. The rate results further reveal that VR and GT methods can effectively eliminate data heterogeneity within and across devices, respectively, enabling the exact convergence of the algorithm to the optimal solution. Numerical experiments confirm the findings in this paper.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization methods differ in how they sample data, compute gradients, and exchange information between devices. This paper puts several such methods into one framework for empirical risk minimization. Its central representation is an augmented graph whose nodes model samples and whose edges encode both local gradient computation and communication across devices.

Choosing different graph topologies recovers methods including Local-SGD and decentralized SGD. The same perspective also covers variance-reduction and gradient-tracking methods such as SAGA, Local-SVRG, and GT-SAGA. A structured Lyapunov function supports a shared convergence analysis for smooth convex and strongly convex objectives, recovering the best known rates for many existing algorithms.

The analysis distinguishes two sources of data heterogeneity. Variance reduction can eliminate its effects within devices, while gradient tracking can eliminate its effects across devices, enabling exact convergence to the optimal solution under the analyzed conditions. Numerical experiments confirm the findings. The framework therefore explains both relationships among algorithms and the different roles their corrective mechanisms play when data are unevenly distributed.
summary.tldr: An augmented sample graph unifies stochastic optimization methods and explains how variance reduction and gradient tracking address different forms of data heterogeneity.

title: Tackling Data Heterogeneity: A New Unified Framework for Decentralized SGD with Sample-induced Topology

abstract: Injecting artificial noise into gradient descent (GD) is commonly employed to improve the performance of machine learning models. Usually, uncorrelated noise is used in such perturbed gradient descent (PGD) methods. It is, however, not known if this is optimal or whether other types of noise could provide better generalization performance. In this paper, we zoom in on the problem of correlating the perturbations of consecutive PGD steps. We consider a variety of objective functions for which we find that GD with anticorrelated perturbations ("Anti-PGD") generalizes significantly better than GD and standard (uncorrelated) PGD. To support these experimental findings, we also derive a theoretical analysis that demonstrates that Anti-PGD moves to wider minima, while GD and PGD remain stuck in suboptimal regions or even diverge. This new connection between anticorrelated noise and generalization opens the field to novel ways to exploit noise for training machine learning models.

paragraphs: Adding random noise to gradient descent can improve how a learned model performs beyond its training data. Usually, the perturbations at different steps are uncorrelated. This paper asks whether the relationship between consecutive perturbations is itself an important design choice, rather than treating independent noise as the default answer.

The proposed method, Anti-PGD, uses anticorrelated perturbations across successive optimization steps. In plain language, consecutive noise contributions tend to oppose one another. Across a variety of objective functions studied in the paper, this method generalizes substantially better than ordinary gradient descent and gradient descent with uncorrelated perturbations.

The authors also provide theoretical analysis supporting these experiments. In the settings analyzed, Anti-PGD reaches wider minima while the comparison methods remain in inferior regions or diverge. This links the temporal structure of injected noise to where optimization ends up. The result suggests a useful direction for training-method design, while the stated experimental and theoretical findings concern the objectives and settings examined.
summary.tldr: Anticorrelating noise across gradient steps improves generalization on the studied objectives, with theory connecting the method to wider minima.

title: Anticorrelated Noise Injection for Improved Generalization

abstract: Training generally-capable agents with reinforcement learning (RL) remains a significant challenge. A promising avenue for improving the robustness of RL agents is through the use of curricula. One such class of methods frames environment design as a game between a student and a teacher, using regret-based objectives to produce environment instantiations (or levels) at the frontier of the student agent’s capabilities. These methods benefit from theoretical robustness guarantees at equilibrium, yet they often struggle to find effective levels in challenging design spaces in practice. By contrast, evolutionary approaches incrementally alter environment complexity, resulting in potentially open-ended learning, but often rely on domain-specific heuristics and vast amounts of computational resources. This work proposes harnessing the power of evolution in a principled, regret-based curriculum. Our approach, which we call Adversarially Compounding Complexity by Editing Levels (ACCEL), seeks to constantly produce levels at the frontier of an agent’s capabilities, resulting in curricula that start simple but become increasingly complex. ACCEL maintains the theoretical benefits of prior regret-based methods, while providing significant empirical gains in a diverse set of environments. An interactive version of this paper is available at https://accelagent.github.io.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning curriculum can improve training by choosing environments near the learner's current capabilities. Regret-based environment design treats this as a game between a student and a teacher. Such methods have theoretical robustness guarantees at equilibrium, but finding useful environments can still be difficult in practice when the space of possible designs is challenging.

ACCEL combines regret-based selection with evolutionary editing of environments. It aims to keep producing levels near the student's capability frontier, beginning with simpler challenges and progressively building complexity. This brings incremental environment modification into a principled curriculum framework, connecting the practical appeal of evolution with the theoretical motivation for regret-based teaching.

The authors report that ACCEL retains the theoretical benefits of earlier regret-based approaches and delivers significant empirical improvements across diverse environments. These results support the combination as a way to discover useful training challenges more effectively. The equilibrium qualification remains relevant to the robustness theory: the abstract's practical gains are experimental findings, alongside theoretical properties inherited from the regret-based framework.
summary.tldr: ACCEL evolves training environments through regret-guided level editing, producing increasingly complex curricula with strong empirical results.

title: Evolving Curricula with Regret-Based Environment Design

abstract: Kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD) is a score-based discrepancy widely used in goodness-of-fit tests. It can be applied even when the target distribution has an unknown normalising factor, such as in Bayesian analysis. We show theoretically and empirically that the KSD test can suffer from low power when the target and the alternative distributions have the same well-separated modes but differ in mixing proportions. We propose to perturb the observed sample via Markov transition kernels, with respect to which the target distribution is invariant. This allows us to then employ the KSD test on the perturbed sample. We provide numerical evidence that with suitably chosen transition kernels the proposed approach can lead to substantially higher power than the KSD test.

paragraphs: Kernelized Stein discrepancy, or KSD, is used to test whether observations fit a target distribution. It remains applicable when the target’s normalizing factor is unknown, which makes it useful in settings such as Bayesian analysis. This paper identifies a situation where the test can have difficulty detecting a real mismatch.

The problematic case occurs when the target and alternative distributions share well-separated modes but assign different proportions to those modes. The authors establish theoretically and empirically that KSD can have low power in this setting. Their solution perturbs the observed sample through Markov transition kernels that leave the target distribution invariant, then applies the KSD test to the perturbed observations.

Target invariance means the perturbation preserves the distribution the test is meant to recognize. Numerical evidence shows that suitably chosen transition kernels can substantially improve detection power compared with the original KSD test. The improvement is conditional on the choice of kernel, and the method directly addresses the identified difficulty with differing mixture proportions.
summary.tldr: Target-preserving sample perturbations can improve KSD test power when distributions share separated modes but differ in their proportions.

title: Using Perturbation to Improve Goodness-of-Fit Tests based on Kernelized Stein Discrepancy

abstract: We show that the stochastic gradient bandit algorithm converges to a globally optimal policy at an $O(1/t)$ rate, even with a constant step size. Remarkably, global convergence of the stochastic gradient bandit algorithm has not been previously established, even though it is an old algorithm known to be applicable to bandits. The new result is achieved by establishing two novel technical findings: first, the noise of the stochastic updates in the gradient bandit algorithm satisfies a strong “growth condition” property, where the variance diminishes whenever progress becomes small, implying that additional noise control via diminishing step sizes is unnecessary; second, a form of “weak exploration” is automatically achieved through the stochastic gradient updates, since they prevent the action probabilities from decaying faster than $O(1/t)$, thus ensuring that every action is sampled infinitely often with probability $1$. These two findings can be used to show that the stochastic gradient update is already “sufficient” for bandits in the sense that exploration versus exploitation is automatically balanced in a manner that ensures almost sure convergence to a global optimum. These novel theoretical findings are further verified by experimental results.

paragraphs: The stochastic gradient bandit algorithm is an established method for learning which actions give better rewards. This paper supplies a global convergence result that had remained unproven: the algorithm approaches an optimal policy at an O(1/t) rate even with a constant step size. The analysis explains how its own updates provide enough noise regulation and exploration.

The first key finding is a growth condition on update noise. Its variance shrinks when progress becomes small, so decreasing the step size is unnecessary for the stated convergence result. The second finding concerns action probabilities: stochastic updates prevent them from decaying faster than O(1/t), ensuring that every action is sampled infinitely often with probability one.

Together, these properties explain how exploration and exploitation remain balanced sufficiently for almost-sure convergence to a global optimum. Continued sampling prevents actions from being permanently neglected, while diminishing update variance supports convergence without an externally shrinking step size. Experiments further verify the theoretical findings. The contribution concerns the analyzed bandit algorithm and establishes why its existing stochastic update mechanism can suffice.
summary.tldr: The stochastic gradient bandit algorithm converges globally at O(1/t) with a constant step size because its updates provide sufficient exploration and shrinking noise.

title: Stochastic Gradient Succeeds for Bandits

abstract: Reconstructing natural images from fMRI recordings is a challenging task of great importance in neuroscience. The current architectures are bottlenecked because they fail to effectively capture the hierarchical processing of visual stimuli that takes place in the human brain. Motivated by that fact, we introduce a novel neural network architecture for the problem of neural decoding. Our architecture uses Hierarchical Variational Autoencoders (HVAEs) to learn meaningful representations of natural images and leverages their latent space hierarchy to learn voxel-to-image mappings. By mapping the early stages of the visual pathway to the first set of latent variables and the higher visual cortex areas to the deeper layers in the latent hierarchy, we are able to construct a latent variable neural decoding model that replicates the hierarchical visual information processing. Our model achieves better reconstructions compared to the state of the art and our ablation study indicates that the hierarchical structure of the latent space is responsible for that performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing images from fMRI measurements requires connecting patterns of brain activity to visual content. The paper argues that existing architectures are held back by how they represent this connection: they do not effectively capture the hierarchical processing of visual information in the brain.

The proposed architecture uses a hierarchical variational autoencoder to learn representations of natural images. Its multiple levels of latent variables then provide a structure for mapping brain measurements into images. Signals from early visual processing stages map to the first latent variables, while signals from higher visual cortex areas map to deeper levels of the hierarchy.

This organization makes the decoding model reflect the hierarchy of visual processing. The authors report better reconstructions than the state of the art, and an ablation study indicates that the latent hierarchy is responsible for the performance advantage. The contribution thus links the architecture's organization to the reconstruction results, rather than merely reporting an improvement from an unspecified decoding model.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical variational autoencoder aligns visual brain regions with latent levels to improve image reconstruction from fMRI.

title: Generative Decoding of Visual Stimuli

abstract: We present CTreeOT, a convergent, differentiable algorithm for matching two trees when each tree is conditioned on some input. Such conditional tree matching is useful for light-weight, few-shot adaptation of tree prediction models without parameter fine-tuning. CTreeOT includes an alignment algorithm that extends the popular Sinkhorn algorithm for matching tree nodes while supporting constraints on tree edges. The algorithm involves alternating between matrix rescaling and message passing updates, and can be efficiently expressed as GPU tensor operations. The second part of CTreeOT is fine-grained relevance-based reweighting of nodes that makes the match scores useful for prediction tasks. We demonstrate the usefulness of CTreeOT for cross-schema adaptation of Text-to-SQL, a popular semantic parsing task. We show that compared to state-of-the-art methods, we achieve significant increase in adaptation accuracy.

paragraphs: Tree prediction models produce structured outputs whose nodes and connections must work together. The paper introduces CTreeOT for matching two trees when each is conditioned on an input. Such matching supports lightweight adaptation from a few examples at inference time, without requiring parameter fine-tuning.

CTreeOT has two main components. Its alignment procedure extends Sinkhorn matching to accommodate constraints on tree edges, so matching can account for relationships beyond individual nodes. The procedure alternates matrix rescaling with message passing and can be implemented efficiently using GPU tensor operations. A second component reweights nodes according to their relevance, making the resulting match scores useful for prediction.

The algorithm is differentiable and has a convergence guarantee. The authors demonstrate it on adapting Text-to-SQL systems across database schemas, where they report a significant accuracy improvement over state-of-the-art methods. The result shows how structured matching and relevance weighting can support few-shot adaptation in this task without changing the prediction model's parameters.
summary.tldr: CTreeOT matches input-conditioned trees to enable few-shot adaptation without fine-tuning, improving cross-schema Text-to-SQL accuracy.

title: Conditional Tree Matching for Inference-Time Adaptation of Tree Prediction Models

abstract: We consider the problem of generating musical soundtracks in sync with rhythmic visual cues. Most existing works rely on pre-defined music representations, leading to the incompetence of generative flexibility and complexity. Other methods directly generating video-conditioned waveforms suffer from limited scenarios, short lengths, and unstable generation quality. To this end, we present Long-Term Rhythmic Video Soundtracker (LORIS), a novel framework to synthesize long-term conditional waveforms. Specifically, our framework consists of a latent conditional diffusion probabilistic model to perform waveform synthesis. Furthermore, a series of context-aware conditioning encoders are proposed to take temporal information into consideration for a long-term generation. Notably, we extend our model’s applicability from dances to multiple sports scenarios such as floor exercise and figure skating. To perform comprehensive evaluations, we establish a benchmark for rhythmic video soundtracks including the pre-processed dataset, improved evaluation metrics, and robust generative baselines. Extensive experiments show that our model generates long-term soundtracks with state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence. Codes are available at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/LORIS.

Existing approaches can be constrained by predefined music representations, while methods that directly generate waveforms have faced short outputs, limited application settings, and unstable quality. LORIS aims to support longer waveform generation conditioned on visual content.

The framework uses a latent conditional diffusion model for waveform synthesis. Context-aware conditioning encoders incorporate temporal information to support generation over longer spans. This makes the evolving video context part of the generation process. The authors also extend the application settings beyond dance to sports, including floor exercise and figure skating.

Alongside the model, the paper introduces a benchmark with preprocessed data, improved evaluation metrics, and generative baselines. Experiments report state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence for long-term soundtracks. These results address two connected requirements: producing convincing music and matching the visual rhythm. The benchmark provides a shared basis for evaluating both aspects of the soundtrack-generation problem.
summary.tldr: LORIS uses temporally conditioned diffusion to generate long musical soundtracks aligned with rhythmic video cues.

title: Long-Term Rhythmic Video Soundtracker

abstract: Despite the success of the Adam optimizer in practice, the theoretical understanding of its algorithmic components still remains limited. In particular, most existing analyses of Adam show the convergence rate that can be simply achieved by non-adative algorithms like SGD. In this work, we provide a different perspective based on online learning that underscores the importance of Adam’s algorithmic components. Inspired by Cutkosky et al. (2023), we consider the framework called online learning of updates/increments, where we choose the updates/increments of an optimizer based on an online learner. With this framework, the design of a good optimizer is reduced to the design of a good online learner. Our main observation is that Adam corresponds to a principled online learning framework called Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL). Building on this observation, we study the benefits of its algorithmic components from the online learning perspective.

paragraphs: Adam performs well in practice, but standard convergence analyses often yield rates that nonadaptive methods such as stochastic gradient descent can also achieve. That leaves a gap between demonstrating convergence and explaining the value of Adam’s particular components. This paper approaches that gap through online learning.

The authors use a framework in which an online learner selects the updates, or increments, made by an optimizer. This reframes optimizer construction as the problem of designing a good learner for those updates. The central observation is that Adam corresponds to Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, a principled online learning framework, when viewed through this formulation.

Building on that correspondence, the paper studies the benefits of Adam’s components from the online learning perspective. The contribution is an alternative explanation of the algorithm’s structure: its update rules can be understood as parts of a coherent learning procedure. This provides a framework for investigating why those components matter beyond what a generic convergence-rate comparison with stochastic gradient descent reveals.
summary.tldr: Viewing optimizer updates as online-learning decisions reveals Adam as a form of Follow-the-Regularized-Leader.

title: Understanding Adam Optimizer via Online Learning of Updates: Adam is FTRL in Disguise

abstract: During the last few years, the field of dynamical systems has been developing innovative tools to study the asymptotic behavior of different optimizers in the context of neural networks. In this work, we redefine an extensively studied optimizer, employing classical techniques from hyperbolic geometry. This new definition is linked to a non-linear differential equation as a continuous limit. Additionally, by utilizing Lyapunov stability concepts, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of its critical points.
