Additionally, by utilizing Lyapunov stability concepts, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of its critical points.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms generate a sequence of changes to a model’s parameters. A dynamical-systems perspective studies the behavior of those changes over time, especially what happens as optimization continues. This paper takes that perspective on an extensively studied optimizer, redefining it through classical techniques from hyperbolic geometry.

The authors connect the resulting definition to a nonlinear differential equation through a continuous limit. This connection provides a mathematical description of the optimizer’s evolution in continuous time. Its role is to make the long-term behavior accessible to tools from differential equations and stability analysis, linking the geometric reformulation of the optimizer to a dynamical model.

The paper then uses Lyapunov stability concepts to analyze the asymptotic behavior of critical points. Such analysis concerns how the dynamics behave around those points over time. The stated contribution is a theoretical treatment of the redefined optimizer: hyperbolic geometry supplies its formulation, the continuous limit supplies the differential equation, and stability theory supplies a way to examine its eventual behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates an optimizer using hyperbolic geometry and studies its continuous-time critical-point behavior through Lyapunov stability.

title: Hyperbolic Optimizer as a Dynamical System

abstract: The local and global interpretability of various ML models has been studied extensively in recent years. However, despite significant progress in the field, many known results remain informal or lack sufficient mathematical rigor. We propose a framework for bridging this gap, by using computational complexity theory to assess local and global perspectives of interpreting ML models. We begin by proposing proofs for two novel insights that are essential for our analysis: (1) a duality between local and global forms of explanations; and (2) the inherent uniqueness of certain global explanation forms. We then use these insights to evaluate the complexity of computing explanations, across three model types representing the extremes of the interpretability spectrum: (1) linear models; (2) decision trees; and (3) neural networks. Our findings offer insights into both the local and global interpretability of these models. For instance, under standard complexity assumptions such as P != NP, we prove that selecting global sufficient subsets in linear models is computationally harder than selecting local subsets. Interestingly, with neural networks and decision trees, the opposite is true: it is harder to carry out this task locally than globally. We believe that our findings demonstrate how examining explainability through a computational complexity lens can help us develop a more rigorous grasp of the inherent interpretability of ML models.

paragraphs: Explaining a single prediction and explaining a model’s behavior across inputs are different computational tasks. This paper gives those local and global perspectives a formal treatment using computational complexity theory. The aim is to determine how difficult particular explanation problems are, moving beyond informal judgments about which model types seem interpretable.

The authors first prove a duality between local and global explanations and establish uniqueness for certain forms of global explanation. They then use these results to analyze linear models, decision trees, and neural networks. These model families provide contrasting cases for examining whether an explanation task becomes easier or harder when its scope changes.

For selecting sufficient subsets, the answer depends on the model family. Under standard complexity assumptions such as P not equaling NP, the global task is harder than the local task for linear models. For decision trees and neural networks, the ordering reverses. This shows that the computational difficulty of explanation depends jointly on the model, the explanation form, and whether the requested explanation is local or global.
summary.tldr: The relative difficulty of local and global explanations reverses across model families for the sufficient-subset task studied.

title: Local vs. Global Interpretability: A Computational Complexity Perspective

abstract: Neural audio synthesis methods now allow specifying ideas in natural language. However, these methods produce results that cannot be easily tweaked, as they are based on large latent spaces and up to billions of uninterpretable parameters. We propose a text-to-audio generation method that leverages a virtual modular sound synthesizer with only 78 parameters. Synthesizers have long been used by skilled sound designers for media like music and film due to their flexibility and intuitive controls. Our method, CTAG, iteratively updates a synthesizer’s parameters to produce high-quality audio renderings of text prompts that can be easily inspected and tweaked. Sounds produced this way are also more abstract, capturing essential conceptual features over fine-grained acoustic details, akin to how simple sketches can vividly convey visual concepts. Our results show how CTAG produces sounds that are distinctive, perceived as artistic, and yet similarly identifiable to recent neural audio synthesis models, positioning it as a valuable and complementary tool.

Its appeal combines recognizable text-driven generation with a sound-making representation that remains accessible to subsequent human editing.
summary.tldr: CTAG generates recognizable, artistic sounds from text by adjusting 78 synthesizer parameters that remain easy to inspect and edit.

title: Creative Text-to-Audio Generation via Synthesizer Programming

abstract: Error correction codes are a crucial part of the physical communication layer, ensuring the reliable transfer of data over noisy channels. The design of optimal linear block codes capable of being efficiently decoded is of major concern, especially for short block lengths. While neural decoders have recently demonstrated their advantage over classical decoding techniques, the neural design of the codes remains a challenge. In this work, we propose for the first time a unified encoder-decoder training of binary linear block codes. To this end, we adapt the coding setting to support efficient and differentiable training of the code for end-to-end optimization over the order two Galois field. We also propose a novel Transformer model in which the self-attention masking is performed in a differentiable fashion for the efficient backpropagation of the code gradient. Our results show that (i) the proposed decoder outperforms existing neural decoding on conventional codes, (ii) the suggested framework generates codes that outperform the analogous conventional codes, and (iii) the codes we developed not only excel with our decoder but also show enhanced performance with traditional decoding techniques.

Designing effective linear block codes that are also efficiently decodable is especially important for short blocks. Although neural decoders have shown advantages, learning the code itself remains difficult. This paper proposes jointly training the encoder and decoder for binary linear block codes.

They also introduce a Transformer whose attention mask is differentiable. This allows gradients associated with the code to propagate through the model, supporting an end-to-end learning process.

Those learned codes also improve performance with traditional decoding methods. This final result matters because it shows that the benefits extend beyond pairing the codes with the particular neural decoder used to develop them.
summary.tldr: Joint differentiable training learns binary linear codes and a Transformer decoder, with learned-code gains also extending to traditional decoders.

title: Learning Linear Block Error Correction Codes

abstract: Fourier analysis has been an instrumental tool in the development of signal processing. This leads us to wonder whether this framework could similarly benefit generative modelling. In this paper, we explore this question through the scope of time series diffusion models. More specifically, we analyze whether representing time series in the frequency domain is a useful inductive bias for score-based diffusion models. By starting from the canonical SDE formulation of diffusion in the time domain, we show that a dual diffusion process occurs in the frequency domain with an important nuance: Brownian motions are replaced by what we call mirrored Brownian motions, characterized by mirror symmetries among their components. Building on this insight, we show how to adapt the denoising score matching approach to implement diffusion models in the frequency domain. This results in frequency diffusion models, which we compare to canonical time diffusion models. Our empirical evaluation on real-world datasets, covering various domains like healthcare and finance, shows that frequency diffusion models better capture the training distribution than time diffusion models. We explain this observation by showing that time series from these datasets tend to be more localized in the frequency domain than in the time domain, which makes them easier to model in the former case. All our observations point towards impactful synergies between Fourier analysis and diffusion models.

The question is whether that representation makes the structure of real time-series data easier for a generative model to learn.

Starting from the standard stochastic differential equation for time-domain diffusion, the authors derive a corresponding frequency-domain process. A key difference is that its noise involves mirrored Brownian motions, whose components have mirror symmetries. The authors explain this through the greater localization of the studied signals in frequency space. The findings support frequency-domain representation as a useful modeling bias for these datasets, linking the empirical improvement to a structural property of the data.
summary.tldr: Frequency-domain diffusion better captures the studied time-series distributions, using a noise process that respects Fourier mirror symmetries.

title: Time Series Diffusion in the Frequency Domain

abstract: In this paper, we study semi-supervised graph classification, which aims at accurately predicting the categories of graphs in scenarios with limited labeled graphs and abundant unlabeled graphs. Despite the promising capability of graph neural networks (GNNs), they typically require a large number of costly labeled graphs, while a wealth of unlabeled graphs fail to be effectively utilized. Moreover, GNNs are inherently limited to encoding local neighborhood information using message-passing mechanisms, thus lacking the ability to model higher-order dependencies among nodes. To tackle these challenges, we propose a Hypergraph-Enhanced DuAL framework named HEAL for semi-supervised graph classification, which captures graph semantics from the perspective of the hypergraph and the line graph, respectively. Specifically, to better explore the higher-order relationships among nodes, we design a hypergraph structure learning to adaptively learn complex node dependencies beyond pairwise relations. Meanwhile, based on the learned hypergraph, we introduce a line graph to capture the interaction between hyperedges, thereby better mining the underlying semantic structures. Finally, we develop a relational consistency learning to facilitate knowledge transfer between the two branches and provide better mutual guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world graph datasets verify the effectiveness of the proposed method against existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Graph classification assigns a category to an entire graph. HEAL addresses settings with few labeled graphs and many unlabeled ones, where effective use of the available structure matters especially strongly. The paper also targets the difficulty of representing relationships that involve groups of nodes beyond ordinary pairwise connections.

Its first branch learns a hypergraph structure adaptively. Hyperedges represent relationships among groups of nodes, allowing the model to explore more complex dependencies. A second branch builds a line graph from the learned hypergraph to represent interactions between those hyperedges. Together, the branches examine relationships within node groups and relationships between the groups themselves.

Relational consistency learning connects the two branches so they can transfer knowledge and guide one another. This makes their distinct structural views part of a shared learning framework for semi-supervised classification. Experiments on real-world graph datasets support HEAL's effectiveness against existing leading methods. The reported contribution combines richer structural representations with a mechanism for coordinating them when labeled examples are scarce.
summary.tldr: HEAL combines learned hypergraphs and interactions between hyperedges to improve graph classification with limited labels.

title: Hypergraph-enhanced Dual Semi-supervised Graph Classification

abstract: Supervised matrix factorization (SMF) is a classical machine learning method that seeks low-dimensional feature extraction and classification tasks at the same time. Training an SMF model involves solving a non-convex and factor-wise constrained optimization problem with at least three blocks of parameters. Due to the high non-convexity and constraints, theoretical understanding of the optimization landscape of SMF has been limited. In this paper, we provide an extensive local landscape analysis for SMF and derive several theoretical and practical applications. Analyzing diagonal blocks of the Hessian naturally leads to a block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm with adaptive step sizes. We provide global convergence and iteration complexity guarantees for this algorithm. Full Hessian analysis gives minimum $L_{2}$-regularization to guarantee local strong convexity and robustness of parameters. We establish a local estimation guarantee under a statistical SMF model. We also propose a novel GPU-friendly neural implementation of the BCD algorithm and validate our theoretical findings through numerical experiments. Our work contributes to a deeper understanding of SMF optimization, offering insights into the optimization landscape and providing practical solutions to enhance its performance.

paragraphs: Supervised matrix factorization learns a low-dimensional representation while also learning to classify examples. Its training objective is difficult to analyze because it is non-convex, has constraints on individual factors, and contains at least three parameter blocks. This paper studies the objective's local geometry to derive both theoretical guarantees and practical training methods.

Analyzing diagonal blocks of the Hessian, which describes curvature, leads to a block coordinate descent algorithm with adaptive step sizes. The authors provide global convergence and iteration complexity guarantees for that algorithm. Analyzing the full Hessian yields a minimum level of L2 regularization sufficient to guarantee local strong convexity and parameter robustness.

The paper also establishes a local estimation guarantee under a statistical model of supervised matrix factorization. For implementation, it proposes a GPU-friendly neural version of the block coordinate descent algorithm and supports the theoretical findings with numerical experiments. The contribution connects local curvature analysis to optimization, regularization, statistical estimation, and an implementation designed to use modern computing hardware.
summary.tldr: Local curvature analysis of supervised matrix factorization yields an adaptive optimization algorithm, regularization guarantees, and a GPU-friendly implementation.

title: Supervised Matrix Factorization: Local Landscape Analysis and Applications

abstract: We study the contextual bandits with knapsack (CBwK) problem under the high-dimensional setting where the dimension of the feature is large. We investigate how to exploit the sparsity structure to achieve improved regret for the CBwK problem. To this end, we first develop an online variant of the hard thresholding algorithm that performs the optimal sparse estimation. We further combine our online estimator with a primal-dual framework, where we assign a dual variable to each knapsack constraint and utilize an online learning algorithm to update the dual variable, thereby controlling the consumption of the knapsack capacity. We show that this integrated approach allows us to achieve a sublinear regret that depends logarithmically on the feature dimension, thus improving the polynomial dependency established in the previous literature. We also apply our framework to the high-dimension contextual bandit problem without the knapsack constraint and achieve optimal regret in both the data-poor regime and the data-rich regime.

We further combine our online estimator with a primal-dual framework, where we assign a dual variable to each knapsack constraint and utilize an online learning algorithm to update the dual variable, thereby controlling the consumption of the knapsack capacity. We also apply our framework to the high-dimension contextual bandit problem without the knapsack constraint and achieve optimal regret in both the data-poor regime and the data-rich regime.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions described by many features when actions also consume limited resources. The learner must discover rewarding choices while staying within resource budgets, represented by knapsack constraints. The central opportunity is sparsity: useful structure can be concentrated in a relatively small portion of a high-dimensional representation.

The authors develop an online hard-thresholding estimator with optimal sparse-estimation performance. They combine it with a primal-dual method that assigns a separate dual variable to each resource constraint. An online learning algorithm updates these variables, allowing the decision process to account for how quickly each resource budget is being consumed.

The resulting method achieves sublinear regret with logarithmic dependence on feature dimension, improving the polynomial dependence of previous results. Regret measures the performance gap accumulated while learning, so sublinear growth means that gap grows more slowly than the decision horizon. The paper also treats the version without resource constraints, obtaining optimal regret in both data-poor and data-rich regimes. These results show how sparse estimation and budget management can be coordinated.
summary.tldr: Combining online sparse estimation with resource-budget control yields bandit regret that depends only logarithmically on feature dimension.

title: High-dimensional Linear Bandits with Knapsacks

abstract: We introduce a new approach for applying sampling-based sketches to two and three mode tensors. We illustrate our technique to construct sketches for the classical problems of $\ell_0$ sampling and producing $\ell_1$ embeddings. In both settings we achieve sketches that can be applied to a rank one tensor in $(\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes q}$ (for $q=2,3$) in time scaling with $d$ rather than $d^2$ or $d^3$. Our main idea is a particular sampling construction based on fast convolution which allows us to quickly compute sums over sufficiently random subsets of tensor entries.

We illustrate our technique to construct sketches for the classical problems of $\ell_0$ sampling and producing $\ell_1$ embeddings. In both settings we achieve sketches that can be applied to a rank one tensor in $(\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes q}$ (for $q=2,3$) in time scaling with $d$ rather than $d^2$ or $d^3$. Our main idea is a particular sampling construction based on fast convolution which allows us to quickly compute sums over sufficiently random subsets of tensor entries.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to apply sampling-based sketches to tensors with two or three modes. A sketch provides a reduced representation for a particular computational task. The authors demonstrate their construction for two classical tasks: zero-norm sampling and producing one-norm embeddings. The focus is the cost of applying these sketches to structured tensor inputs.

The key setting is a rank-one tensor built from vectors of dimension d. Although the corresponding tensor has d squared or d cubed entries, the proposed sketches can be applied in time that scales with d. The stated speed result specifically concerns rank-one inputs and tensors with two or three modes.

The construction uses fast convolution to calculate sums over subsets of tensor entries. Those subsets are sufficiently random for the sampling-based sketches, while their construction makes the sums efficient to compute. This is the central algorithmic contribution: it combines the randomness needed by the sketch with computation that exploits the tensor's structure, avoiding a running time tied to the full number of entries in the stated setting.
summary.tldr: Fast-convolution sampling lets sketches for two- and three-mode rank-one tensors be applied in time scaling with vector dimension rather than tensor size.

title: Fast Sampling-Based Sketches for Tensors

abstract: Tensor networks are efficient for extremely high-dimensional representation, but their model selection, known as tensor network structure search (TN-SS), is a challenging problem. Although several works have targeted TN-SS, most existing algorithms are manually crafted heuristics with poor performance, suffering from the curse of dimensionality and local convergence. In this work, we jump out of the box, studying how to harness large language models (LLMs) to automatically discover new TN-SS algorithms, replacing the involvement of human experts. By observing how human experts innovate in research, we model their common workflow and propose an automatic algorithm discovery framework called tnGPS. The proposed framework is an elaborate prompting pipeline that instruct LLMs to generate new TN-SS algorithms through iterative refinement and enhancement. The experimental results demonstrate that the algorithms discovered by tnGPS exhibit superior performance in benchmarks compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChaoLiAtRIKEN/tngps.

paragraphs: Tensor networks offer efficient representations of extremely high-dimensional objects, but choosing their structure is difficult. Existing structure-search algorithms are often manually designed heuristics, and the paper identifies dimensionality and local convergence as persistent obstacles. It investigates whether language models can help discover better search algorithms automatically.

The proposed tnGPS framework models aspects of how human researchers develop algorithms. An elaborate prompting pipeline guides a language model through repeated generation, refinement, and enhancement of tensor-network structure-search algorithms. The object being improved is the search procedure itself, rather than just a single tensor-network structure.

In benchmark experiments, algorithms discovered through tnGPS outperform current state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the use of an iterative language-model workflow for algorithm discovery in this particular problem area. The contribution is both the discovery framework and evidence that its generated algorithms can be competitive: the language model participates in designing how the search is performed, reducing reliance on manually crafting each new heuristic.
summary.tldr: tnGPS uses iterative language-model prompting to discover tensor-network structure-search algorithms that outperform existing methods on evaluated benchmarks.

title: tnGPS: Discovering Unknown Tensor Network Structure Search Algorithms via Large Language Models (LLMs)

abstract: Normalizing flows are a flexible class of probability distributions, expressed as transformations of a simple base distribution. A limitation of standard normalizing flows is representing distributions with heavy tails, which arise in applications to both density estimation and variational inference. A popular current solution to this problem is to use a heavy tailed base distribution. We argue this can lead to poor performance due to the difficulty of optimising neural networks, such as normalizing flows, under heavy tailed input. We propose an alternative, "tail transform flow” (TTF), which uses a Gaussian base distribution and a final transformation layer which can produce heavy tails. Experimental results show this approach outperforms current methods, especially when the target distribution has large dimension or tail weight.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows describe probability distributions by transforming samples from a simple starting distribution. Standard versions struggle with heavy tails, where unusually extreme values retain substantial probability. This matters for both density estimation and variational inference. A common response is to start with a heavy-tailed distribution, so the model receives those properties at its input.

The authors argue that this remedy can make neural-network optimization difficult and lead to poor performance. Their alternative, tail transform flow, starts from a Gaussian distribution and adds a final transformation capable of producing heavy tails. The design changes where tail behavior enters the model: it is introduced at the output rather than imposed on the input.

Experiments show that this approach outperforms current methods, particularly for targets with many dimensions or greater tail weight. The findings support separating the choice of an input distribution for optimization from the tail behavior needed in the final distribution. The reported advantage is especially relevant to the demanding targets identified in those experiments.
summary.tldr: Tail transform flows combine a Gaussian base with a final heavy-tail transformation, improving reported performance especially on high-dimensional or heavier-tailed targets.

title: Flexible Tails for Normalizing Flows

abstract: A key paradigm to improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) is to allocate more inference-time compute to search against a verifier or reward model. This process can then be utilized to refine the pretrained model or distill its reasoning patterns into more efficient models. In this paper, we study inference-time computation by viewing chain-of-thought (CoT) generation as a metastable Markov process: easy reasoning steps (e.g., algebraic manipulations) form densely connected clusters, while hard reasoning steps (e.g., applying a relevant theorem) create sparse, low-probability edges between clusters, leading to phase transitions at longer timescales. Under this framework, we prove that implementing a search protocol that rewards sparse edges improves CoT by decreasing the expected number of steps to reach different clusters. In contrast, we establish a limit on reasoning capability when the model is restricted to local information of the pretrained graph. We also show that the information gained by search can be utilized to obtain a better reasoning model: (1) the pretrained model can be directly finetuned to favor sparse edges via policy gradient methods, and moreover (2) a compressed metastable representation of the reasoning dynamics can be distilled into a smaller, more efficient model.

paragraphs: This paper models chain-of-thought reasoning as a Markov process with regions that are easy to move within but difficult to leave. Routine reasoning steps create densely connected clusters. Harder moves, such as selecting a relevant theorem, form sparse connections between clusters. This metastable structure explains how progress can depend on rare transitions.

Within this framework, the authors prove that a search protocol rewarding sparse connections reduces the expected number of steps needed to reach other clusters. They also establish a limit on reasoning when a model uses only local information from the pretrained graph. The benefit of search is therefore tied to finding consequential connections that local information alone cannot adequately exploit.

The paper further shows how information acquired through search can improve a reasoning model. Policy-gradient fine-tuning can encourage the pretrained model to take sparse connections, while distillation can transfer a compressed representation of the metastable dynamics into a smaller model. These are theoretical results within the proposed framework, linking inference-time search to subsequent reinforcement learning and more efficient representations of reasoning.
summary.tldr: A metastable model of reasoning explains provable benefits of searching for rare transitions and transferring that knowledge through fine-tuning or distillation.

title: Metastable Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Provable Benefits of Search, RL and Distillation

abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation has emerged as a promising solution for generating accurate object masks in complex 3D scenes by incorporating user-provided clicks. However, two critical challenges remain underexplored: (1) effectively generalizing from sparse user clicks to produce accurate segmentations and (2) quantifying predictive uncertainty to help users identify unreliable regions. In this work, we propose NPISeg3D, a novel probabilistic framework that builds upon Neural Processes (NPs) to address these challenges. Specifically, NPISeg3D introduces a hierarchical latent variable structure with scene-specific and object-specific latent variables to enhance few-shot generalization by capturing both global context and object-specific characteristics. Additionally, we design a probabilistic prototype modulator that adaptively modulates click prototypes with object-specific latent variables, improving the model’s ability to capture object-aware context and quantify predictive uncertainty. Experiments on four 3D point cloud datasets demonstrate that NPISeg3D achieves superior segmentation performance with fewer clicks while providing reliable uncertainty estimations.

Specifically, NPISeg3D introduces a hierarchical latent variable structure with scene-specific and object-specific latent variables to enhance few-shot generalization by capturing both global context and object-specific characteristics. paragraphs: Interactive 3D segmentation uses a person’s clicks to identify an object within a complex scene. A useful system must infer the rest of the object from limited guidance and indicate where its predictions may be unreliable. NPISeg3D addresses both needs through a probabilistic framework based on Neural Processes.

The model uses a hierarchy of latent variables: one level represents the scene, while another captures characteristics of individual objects. This lets sparse clicks be interpreted using both broader context and object-specific information. A probabilistic prototype modulator further adapts the representations associated with clicks using the object-level latent variables, supporting object-aware predictions and uncertainty estimation within the same framework.

Experiments on four 3D point-cloud datasets report better segmentation with fewer clicks, alongside reliable uncertainty estimates. The results support combining contextual inference and uncertainty modeling rather than treating user guidance only as a set of isolated labels. For interaction, the two benefits are complementary: fewer clicks can produce useful masks, and uncertainty can help users recognize regions that merit further attention.
summary.tldr: NPISeg3D uses scene- and object-level latent variables to improve 3D segmentation from sparse clicks while estimating prediction uncertainty.

title: Probabilistic Interactive 3D Segmentation with Hierarchical Neural Processes

abstract: Neural operators generalize neural networks to learn mappings between function spaces from data. They are commonly used to learn solution operators of parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) or propagators of time-dependent PDEs. However, to make them useful in high-stakes simulation scenarios, their inherent predictive error must be quantified reliably. We introduce LUNO, a novel framework for approximate Bayesian uncertainty quantification in trained neural operators. Our approach leverages model linearization to push (Gaussian) weight-space uncertainty forward to the neural operator’s predictions. We show that this can be interpreted as a probabilistic version of the concept of currying from functional programming, yielding a function-valued (Gaussian) random process belief. Our framework provides a practical yet theoretically sound way to apply existing Bayesian deep learning methods such as the linearized Laplace approximation to neural operators. Just as the underlying neural operator, our approach is resolution-agnostic by design. The method adds minimal prediction overhead, can be applied post-hoc without retraining the network, and scales to large models and datasets. We evaluate these aspects in a case study on Fourier neural operators.

We introduce LUNO, a novel framework for approximate Bayesian uncertainty quantification in trained neural operators. Our approach leverages model linearization to push (Gaussian) weight-space uncertainty forward to the neural operator’s predictions. We show that this can be interpreted as a probabilistic version of the concept of currying from functional programming, yielding a function-valued (Gaussian) random process belief. Our framework provides a practical yet theoretically sound way to apply existing Bayesian deep learning methods such as the linearized Laplace approximation to neural operators. Just as the underlying neural operator, our approach is resolution-agnostic by design. The method adds minimal prediction overhead, can be applied post-hoc without retraining the network, and scales to large models and datasets. We evaluate these aspects in a case study on Fourier neural operators.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions, such as mappings associated with partial differential equation solutions. LUNO adds approximate Bayesian uncertainty quantification to an already trained neural operator.

The method linearizes the model and propagates Gaussian uncertainty over its weights into uncertainty over predicted functions. The resulting belief is a function-valued Gaussian random process. This creates a theoretical bridge from existing Bayesian deep learning techniques, including the linearized Laplace approximation, to models whose outputs are functions rather than fixed collections of numbers.

A Fourier neural operator case study evaluates these properties. title: Linearization Turns Neural Operators into Function-Valued Gaussian Processes

abstract: Despite their success in many domains, large language models (LLMs) remain under-studied in scenarios requiring optimal decision-making under uncertainty. This is crucial as many real-world applications, ranging from personalized recommendations to healthcare interventions, demand that LLMs not only predict but also actively learn to make optimal decisions through exploration. In this work, we measure LLMs’ (in)ability to make optimal decisions in bandits, a state-less reinforcement learning setting relevant to many applications. We develop a comprehensive suite of environments, including both context-free and contextual bandits with varying task difficulties, to benchmark LLMs’ performance. Motivated by the existence of optimal exploration algorithms, we propose efficient ways to integrate this algorithmic knowledge into LLMs: by providing explicit algorithm-guided support during inference; and through algorithm distillation via in-context demonstrations and fine-tuning, using synthetic data generated from these algorithms. Impressively, these techniques allow us to achieve superior exploration performance with smaller models, surpassing larger models on various tasks. We conducted an extensive ablation study to shed light on various factors, such as task difficulty and data representation, that influence the efficiency of LLM exploration. Additionally, we conduct a rigorous analysis of the LLM’s exploration efficiency using the concept of regret, linking its ability to explore to the model size and underlying algorithm.

paragraphs: An effective decision-maker must sometimes choose an action to learn about its consequences, rather than simply select the option that currently looks best. EVOLvE investigates how well language models perform this exploration in bandit problems, a reinforcement learning setting without evolving states. Its evaluation suite includes both context-free and contextual tasks at different difficulty levels.

The authors use knowledge from exploration algorithms to improve language-model decisions. One approach supplies explicit algorithmic guidance during inference. Another transfers algorithm behavior through demonstrations in the prompt or fine-tuning on synthetic examples generated by those algorithms. These routes test whether established decision rules can strengthen exploration without relying only on model scale.

The techniques enable smaller models to outperform larger models on various evaluated tasks. Additional experiments examine how difficulty and data representation influence exploration efficiency. A regret-based analysis links exploration performance to model size and the underlying algorithm. Together, these results show that incorporating algorithmic knowledge can materially improve the decision-making behavior measured by this benchmark.
summary.tldr: EVOLvE benchmarks language-model exploration and shows that algorithmic guidance can help smaller models outperform larger ones.

title: EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For In-Context Exploration

abstract: Designing effective reward functions in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a significant challenge, often leading to suboptimal or misaligned behaviors in complex, coordinated environments. We introduce Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning from Multi-phase Human Feedback of Mixed Quality ($\text{M}^3\text{HF}$), a novel framework that integrates multi-phase human feedback of mixed quality into the MARL training process. By involving humans with diverse expertise levels to provide iterative guidance, $\text{M}^3\text{HF}$ leverages both expert and non-expert feedback to continuously refine agents’ policies. During training, we strategically pause agent learning for human evaluation, parse feedback using large language models to assign it appropriately and update reward functions through predefined templates and adaptive weights by using weight decay and performance-based adjustments. Our approach enables the integration of nuanced human insights across various levels of quality, enhancing the interpretability and robustness of multi-agent cooperation. Empirical results in challenging environments demonstrate that $\text{M}^3\text{HF}$ significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, effectively addressing the complexities of reward design in MARL and enabling broader human participation in the training process.

paragraphs: Designing rewards for cooperating reinforcement learning agents is difficult because a reward can encourage ineffective or misaligned behavior. M³HF addresses this problem through repeated human involvement during training. It accepts guidance from people with different levels of expertise, aiming to use both expert and non-expert feedback to improve the agents' policies.

The training process pauses at selected points for human evaluation. Large language models interpret that feedback and assign it appropriately, after which reward functions are updated through predefined templates. Adaptive weights, weight decay, and performance-based adjustments manage the feedback's influence. This creates a recurring connection between human judgments about cooperation and the rewards that shape subsequent agent learning.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in challenging environments, alongside enhanced interpretability and robustness of cooperation. The approach matters because it makes reward design an iterative process that can incorporate nuanced feedback of mixed quality. Its broader participation claim rests on explicitly including non-experts, while its empirical findings support the usefulness of that feedback-driven training framework.
summary.tldr: M³HF repeatedly translates expert and non-expert human feedback into reward updates to improve multi-agent cooperation.

title: M$^3$HF: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning from Multi-phase Human Feedback of Mixed Quality

abstract: The quest for analytical solutions to differential equations has traditionally been constrained by the need for extensive mathematical expertise. Machine learning methods like genetic algorithms have shown promise in this domain, but are hindered by significant computational time and the complexity of their derived solutions. This paper introduces SSDE (Symbolic Solver for Differential Equations), a novel reinforcement learning-based approach that derives symbolic closed-form solutions for various differential equations. Evaluations across a diverse set of ordinary and partial differential equations demonstrate that SSDE outperforms existing machine learning methods, delivering superior accuracy and efficiency in obtaining analytical solutions.

paragraphs: Finding an analytical solution to a differential equation traditionally requires substantial mathematical expertise. The desired result is a symbolic expression describing the solution, making the search for a suitable formula central to the task. This paper presents SSDE, a Symbolic Solver for Differential Equations, as a machine-learning approach to that search.

SSDE uses reinforcement learning to derive symbolic closed-form solutions for various differential equations. The motivation comes from difficulties with earlier machine-learning approaches, including genetic algorithms: their searches can require considerable computation and produce complicated solutions. SSDE investigates reinforcement learning as another way to obtain analytical expressions efficiently.

The evaluations include both ordinary and partial differential equations across a diverse test set. The authors report better accuracy and efficiency than existing machine-learning methods for obtaining analytical solutions. These findings support reinforcement learning as a promising tool for symbolic equation solving in the evaluated settings. The scope of the stated result is the successful treatment of various equations, rather than a claim that every differential equation admits a solution SSDE can find.
summary.tldr: SSDE uses reinforcement learning to find symbolic solutions to differential equations, improving accuracy and efficiency in the reported evaluations.

title: Closed-form Solutions: A New Perspective on Solving Differential Equations

abstract: In silico modeling of transcriptional responses to perturbations is crucial for advancing our understanding of cellular processes and disease mechanisms. We present PertEval-scFM, a standardized framework designed to evaluate models for perturbation effect prediction. We apply PertEval-scFM to benchmark zero-shot single-cell foundation model (scFM) embeddings against baseline models to assess whether these contextualized representations enhance perturbation effect prediction. Our results show that scFM embeddings offer limited improvement over simple baseline models in the zero-shot setting, particularly under distribution shift. Overall, this study provides a systematic evaluation of zero-shot scFM embeddings for perturbation effect prediction, highlighting the challenges of this task and the limitations of current-generation scFMs. Our findings underscore the need for specialized models and high-quality datasets that capture a broader range of cellular states. Source code and documentation can be found at: https://github.com/aaronwtr/PertEval.

paragraphs: Predicting how cellular gene expression responds to perturbations could help researchers study cell processes and disease mechanisms computationally. PertEval-scFM provides a standardized framework for evaluating models on this task. Its central question is whether representations from single-cell foundation models improve prediction of these responses compared with simpler baseline models.

The evaluation specifically examines foundation-model embeddings used in a zero-shot setting. These embeddings provide contextualized representations, but the benchmark asks whether that representation translates into useful predictive gains. The authors find only limited improvement over simple baselines, with the problem particularly apparent under distribution shift, when the prediction setting differs from the data conditions supporting the model.

The result identifies a task-specific limitation of the evaluated zero-shot embeddings rather than establishing that every use of single-cell foundation models is ineffective. The authors argue for specialized models and higher-quality datasets covering a broader range of cellular states. Their contribution is both an evaluation framework and evidence that broad pretraining alone has not resolved perturbation-effect prediction in this setting.
summary.tldr: PertEval-scFM finds limited gains from zero-shot single-cell foundation-model embeddings for perturbation prediction, especially under distribution shift.

title: PertEval-scFM: Benchmarking Single-Cell Foundation Models for Perturbation Effect Prediction

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex reasoning tasks, particularly in mathematics. However, the domain of physics reasoning presents unique challenges that have received significantly less attention. Existing benchmarks often fall short in evaluating LLMs’ abilities on the breadth and depth of undergraduate-level physics, underscoring the need for a comprehensive evaluation. To fill this gap, we introduce UGPhysics, a large-scale and diverse benchmark specifically designed to evaluate UnderGraduate-level Physics (UGPhysics) reasoning with LLMs. UGPhysics includes 5,520 undergraduate-level physics problems in both English and Chinese across 13 subjects with seven different answer types and four distinct physics reasoning skills, all rigorously screened for data leakage. Additionally, we develop a Model-Assistant Rule-based Judgment (MARJ) pipeline specifically tailored for assessing physics problems, ensuring accurate evaluation. Our evaluation of 31 leading LLMs shows that the highest overall accuracy, 49.8% (achieved by OpenAI-o1-mini), emphasizes the need for models with stronger physics reasoning skills, beyond math abilities. We hope UGPhysics, along with MARJ, will drive future advancements in AI for physics reasoning. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/YangLabHKUST/UGPhysics.

paragraphs: UGPhysics evaluates language models on undergraduate physics reasoning, a domain the authors argue is insufficiently covered by existing benchmarks. The motivation is that success in mathematics does not by itself establish broad physics reasoning ability. The benchmark is designed to examine both the range and depth of that ability.

It contains 5,520 problems in English and Chinese, spanning 13 subjects, seven answer types, and four physics reasoning skills. The problems undergo rigorous screening for data leakage. The contribution is therefore both a broad test collection and a specialized assessment pipeline, providing a basis for measuring progress in physics reasoning beyond mathematical problem-solving performance.
summary.tldr: UGPhysics tests undergraduate physics reasoning across 5,520 problems, with the best of 31 evaluated models reaching 49.8% accuracy.

title: UGPhysics: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Undergraduate Physics Reasoning with Large Language Models

abstract: ANN-to-SNN conversion has emerged as a key approach to train Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), particularly for Transformer architectures, as it maps pre-trained ANN parameters to SNN equivalents without requiring retraining, thereby preserving ANN accuracy while eliminating training costs. Among various coding methods used in ANN-to-SNN conversion, time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding, which allows each neuron to at most one spike, offers significantly lower energy consumption. However, while previous TTFS-based SNNs have achieved comparable performance with convolutional ANNs, the attention mechanism and nonlinear layers in Transformer architectures remains a challenge by existing SNNs with TTFS coding. This paper proposes a new neuron structure for TTFS coding that expands its representational range and enhances the capability to process nonlinear functions, along with detailed designs of nonlinear neurons for different layers in Transformer. Experimental results on different models demonstrate that our proposed method can achieve high accuracy with significantly lower energy consumption. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to focus on converting Transformer to SNN with TTFS coding.

paragraphs: Converting a pretrained artificial neural network into a spiking network offers a way to use existing learned parameters without retraining. Time-to-first-spike coding is particularly attractive for energy efficiency because each neuron emits at most one spike. However, applying this coding to transformers is difficult because attention and nonlinear layers require representations that existing approaches struggle to provide.

TTFSFormer introduces a neuron structure that expands the representational range of time-to-first-spike coding and improves its ability to process nonlinear functions. The paper also provides nonlinear neuron designs tailored to different transformer layers. These components address the operations that make transformer conversion more challenging than earlier applications of the coding scheme to convolutional networks.

Experiments across different models show high accuracy with significantly lower energy consumption. The authors describe the work as the first focused on transformer-to-spiking conversion using time-to-first-spike coding. The reported findings connect architectural changes at the neuron level with the broader goal of efficient transformer execution, extending a low-spike coding approach to attention-based models.
summary.tldr: TTFSFormer introduces neuron designs that support transformer conversion to time-to-first-spike networks with high accuracy and lower measured energy consumption.

title: TTFSFormer: A TTFS-based Lossless Conversion of Spiking Transformer

abstract: Language models are extensively evaluated, but correctly interpreting evaluation results requires knowledge of train-test overlap, which refers to the extent to which the language model is trained on the very data it is being tested on. The public currently lacks adequate information about train-test overlap: most models have no public train-test overlap statistics, and third parties cannot directly measure train-test overlap since they do not have access to the training data. To make this clear, we document the practices of 30 models, finding that just 9 models report train-test overlap: 4 models release training data under open-source licenses, enabling the community to directly measure train-test overlap, and 5 models publish their train-test overlap methodology and statistics. By engaging with language model developers, we provide novel information about train-test overlap for three additional models. Overall, this position paper argues that language model developers should publish train-test overlap statistics and/or training data whenever they report evaluation results on public test sets. We hope our work increases transparency into train-test overlap to increase the community-wide trust in model evaluations.

The paper’s goal is to make model evaluations easier to interpret and strengthen community trust in the results developers report.
summary.tldr: An examination of 30 models motivates a call for developers to disclose training–test overlap alongside public benchmark results.

title: Position: Language model developers should report train-test overlap

abstract: This paper is concerned with differentiable resampling in the context of sequential Monte Carlo (e.g., particle filtering). Drawing on reparametrisation, we propose a new resampling method that is informative and instantly differentiable, based on a training-free diffusion model surrogate. We theoretically prove that our diffusion resampling method provides a consistent resampling distribution, and we show empirically that it outperforms the state-of-the-art differentiable resampling methods on multiple filtering and parameter estimation benchmarks. Finally, we show that it achieves competitive end-to-end performance when used in learning a complex dynamics-decoder model with high-dimensional image observations.

paragraphs: Particle filtering represents uncertainty about a changing system with a collection of candidate states. Resampling is an important part of that process, and making it differentiable allows it to participate in gradient-based learning. This paper introduces a resampling method designed to provide informative derivatives within sequential Monte Carlo.

The method combines reparameterization with a diffusion-model surrogate that requires no training. This makes the resampling operation immediately differentiable without first fitting a separate diffusion model. The authors also prove that its resampling distribution is consistent, providing a theoretical property alongside the proposed mechanism for passing learning signals through resampling.

On multiple filtering and parameter-estimation benchmarks, the method empirically outperforms the state-of-the-art differentiable resampling approaches used in the comparison. It also achieves competitive end-to-end results when learning a complex dynamics-and-decoder model from high-dimensional images. These findings connect the local resampling improvement to a larger learning pipeline: the method can support both state estimation and the training of models whose observations require substantial decoding.
summary.tldr: A training-free diffusion surrogate enables differentiable particle resampling with a consistency proof and strong empirical results.

title: Diffusion Differentiable Resampling

abstract: Graph coarsening is a graph dimensionality reduction technique that aims to construct a smaller and more tractable graph while preserving the essential structural and semantic properties of the original graph. However, most existing methods rely on pair-wise similarity matching, where each node independently searches for its best partner based on global information. This selfishness matching paradigm incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. To address this problem, we shift to a non-selfishness principle that prioritizes the collective interference of neighborhood in coarsening, and propose an efficient method named NOPE, which achieves linear memory consumption and near-linear computational complexity in the number of nodes. Furthermore, we derive a faster variant NOPE, which reduces O($\Delta$\cdotd) interference evaluation to O(d) based on the local isotropy assumption, and consequently alleviates the computational bottleneck for high-degree nodes. Experimental results show that NOPE achieves $1.8–10\times$ speedup over NOPE and surpass almost all baselines with 1-3 orders of magnitude acceleration. Meanwhile, learning on coarsened graphs yields comparable performance to original graphs, and can even show superior performance over LLM-based graph reasoning owing to compact graph information. The code can be available at https://github.com/dazonglian/NOPE-main.

paragraphs: Graph coarsening creates a smaller graph while aiming to preserve important structure and meaning. Many methods match nodes in pairs, with each node searching for its preferred partner using global information. The authors argue that this individually focused matching creates substantial computation and memory costs.

NOPE replaces that approach with a principle that considers collective neighborhood interference during coarsening. It achieves linear memory use and near-linear computation in the number of nodes. A faster variant, NOPE*, assumes local isotropy to simplify interference evaluation from O(Δ·d) to O(d), reducing the bottleneck associated with high-degree nodes.

Learning on the resulting smaller graphs gives performance comparable to learning on the originals. The authors also report that compact graph information can outperform LLM-based graph reasoning. These findings support considering neighborhood effects jointly when seeking efficient graph compression that retains useful information.
summary.tldr: NOPE coarsens graphs efficiently by considering collective neighborhood effects, with a faster variant based on local isotropy.

title: Rethinking Efficient Graph Coarsening via a Non-Selfishness Principle

abstract: Planning collaboration strategies for multi-agent embodied systems remains a core challenge for LLM-based planners, which often fail to capture the physical and coordination constraints of realworld environments. To address this, we present EvoCF, an agentic memory-driven evolutionary counterfactual planning framework for discovering improved multi-agent collaboration strategies through counterfactual plan generation and evaluation. First, we propose a symbolic constraint inductor that induces reusable symbolic constraints from failures, forming an evolving rule library. Then, we propose an evolutionary counterfactual plan generator that systematically explores semantically consistent plan variants through rule-conditioned mutations, enabling robust collaboration strategies beyond short-sighted one-shot LLM plans. Finally, we design an agentic memory-grounded evaluator that ranks candidate plans using retrieval-augmented evidence, producing interpretable, constraint-aware selections. Across multi-agent embodied simulation benchmarks, EvoCF consistently discovers more robust and executable plans compared to baseline approaches. Our results demonstrate that grounding multi-agent planning in agentic memory and counterfactual reasoning significantly enhances both effectiveness and robustness.

paragraphs: EvoCF addresses collaboration planning for embodied agents, where a plausible language-model plan can still fail because it overlooks physical or coordination constraints. The framework searches for improved strategies by generating alternative plans and evaluating them using remembered evidence. This makes previous experience part of both the search process and the final selection.

Its first component extracts reusable symbolic constraints from failures and accumulates them in an evolving rule library. A counterfactual plan generator then creates semantically consistent alternatives through mutations conditioned on those rules. Finally, an evaluator retrieves evidence from agentic memory to rank candidates, producing selections that are interpretable and attentive to constraints.

Across embodied multi-agent simulation benchmarks, EvoCF consistently finds plans that are more robust and executable than baseline approaches. The reported results support combining failure-derived rules, systematic plan variation, and evidence-based evaluation. The contribution lies in connecting these stages: failures inform future candidates, and remembered evidence helps judge which alternatives are likely to work within the simulated environments.
summary.tldr: EvoCF uses failure-derived constraints, alternative plan generation, and memory-based evaluation to improve multi-agent planning in simulations.

title: EvoCF: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Agentic Memory-Driven Evolutionary Counterfactual Planning

abstract: NVIDIA’s 2:4 Sparse Tensor Cores deliver $2\times$ throughput but demand strict 50% pruning—a ratio that causes severe accuracy loss in LLMs. Milder $(2N-2):2N$ patterns (e.g., 6:8, 25% pruning) preserve accuracy far better—within 0.4–1.8 average points of dense in our Qwen2.5-7B/14B study—yet receive NO hardware support and fall back to dense execution. We present SlideSparse, the first system to unlock Sparse Tensor Core acceleration for the $(2N-2):2N$ model family on commodity GPUs. Our Sliding Window Decomposition rewrites any $(2N-2):2N$ weight block into $N-1$ overlapping 2:4-compliant windows without changing the underlying dot product; in addition, our Activation Lifting fuses the corresponding activation rearrangement into per-token quantization at low marginal cost. Integrated into vLLM, SlideSparse is evaluated across various GPUs (A100, H100, B200, RTX 4090, RTX 5080, DGX-spark), precisions (FP4, INT8, FP8, BF16, FP16), and model families (Llama, Qwen, BitNet). On compute-bound workloads, the measured speedup ($1.33\times$) matches the theoretical upper-bound $N/(N-1)=4/3$ at 6:8 weight sparsity in Qwen2.5-7B, establishing $(2N-2):2N$ as a practical path to better accuracy–speedup trade-offs in LLM acceleration. Code available at https://github.com/bcacdwk/vllmbench.

paragraphs: NVIDIA's sparse hardware supports 2:4 weight patterns, requiring half the weights to be removed. That level of pruning can substantially hurt language-model accuracy. Milder patterns such as 6:8 remove only a quarter of the weights, but normally lack direct hardware acceleration. SlideSparse makes this broader sparsity family usable on existing Sparse Tensor Cores.

Its Sliding Window Decomposition rewrites each supported weight block as overlapping 2:4-compatible windows while preserving the underlying dot product. Activation Lifting performs the corresponding activation rearrangement within per-token quantization at low additional cost. The decomposition therefore connects a less aggressive pruning pattern to hardware designed for a stricter one.

In the reported Qwen2.5 study, milder sparsity preserves accuracy within 0.4–1.8 average points of dense models. For compute-bound Qwen2.5-7B workloads at 6:8 sparsity, measured acceleration reaches 1.33 times, matching the stated theoretical bound of 4/3. That result establishes a concrete accuracy–speed trade-off in the evaluated workload regime.
summary.tldr: SlideSparse translates milder pruning patterns into hardware-supported sparse operations, reaching 1.33-fold acceleration in a reported compute-bound setting.

title: SlideSparse: Fast and Flexible (2N-2):2N Structured Sparsity

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a small, high-quality set of long reasoning traces is an effective approach for eliciting strong reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods for curating high-quality SFT data rely heavily on strong reasoning models to filter examples based on diversity and difficulty, making the curation process costly while often yielding suboptimal data quality. In this work, we show that diverse and challenging reasoning examples can be identified using only the initial reasoning tokens. Specifically, we demonstrate that difficult problems can be reliably detected based on the loss of the first 100 reasoning tokens evaluated at a randomly perturbed checkpoint of the pretrained model. We further show that examples exhibiting similar loss patterns over their first 1k reasoning tokens across a small number of perturbed checkpoints extrapolating along the fine-tuning trajectory provably induce similar gradients. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B models on the M23K medical reasoning and OpenThoughts-Math datasets. Our method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while being 91% more token efficient.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning on a small collection of strong reasoning examples can elicit substantial reasoning ability, but selecting those examples can be expensive. This paper investigates how much selection information is already present near the beginning of a reasoning trace. It finds that short prefixes can reveal both difficulty and relationships between examples.

For difficulty, the method evaluates the loss on the first 100 reasoning tokens using a randomly perturbed pretrained checkpoint. For diversity, it compares loss patterns over the first 1,000 tokens across several perturbed checkpoints extrapolated along the fine-tuning trajectory. The authors prove that examples with similar patterns induce similar gradients, connecting this selection signal to how examples affect training.

Experiments fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B on medical and mathematical reasoning datasets. The approach outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while being 91% more token efficient. These findings support using early reasoning signals to curate useful training data with much less token processing, instead of depending heavily on strong reasoning models to evaluate examples.
summary.tldr: Early reasoning-token losses identify difficult and related examples, enabling data curation that improves performance while using substantially fewer tokens.

title: Reasoning Quality Emerges Early: Data Curation for Reasoning Models

abstract: A key challenge in probabilistic regression is ensuring that predictive distributions accurately reflect true empirical uncertainty. Minimizing overall prediction error often encourages models to prioritize informativeness over calibration, producing narrow but overconfident predictions. However, in safety-critical settings, trustworthy uncertainty estimates are often more valuable than narrow intervals. Realizing the problem, several recent works have focused on post-hoc corrections; however, existing methods either rely on weak notions of calibration (such as PIT uniformity) or impose restrictive parametric assumptions on the nature of the error. To address these limitations, we propose a novel nonparametric re-calibration algorithm based on conditional kernel mean embeddings, capable of correcting calibration error without restrictive modeling assumptions. For efficient inference with real-valued targets, we introduce a novel characteristic kernel over distributions that can be evaluated in $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ time for empirical distributions of size $n$. We demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms prior re-calibration approaches across a diverse set of regression benchmarks and model classes.

paragraphs: A regression model can produce precise-looking predictions whose uncertainty is too small. Optimizing overall predictive error may favor informative, narrow distributions without ensuring that those distributions match empirical uncertainty. This paper addresses post-hoc recalibration, where an existing model’s predictive distributions are corrected to better reflect uncertainty.

The authors argue that prior corrections either use weak calibration criteria, such as uniformity of the probability integral transform, or assume a restrictive parametric form for calibration errors. Their algorithm instead uses conditional kernel mean embeddings to perform a nonparametric correction. The goal is to correct calibration error without imposing those restrictive modeling assumptions on its shape.

For real-valued targets, the paper also introduces a characteristic kernel over distributions that can be evaluated in O(n log n) time for empirical distributions containing n samples. This computational contribution supports efficient inference within the recalibration method. Across diverse regression benchmarks and model classes, the authors report consistent improvements over prior recalibration approaches. The findings support correcting the predicted uncertainty itself, alongside the usual concern with prediction accuracy.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric recalibration method uses conditional kernel embeddings to improve predictive uncertainty across regression benchmarks and model classes.

title: Nonparametric Distribution Regression Re-calibration

abstract: Temporal straightening describes how, across layers in autoregressive LLMs, the trajectory traced by the token representations of an input sequence becomes straighter, potentially enabling next-token prediction by linear extrapolation. However, a direct link between this trajectory and token-level behavior has been missing. We provide such a link by relating contextual curvature—a geometric measure of how sharply the representational trajectory bends over recent context—to next-token entropy. Across two models (GPT-2 XL and Pythia-2.8B), contextual curvature is correlated with entropy, and this relationship emerges during training. Perturbation experiments reveal selective dependence: manipulating curvature through trajectory-aligned interventions reliably modulates entropy, while geometrically misaligned perturbations have no effect. Finally, regularizing representations to be straighter during training modestly reduces token-level entropy without degrading validation loss. These results identify trajectory curvature as a task-aligned representational feature that influences behavioral uncertainty in LLMs.

paragraphs: Token representations form a trajectory through a language model's internal space. Earlier observations of temporal straightening suggested that this trajectory becomes straighter across layers, potentially helping next-token prediction through linear extrapolation. This paper connects the geometry of recent context to a behavioral quantity: the entropy of the model's next-token distribution.

Across GPT-2 XL and Pythia-2.8B, contextual curvature correlates with next-token entropy, and the relationship develops during training. The authors then test interventions to distinguish a purely observational association from a feature that can influence behavior. Perturbations aligned with the representational trajectory reliably change entropy, while geometrically misaligned perturbations have no effect in the reported experiments.

The paper also regularizes representations toward straighter trajectories during training. This modestly lowers token-level entropy without worsening validation loss. Together, the results identify curvature as a task-aligned feature that influences predictive uncertainty in the studied models. The selective intervention results matter because the effect depends on how the representation is changed.
summary.tldr: In two language models, contextual representation curvature relates to next-token entropy, and trajectory-aligned interventions can selectively change that uncertainty.

title: Representational Curvature Modulates Behavioral Uncertainty in Large Language Models

abstract: Knowledge distillation is crucial for compressing large Vision–Language Models (VLMs) into efficient architectures. While prior VLM research has primarily focused on reasoning tasks like visual question answering, multimodal embedding learning, a key component for large-scale retrieval, has received comparatively less attention. Existing distillation methods typically align static global representations, overlooking hierarchical feature structure and fine-grained cross-modal interactions. This leads to a structural gap where student models fail to inherit object-level semantics and spatial relationships from teachers. To address this limitation, we propose HieRD, a Hierarchical Representation Distillation framework that preserves hierarchical structure within and across modalities throughout the distillation process by leveraging clustered visual tokens and multi-granular alignment with phrase-level text. Experimental results on multimodal embedding and downstream tasks show that HieRD consistently outperforms strong baselines, reflecting the effectiveness of its fine-grained semantic and spatial modeling, while enabling compact and efficient embedding models.

paragraphs: Vision-language embedding models support retrieval by representing images and text in forms that can be compared. Compressing these models requires transferring useful structure from a larger teacher to a smaller student. The paper argues that matching only global representations can leave students without the teacher’s object-level meaning and spatial relationships.

HieRD addresses this gap with hierarchical distillation within and across the visual and language modalities. It groups visual tokens and aligns information at multiple levels of detail with phrase-level text. This makes the transfer process sensitive to finer semantic and spatial structure, instead of relying only on a single overall representation.

Experiments on multimodal embedding and downstream tasks show consistent improvements over strong baselines. The stated findings support the value of preserving relationships at several levels during compression, while enabling compact and efficient embedding models. For retrieval-oriented modeling, the contribution is a distillation method that explicitly transfers internal organization and cross-modal correspondence alongside the representations used for comparison.
summary.tldr: HieRD improves compact vision-language embeddings by distilling hierarchical visual structure and phrase-level cross-modal relationships.

title: HieRD: Hierarchical Relational Distillation for Vision-Language Embedding Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as scalable evaluators of model responses in lieu of human annotators. However, imperfect sensitivity and specificity of the LLM judges induce bias in naive evaluation scores. We propose a simple plug-in framework that corrects this bias and enables statistically principled uncertainty quantification. Our framework constructs confidence intervals that account for uncertainty from both the test dataset and a human-labeled calibration dataset. Additionally, it uses an adaptive strategy to allocate calibration samples for tighter intervals. Importantly, we characterize parameter regimes defined by the true evaluation score and the LLM judge’s sensitivity and specificity in which our LLM-based evaluation yields more reliable estimates than human-only evaluation. Moreover, we show that our framework remains unbiased under distribution shift between the test and calibration datasets, in contrast to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Using a language model to judge responses makes evaluation scalable, but its mistakes can systematically distort the reported score. This paper proposes a plug-in correction based on the judge’s sensitivity and specificity: how well it recognizes positive cases and rejects negative ones. The framework aims to correct biased scores while also reporting statistically principled uncertainty.

Its confidence intervals account for two sources of uncertainty: the sampled test data and the human-labeled calibration data used to characterize the judge. This matters because a correction estimated from limited human labels is itself uncertain. An adaptive allocation strategy selects how calibration samples are distributed to obtain tighter intervals, making calibration design part of the evaluation procedure.

The authors characterize parameter regimes in which their LLM-based evaluation produces more reliable estimates than human-only evaluation. That advantage depends on the true score and the judge’s sensitivity and specificity. They also show unbiasedness under distribution shift between calibration and test data in their framework. The contribution therefore combines score correction, uncertainty reporting, and conditions for deciding when assisted evaluation is beneficial.
summary.tldr: A calibration framework corrects LLM-judge score bias and accounts for uncertainty in both test and human calibration data.

title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve impressive performance across domains but face significant challenges when deployed on consumer-grade GPUs or personal devices such as laptops, due to high memory consumption and inference costs. Post-training quantization (PTQ) of LLMs offers a promising solution that reduces their memory footprint and decoding latency. In practice, PTQ with uniform quantization representation is favored due to its efficiency and ease of deployment, as uniform quantization is widely supported by mainstream hardware and software libraries. Recent studies on low-bit uniform quantization have led to noticeable improvements in post-quantization model performance; however, they mainly focus on quantization methodologies, while the initialization of quantization parameters remains underexplored and still relies on the conventional Min-Max formula. In this work, we identify the limitations of the Min-Max formula, move beyond its constraints, and propose NeUQI, a method that efficiently determines near-optimal initialization for uniform quantization. Our NeUQI simplifies the joint optimization of the scale and zero-point by deriving the zero-point for a given scale, thereby reducing the problem to a scale-only optimization. Benefiting from the improved quantization parameters, our NeUQI consistently outperforms existing methods in the experiments with the LLaMA and Qwen families on various settings and tasks. Furthermore, when combined with a lightweight distillation strategy, NeUQI even achieves superior performance to PV-tuning, a considerably more resource-intensive method.
